en: The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.

1. The Introduction, Chapter One. At that time, the Bhagavat was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All of them were great arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; who were tamed like great dragons, had laid down their heavy burdens, and were no longer subject to future existence; who had accomplished what was to be done and attained their own true benefit; who dwelt in the knowledge of equality and entered the gate of liberation, having attained mastery and crossed to the other shore beyond all suffering—with the sole exception of the Venerable Ānanda.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had all come from the worlds of the ten directions, each accompanied by a host of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable devaputras from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, whose names were:
Devaputra Nanda, Devaputra Sunanda, Devaputra Candanama, Devaputra Sumana, Devaputra Īśvara, Devaputra Maheśvara, Devaputra Durjaya, and Devaputra Sutejaprabha.
After midnight had passed, this host of devaputras emitted a great radiance that shone directly upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
they all then proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his venerable feet,
and immediately offered celestial tamālapatra incense, celestial agallochum incense, celestial tagara incense, and celestial powdered sandalwood.
Having diligently scattered various kinds of incense, such as ox-head sandalwood incense and others,
over the Buddha three times, they further offered celestial flowers, celestial kovidāra flowers,
mahākovidāra flowers, māndārava flowers, and mahāmāndārava flowers.
Having scattered various kinds of flowers— such as *śubhaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, and *adhimukta* flowers—
upon the Buddha with earnest devotion three times, they again gradually advanced toward the Buddha’s presence,
circumambulated him three times to the right, and with single-minded reverence joined their ten fingers in palms-together salutation.
They prostrated themselves before the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the assembly of devaputras each thought to themselves:

"This bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of All Buddhas was previously proclaimed by past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas amidst assemblies of devas and humans, for the sake of analyzing and benefiting all sentient beings."

Does our World-Honored One not now expound and proclaim such a sublime scripture for this great assembly of devas and humans—Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans?
"Because we desire to benefit all the multitudes of gods and humans in the world, and so that all sentient beings in future ages may likewise receive this benefit.

At that time, the devaputra Nanda, the devaputra Sunanda, the devaputra Candana, the devaputra Sumana, the devaputra Īśvara, the devaputra Maheśvara, the devaputra Durjaya, and the devaputra Su-tejas—this entire assembly of devaputras, having reflected thus, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"Bhagavān! This Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of All Buddhas was previously expounded and proclaimed by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past for the great assemblies of devas and humans—Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas... and even all humans and non-humans—for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings in the world."

I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will now likewise expound such a Vaipulya Dharma-door for this great assembly of devas and humans—the Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as all those who are human and non-human—so that the worlds may obtain abundant benefit, peace, and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with great compassion perfuming his heart and desiring to benefit all sentient beings in the world, silently accepted the request of these sons of the gods.

At that time, the sons of the gods, seeing that the Buddha remained silent, knew that the Holy One had compassionately granted his consent. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then suddenly vanished from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, returning to their celestial palaces.
At that time, after the latter part of the night had passed and as dawn was breaking, the World-Honored One let out a cough like the roar of a great lion king and then smiled.

When the Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—had suddenly emitted such an extraordinary sound, in an instant, all the bhikṣus residing in the vihāra on Vulture Peak Mountain, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, gathered together at the place where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was.

At that time, there were also many other bhikṣus from various aranya dwellings—possessing great supernormal powers and great majestic virtue—who, likewise sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all came together from their respective aranyas and entered Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to assemble at the place where the Tathāgata was.

At that time, all the bhikṣuṇīs of the great city of Rājagṛha, likewise sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, entered Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and assembled at the place where the Tathāgata was.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, surrounded by an entourage of immeasurable hundreds of thousands before and behind him, entered Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and gathered at the place where the Tathāgata was.
At that time, there were also various yakṣa generals, whose names were:

the yakṣa general Aṭavaka, Dweller in the Wilderness; the yakṣa general Ghaṭāpaka, Donkey-shaped; the yakṣa general Kumbhīra, Makara-fish; the yakṣa general Sūciloma, Needle-hair; and the yakṣa general Mālādhārin, Flower-garland-holder. With these yakṣas as their leaders, along with other hosts of yakṣas—possessing great majesty and power—each surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of attendants before and behind, they entered Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and gathered at the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, there were also various asura kings, namely:

the asura king Mahārahu, the asura king Vemacitra of various fearsome forms, the asura king Subāhu, and the asura king Prahārasundara—possessing great majestic power and endowed with great might—who, upon hearing the Buddha’s call of warning, felt a surge of alarm and terror such that the hair on their bodies stood on end. Each, surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of retinues, came to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and assembled at the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, all the great nāga kings and their retinues throughout this trichiliocosm, upon each hearing the sound of the Buddha’s coughing and clearing of his throat, felt a surge of awe and trepidation such that the hair on their bodies stood on end; sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they came to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and gathered at the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada of the great city of Śrāvastī, surrounded by an entourage of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, departed from Śrāvastī for Rājagṛha. He ascended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and gathered at the place where the Buddha was, desiring to pay respectful homage and offerings to the Tathāgata and to hear the True Dharma.
At that time, there were also immeasurable Licchavis in the great city of Vaiśālī, all born into families of great, pure Brahmins. Their names were:
the Licchavi Susīma, the Licchavi Kumārabhūta Vairasena, the Licchavi Puṇyālaṃkāra, the Licchavi Anantahasta, the Licchavi Uddhastahasta, and the son of the householder Dīptahasta.

With these as their leaders, all of whom had long been established in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, each surrounded by hundreds of thousands of immeasurable retinues, they traveled from Vaiśālī to Rājagṛha and entered Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to assemble at the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, there were also immeasurable sons of elders from the great city of Campā who, having already made offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas in the past, had planted various roots of goodness, possessed great majesty and power, and were known by such names as the elder’s son Suvihita, the elder’s son Hitaiṣin, and the brahmin’s son Anantavīrya.

With these as their leaders, along with other immeasurable elders and householders, each surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of attendants, they went from the city of Campā to the city of Rājagṛha and entered Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to assemble at the place where the Buddha was, desiring to pay respect and make offerings to the Tathāgata and to hear the True Dharma.

At that time, there were immeasurable multitudes of diverse people in the city of Vārāṇasī who, having already made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in the past and planted various roots of goodness, had all reached full maturity. From Vārāṇasī they proceeded to the city of Rājagṛha and entered Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, gathering at the place where the Buddha was, desiring to pay respectful homage and make offerings to the Tathāgata and to hear the True Dharma.

At that time, there were also immeasurable Malla youths from the city of Kuśinagara who had likewise made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Because they had long cultivated various roots of goodness, they possessed great majesty and power, and were surrounded by immeasurable retinues. From Kuśinagara, they proceeded to Rājagṛha and entered Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to assemble at the Buddha’s dwelling, also for the sake of reverently making offerings to the Tathāgata and hearing the True Dharma.

At that time, throughout all the worlds in the eastern direction—passing beyond as many worlds as there are sands in immeasurable Ganges Rivers—all the Great Brahma Kings and their retinues of other devas, who possessed great majesty and were endowed with great supernormal powers, heard the sound of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Great Lion King, clearing his throat. They were all greatly startled, and the hair on their bodies stood on end. Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, each surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable thousands of millions of devas, they all departed from their respective abodes and came to this Sahā world, arriving at the great city of Rājagṛha and entering Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to assemble at the place where the Buddha was.

In this same way, in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, there were likewise immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. All the Great Brahma Kings and other celestial hosts therein—possessing great majesty and great supernormal powers—upon hearing the sound of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that Great Lion King’s coughing, were likewise struck with awe and their hair stood on end. Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spirit, each surrounded by retinues of immeasurable tens of millions of celestial beings, they all departed from their respective abodes and came to this Sahā world, to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the great city of Rājagṛha, assembling at the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the ground of Vulture Peak was vast and expansive, equal in length and breadth to this trichiliocosm;
it was filled with a great assembly such that there was not even a space as large as the tip of a staff left empty.

Yet, that great assembly all possessed immeasurable power of great majesty and great supernormal powers; it was completely filled with devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other beings, both human and non-human.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great assembly of devas and humans of the world had all gathered, again let forth such a sound of coughing like that of a great lion king;
having let forth this great sound, he emerged from his vihāra, went to a certain place, and smiled once more.

At that time, when the great assembly of gods, humans, and others in the world beheld this event, each discarded their own garments and various flower garlands, scattering diverse fragrances over the Buddha as an offering of reverence; they gazed upon him with utmost sincerity.

At that time, among the great assembly were the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Rāhula, the Venerable Mahākausthila, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Lokapāla, the Venerable Kṣemaka, the Venerable Nanda, the Venerable Ānanda, and others as their leaders, along with all the other great śrāvakas—all of whom were of great virtue and possessed of great supernormal powers—who had all come and sat together in this assembly.
At that time, within the great assembly, there were also the venerable Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
Vyatīta-trailokya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Vikrānta-gāmin Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
Sadyaḥ-prathama-cittotpāda-dharma-cakra-pravartaka Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Sudhīra Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, and Mahā-svara Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Well-Walking (Sucaritacara),
Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Transcending the Three Times (Trailokyasamatikrānta), Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Sustainer of the World (Lokadhara),
Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, and others as their leaders, along with countless others.
Countless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had all planted roots of goodness under countless Tathāgatas of the past;
having cultivated various practices until their merit was fully perfected, they had long ago attained abiding in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Venerable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, seeing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had smiled once more, rose from his seat, adjusted his appearance and robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"O Supreme, Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, It is not without cause that you manifest a smile.
Peerless throughout all the worlds, I pray that you will explain to me the reason for your smile."
You constantly bestow upon the poor whatever they require, and you also preach the most wondrous treasure of the Mahāyāna;
you can remove the cataracts from those born blind—what is the cause and condition for your smile now?
The World-Honored One has no equal even within the three realms, let alone anyone in the world who could be said to surpass you.
You are the Great Guide of the world; for what reason do you now manifest a smile?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, saying:
“Amoghadarśin! Do you now behold this supreme location, with its surroundings and flanks shaken and adorned with manifold signs, and do you find it delightful?”
Amoghadarśin said:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Bhagavān!”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Aśūnyadarśin! You should know that this place was formerly utilized by various Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, who taught, dwelt, and traveled here."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin proceeded swiftly toward that region;
having arrived there, he immediately entered into samādhi.
While abiding in samādhi, a most excellent and wondrous jewel throne was spontaneously manifested, complete with all manner of various adornments.
Having finished adorning the seat, he returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since this place is now adorned in such a manner, I pray that the World-Honored One will also deign to occupy this excellent site at this opportune time.”
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to that place; having arrived, he ascended the seat in accordance with the Dharma.

Then, as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha ascended this seat, this entire great trichiliocosm shook in six ways—namely: it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere—rising in the east and sinking in the west, rising in the west and sinking in the east, rising in the south and sinking in the north, rising in the north and sinking in the south, rising in the center and sinking at the periphery, and rising at the periphery and sinking in the center.
When this great earth had thus shaken, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, a great radiance pervaded this world, causing all sentient beings to experience happiness;
even down to the sentient beings within the Avīci Great Hell, when their bodies were touched by the light, all their sufferings were extinguished, and they equally experienced happiness.

In this way, all sentient beings suffering within the various hells, as well as the various classes of animals who prey upon one another, and the hungry ghosts in the realm of King Yama—once they encountered this light—all their instruments of torment were completely eliminated, and their hunger and thirst were fully satisfied; there was not a single being who did not experience bliss.

At that time, all sentient beings completely abandoned evil thoughts and gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness; they took delight in one another and each harbored compassion, like close relatives, looking upon each other with joy as they sat together in harmony.
Thereupon, he praised him, saying:
“The World-Honored One, seated upon this throne, Is able to emit great radiance;
The great earth trembles in six ways, Causing all sentient beings to rejoice.”
When the Tathāgata occupies this seat, the Dharma King emits radiance;
know that at such a time, all sentient beings equally receive joy.
When the Perfectly Awakened One occupies this seat, the refuge of great wisdom,
Emitting light to benefit the world, it shines everywhere throughout this buddha-field.
How marvelous!
This Great Vehicle, the most supreme and unsurpassed vehicle—when the Tathāgata occupies this seat, his benefit for beings is inconceivable.
How marvelous!
This Great Vehicle, the most supreme and unsurpassed vehicle, cannot be fathomed by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue until it completely covered this trichiliocosm, and then addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the great assembly of śrāvakas, saying:
"O sons of good family!

"You all should know that after midnight yesterday, suddenly there appeared the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—Nanda, Sunanda, Candana, Sumana, Durjaya, and even Sūtpala—and together with immeasurable other sons of gods who possessed great majesty and were endowed with great supernormal powers, they emitted a brilliant light that shone directly upon Vulture Peak Mountain and came to where I was."
They immediately scattered various kinds of exquisite celestial incenses—namely, celestial powdered sandalwood up to celestial tamāla-leaf incense and so forth—over me.
Furthermore, they made offerings to me with various kinds of celestial flowers, namely the *utpala* flower up to the great *mañjūṣaka* flower and so forth.
They circumambulated me three times to the right, prostrated at my feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having withdrawn and remained there, he further developed a heart of increased reverence toward me and stood silently with his ten fingers joined in *añjali*.
Having so stood, he immediately reflected thus:

"This entire Dharma-gate of the Buddhas' mindfulness of the Buddha was previously proclaimed and explained by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past for those great assemblies of devas and humans, solely desiring to bring peace and happiness to all those sentient beings."

Now our World-Honored One shall likewise expound for this great assembly of devas and humans such a Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, for the sake of bringing peace, happiness, and benefit to all sentient beings.
After those devaputras had thought thus, they immediately requested me to preach this Dharma-gate.
At that time, I remained silent, granting them my consent to speak.
Once the devas knew this, they disappeared from sight.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When the bhikṣu knows that after the middle watch of the night has passed, The Mahārāja of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, Māhendra,
Together with the hosts of devas and his retinue— Nanda and Sunanda— [arrive]."
Sumāgadhā, Candana, and the rest, up to Duṣprasaha and Sūtpala,
universally radiate supreme light throughout the world, shining directly upon this land of Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Once that deva had come to where I was, he made offerings with celestial flowers and incense;
only then did he circumambulate me three times to the right, prostrate in reverence, and stand to one side.
Those devaputras silently gave rise to this thought:
"In the past, the Most Victorious One extensively proclaimed this Sūtra on Mindfulness of the Buddha out of compassion for the sentient beings of the world;
now that our Śākyamuni Buddha is endowed with the ten powers, would he not surely expound this Dharma-gate?"

To benefit all sentient beings in the world and to bring peace and security to all devas and humans, the devas, having reflected thus, offered their request; at that time, I remained silent and then granted my consent.
Therefore, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, I shall speak as the previous Buddhas have expounded.
Knowing that I had granted my consent, the devas gave rise to great joy and a heart of reverence;
they all once again paid their respects with prostrations, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then departed.
"O bhikṣus, you should listen well: I have heard what the Buddhas of the past have taught.
Do not give rise to alarm or doubt regarding this matter; the wisdom of the Tathāgatas is difficult to fathom."
The path traversed by all Buddhas of the past, I have known it entirely and am no longer in doubt;
the awakening attained by all Honored Ones among men in the present, I have already realized;
and the natural Dharma-body of those who will appear in the future, compassionate toward the world, I have awakened to.
I now possess fully perfected, unimpeded wisdom; such great wisdom is difficult to measure.
It transcends the world with no equal, and no sentient being can fathom it.

Chapter Two: The Previous Life of Amoghadarśin, Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and other such great disciples who were endowed with supernormal powers and possessed of great majestic virtue, saying:
"O you bhikṣus!"
According to what you know and within the scope of your own realization, each of you should now roar the lion’s roar before me. Why is this?
If you speak, it will cause all these great assemblies of gods and humans, as well as all the śrāvakas, to attain faith and understanding.

At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Transcender of the Three Realms, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Surpasser of the Inconceivable, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Steadfast Gait, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Turning the Wheel of Dharma upon Initial Resolve, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Skillful Contemplation, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Sound, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sustainer of the World, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, saying:
“Amoghadarśin!
You should now let out a great lion’s roar and resolutely request that he explain the true characteristics of the merits attained by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
If you make this request, you will be able to benefit all sentient beings throughout the world.
"Therefore, I now personally exhort you.
At that time, having heard the holy teaching, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin immediately praised the Buddha in verse before him:
"The World-Honored One’s body of golden hue, adorned with a hundred merits, Is the supreme ultimate truth of compassionate and wondrous awakening."
Your merit and wisdom have never diminished; for what reason do you suddenly urge me to make this request?
You are the Honored One among men, without equal; there is no one in the world whose supreme wisdom surpasses yours.
Having perfected the virtues of a Dharma King, for what reason do you exhort me today to make this request?
The Buddha’s extinction is pure, his dhyāna supreme; his wisdom is profound and subtle, his liberation true.
Since his knowledge and vision of liberation were already perfected long ago, for what reason does he now urge you to inquire?
The Dharma King is fully endowed with majestic deportment; he is the most honored and heroic being in all worlds.
Since he is able to benefit both himself and others, for what reason does the Great Teacher urge me to make this request?
The World-Honored One’s compassion has long been pure and ultimate; throughout vast eons, he has always acted without distinction between enemy and kin.
His unimpeded eloquence is beyond measure; for what reason does the World-Honored One prompt me to make this request?
You who can bestow wealth upon all the destitute, And open the eyes of those born blind in this world;
O Supreme Honored One, you who bring peace to the fearful— For what reason does the World-Honored One urge me to make this request?
The Buddha’s body cannot be defiled by impurities; his robes are inherently free from dust and grime.
Born into the royal lineage of the Sage-King’s family, for what reason do you now offer this exhortation?
The sacred robes remain four finger-widths away from the body, never touching it as they abide;
even the swirling gale of a great wind cannot move them—O Holy Honored One, for what purpose do you exhort us to make this request?
When the World-Honored One usually travels along the road, The hollows and elevations he reaches become naturally level and full;
Or when he passes over high mounds, they immediately become smooth and even. For what reason does he cause me to make this request today?
The World-Honored One’s physical marks are all perfectly complete; his gait and every joint are unshakable.
Having attained the inconceivable state of indestructibility, should he not be the one whom I should request today?
When I observed the World-Honored One turning his gaze back, the great earth shook in six ways;
there is no one with supernormal powers like the Tathāgata, for such is the sovereign among men.
Touched by the radiance of the World-Honored One’s light, even the mad do not lose their minds;
merely by catching a glimpse of the Tathāgata’s light, those who have momentarily lost mindfulness immediately regain it.

When the World-Honored One walks, his feet stir up dust; any sentient being who encounters it finds joy for seven days, and even at the end of their life, they are reborn according to their wishes. Therefore, I take refuge in the one who bestows happiness.
If a person encounters illness and undergoes great suffering, Oppressed by manifold pains and aches beyond endurance,
Should they briefly receive the World-Honored One’s touch with his hand, They immediately attain an inconceivable state of peace and stability.
The World-Honored One’s Dharma-body possesses such power, all attained through cultivation over vast eons;
there is no room for doubt in this matter, so the Teacher need not urge me to make a request.
Supreme among men, possessing manifold powers, the Great Sage who tames and delivers all—
now I address the Teacher of Gods and Men: "Therefore,
you should not urge me to make a request."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You, Amoghadarśin, have eloquently explained this matter."
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it.
Vimaladarśana said, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that you will explain this extensively; I shall now receive it with careful attention.
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:

"I recall that in the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a king named Anantavīrya. He possessed great supernormal powers and was endowed with majestic virtue, ruling and transforming the world through the True Dharma."
The great city where he dwells is named Suvikrānta; that city is vast and expansive, measuring twelve yojanas from east to west and seven and a half yojanas from south to north.

The city has seven tiers; each successive tier of the city is composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, musaragalva, pearl, and coral—all interspersed with these various precious gems.
Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
You should know that the city has four sides, with three gates on each side, and each gate has two towers facing one another.
The pavilions were lofty and expansive, magnificently adorned and complete in their exquisite beauty, all fashioned from wondrous jewels.
At the center of each gate stood the victory banner of Śakra as the threshold; furthermore, all the lintels, doorposts, hinges, and panels were inlaid with every kind of precious gem.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

All the gates of that city were covered above with nets made of both gold and silver. Furthermore, the nets were variously adorned—gold nets with silver bells and silver nets with gold bells—and when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced subtle and wondrous sounds, perfectly harmonious and elegant like celestial music."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāsa!
That city has seven tiers, and within these seven tiers are complete jeweled stairways.

There are railings exquisitely carved and clearly defined, made of the seven treasures in various lovely colors—where there are golden railings, white silver tassels hang; where there are silver railings, pearls are suspended; where there are pearl railings, lapis lazuli tassels hang; and so on, with various colored silks interlaced—suspended among the many jewels, they reflect and illuminate one another."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

That city has sevenfold walls, all of which are surrounded on every side by precious moats—namely, of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and agate—all its various adornments being made of these jewels. Each moat has stairways made of the seven treasures, variegated and brilliantly colored, exquisite and beautiful to behold."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

In the moat waters of that King Vīrya, exquisite flowers were in full bloom—namely, the udumbara, the padma, the kumuda, and the puṇḍarīka. These various flowers possessed lovely radiance, were fresh, pure, and soft, and their fragrance wafted far; they were enjoyed by sentient beings without any restriction or protection."
"Furthermore, Aśūnya-darśin!

On the banks of that King Vīrya’s moat, he planted various kinds of flowers—namely, the *nikaca* flower, the *pāṭala* flower, the *atimuktaka* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *bālasika* flower, the *kubiradhara* flower, and the *dhanukālika* flower. These flowers were fragrant, fresh, and lovely, like celestial blossoms; the people took them for their use without any restriction."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyatādarśin!

That city is surrounded on all sides by seven rows of *tāla* jewel-trees, bright and lovely, composed of the seven precious substances. Among them, the golden trees have leaves, flowers, and fruits of white silver;
the silver trees have leaves, flowers, and fruits of pearls."
The pearl trees have lapis lazuli for their leaves, flowers, and fruits;
the lapis lazuli trees have crystal for their leaves, flowers, and fruits;
the crystal trees have agate for their leaves, flowers, and fruits.
The agate trees have musaragalva for their leaves, flowers, and fruits;
the musaragalva trees have red pearls for their leaves, flowers, and fruits;
the red pearl trees have coral for their leaves, flowers, and fruits.
As for the coral trees, their leaves, flowers, and fruits are made of pure gold.
Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!
The numerous tala trees are lush and magnificent to behold; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce exquisite sounds.
Those who hear it receive joy and delight.
Just as when a person plays music that can produce various subtle and exquisite sounds, there is no one who does not find pleasure upon hearing them;
so too it is with those *tāla* trees, for when the wind touches them, they emit subtle sounds that people delight to hear.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

Within that royal city, there were always such various sounds that never ceased, namely: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of foot-soldiers; the sound of drums, the sound of conchs, the sound of *vīṇās*, the sound of lutes, *sarasvatīs*, *bīṇās*, *kinnarīs*, *tūṇavas*, flutes, *piṅgalas*, and *pāṇavas*. All such various sounds never paused for even a moment."
The king constantly issued a proclamation throughout the realm:
"Whoever has any need—be it food and drink, clothing, elephants and horses, or carriages—I shall provide all that is required according to their wishes."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

Outside that king’s city, in the Tāla grove where travelers pass and rest—whether drinking, eating, lying down, or sitting—they hear the various subtle and wondrous sounds of these precious trees and do not fail to experience the exquisite pleasures of the five desires."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

Within that great city, at a distance of no more than a single arrow-shot from near or far, King Vīrya established a flower pond. Its four banks and its floor were all composed of the four precious substances, and its stairways on the four sides were adorned with the seven treasures—namely, golden stairways adorned with silver, silver stairways adorned with lapis lazuli, lapis lazuli stairways adorned with crystal, crystal stairways adorned with agate, agate stairways adorned with coral, and coral stairways adorned with amber. Interspersed with various jewels, it brought joy to all who beheld it."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

That pond also possesses various kinds of exquisite flowers—namely, the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, and the puṇḍarīka. The fragrance of these many flowers is so rich and pervasive that there are no sentient beings who, upon smelling it, do not feel love and joy."
Upon the banks of the pond, various flowers were further planted—namely, from the *aineya* flower up to the *dhanuṣkāri* flower—all of which were as lovely as celestial blossoms.
The gates of those lotus ponds were always open and never closed; people came and went without any restrictions or prohibitions.
"Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!

Within that great city, King Vīrya established pleasure gardens. Within these gardens, there were various groves of trees made of the seven precious substances, which were always laden with flowers and fruit."
The king, together with his consort, the ladies of the inner palace, and the attendants, dwelt there in harmony, taking delight in joyous pleasures.
There were no restrictions at the gates; the people were free to come and go as they pleased, enjoying sightseeing, play, and shared happiness.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyatādarśin!

Moreover, within that garden, at a distance of one arrow-shot from each side, separate lotus ponds were established, likewise composed of the four jewels such as gold. Furthermore, their steps and stairways were adorned with the seven precious gems; they were radiant with manifold colors, so beautiful that all who saw them delighted in gazing upon them."
Within the waters of that pond were various kinds of flowers—namely, the utpala lotus up to the puṇḍarīka lotus—all of which were fragrant, fresh, and lovely.

"On the banks of the pond there are also many kinds of forest trees and various flowers and fruits—namely, the pāṇi-jaṅka flower, the dhāmārgava, and even the dhanu-kārī flower. These flowers and fruits are fragrant, fresh, and lovely; when the people take them for use, there is no one to forbid or restrict them."
"Furthermore, Aśūnya-darśin!
That King Vīrya was by nature benevolent and compassionate, cherishing all sentient beings with the same affection as a mother loves her child;
he also constantly served śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and elders with a profound heart, just as a son serves his father."
"Furthermore, Aśūnya-darśin! That king was of imposing stature, towering above ordinary men;

his body was perfectly formed and endowed with all the marks of excellence; his countenance was upright and his complexion radiant; his majesty and virtue were vast and universal, such that gods and humans alike loved and revered him."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

That king, having planted the roots of virtue in his past lives, was born into a Kṣatriya family of noble lineage, unsurpassed by anyone in the world. His parents for seven generations had been pure, and his wife, children, and retinue shared in a convergence of blessings and prosperity; not a single person among them ever committed a transgression or wrong."
"Furthermore, Aśūnya-darśin!

By virtue of that king’s meritorious karma, the world was abundant; all manner of the hundred flavors were constantly filling his granaries and kitchens, while silks, brocades, and various treasures overflowed his treasuries."
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Chapter One:
The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Chapter Two: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
The Remainder of the Chapter on the Past Deeds of Amoghadarśin: "Furthermore, Amoghadarśin!

That King Vīryavat, out of loving-kindness and compassion, was one who delighted greatly in practicing *dāna*. He constantly served as an unimpeded donor for great assemblies; to all the śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the sick, and all seekers throughout the world, he gave according to their needs without ever growing weary or tired."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
All eighty-four thousand cities and villages over which that King Vīrya ruled were produced by the superior causes of pure karma and were composed of the seven treasures."

Upon each of the city walls, he further constructed eighty-four thousand sandalwood pavilions, gates, and adjacent watchtowers and rest stations; all were provided with halls and residences, magnificently adorned with various jewels.
The gates have no distinction between day and night; they remain perpetually open and never closed, intended so that all may equally attain great peace.

Furthermore, within all the cities, lanes, alleys, and thoroughfares, lamps and candles are constantly lit with great radiance, causing the people there to each exert their efforts in labor and together enjoy this security and happiness.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, King Vīrya had two sons:

the first was named Siṃha and the second was named Siṃhamati. Their faculties were keen and sharp, their physical marks were perfect, they possessed great majesty and power, and they were endowed with supernatural powers; all had already previously resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Ratnasaṃcaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, World-Honored One. He constantly proclaimed and elucidated the True Dharma for gods, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and even all humans and non-humans; it was good in the beginning, middle, and end, profound in meaning and flavor, excellent in its phrasing, pure and complete without admixture, the pristine holy life."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaskandha was constantly teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings near the city of Suvihita, accompanied by seventy-two billion hundred thousand great śrāvakas—all of whom were arhats, endowed with supernatural powers, and possessed of great majestic virtue."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaskandha, having dressed and taken up his bowl at the hour of eating, was surrounded on all sides by a great assembly of seventy-two billion hundred thousand śrāvakas. With a majestic and serene demeanor, he entered the city of Suvihita to beg for alms in due order."

Just as King Vīryarāja was with his two sons atop a high tower, he gazed afar and beheld the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha, surrounded by a great assembly; he was most exceptionally dignified and sublime, his majestic virtue towering and magnificent.

All who behold this practitioner find joy in seeing them; their faculties are purified, their mental deliberations are serene, and they possess a superior *śamatha* that brings both upper and lower realms under control. Having reached the further shore of the foremost merit, they are fully perfected in all stages (*bhūmi*).

Having seen this, the king was struck with wonder and felt immeasurable joy and courage. He immediately took his two sons and, carrying various flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, and other famous perfumes, they all went out through the palace gate. With great haste, they proceeded to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnasaṃcaya was, to present these offerings to the Buddha and the great assembly. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

That King Vīrya and his two sons then entreated the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha and the great assembly to accept their offerings for as long as they lived—namely, clothing, utensils, food and drink, and medicine—providing everything that was required. Their provisions were abundant and generous, so that the noble assembly attained peace and security."

This King Vīradatta and his two sons had planted roots of virtue in the past and constantly sought the Buddha-dharma; now that they have encountered it and received this invitation, their hearts are filled with joy, and their sense of celebration is especially profound.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnarāśi, having taught the Dharma and transformed sentient beings among gods and humans, and having completed all that was to be done, entered parinirvāṇa without remainder during the middle watch of the night."

"Aśūnyadarśin! When King Vīrya heard that the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa, he immediately, together with his queen and his two sons, personally led his ministers and the common people to the place where the World-Honored One had passed into parinirvāṇa."

Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One; wailing and weeping piteously, beating his breast and crying out, he threw his entire body to the ground like a tree snapped in the wind. Rolling about on the earth, he lamented with grief, saying:
"How swift is the passing into parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One!"
The Great Sage has entered nirvana and abandoned us;
the world is now left blind as the Guide has passed away;
sentient beings are impoverished as the Caravan Leader has reached his end.
“The world is about to fall into darkness; the lamp of wisdom has suddenly been extinguished. “Vimalakīrti!

After King Saṃpradīpta had thus mourned his beloved with the utmost lamentation, he then went with his two sons to the place where the World-Honored One was. They bathed the Holy Body with various scented waters and further anointed the Venerable’s body with all kinds of fragrances. Moreover, they made offerings with the utmost devotion using various extraordinary flower garlands and subtle, wonderful music. Only then did they wrap the body in exquisite Kāśika cloth and fine cotton, place it within a golden coffin and an iron outer casing, and decorate that coffin with an intermingling of the seven precious gems.”

Having thus placed the body of that Buddha within it, they then gathered pure and exquisite red sandalwood—reaching one yojana in height and one krośa in length and breadth, forming a perfect square—and scattered various kinds of flowers and floral garlands upon it. They burned superior unguents, powdered incense, and the like, and poured ghee over it; thereafter, they ignited the fire and cremated the physical body of the Tathāgata Ratnākara.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
At that time, having witnessed the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Prince Siṃha reflected thus:
'The Great Teacher of gods and humans has abandoned me and entered extinction; for what purpose should I continue to exist today?'"
"Now, if I were to attain parinirvāṇa while following the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, would that not be joyful?
"Aśūnyadarśin!..."

Then, having thought thus, the prince anointed his body with various famous incenses, perfumed his garments with various fragrances, wrapped them in fine cotton cloth, and thereafter set a great, fierce fire all around to burn his body.

Once the fire had blazed up intensely, the Lion then, amidst the fierce flames, made a great and solemn vow to save all sentient beings, praising and taking refuge in the merits of the Tathāgata with these verses:
"Most honored and supreme among the treasures of the world, Today you relinquish us and enter into *nirupadhiśeṣa*;
Great Teacher of gods and humans who turns the Wheel of Dharma, From this day forth, we shall no longer behold you."
The Dharma King has benefited immeasurable multitudes, But now he has cast them aside and entered nirvana;
Having roared forth this Great Bodhi, He shall forever no longer be seen surrounded by his assembly.
The inconceivable Great Guide, whose preaching of the Dharma brings joy to all who hear it—now all devas, humans, māras, and brahmās shall forever be deprived of hearing his voice.
He bestows the treasures of the Dharma's wealth upon the poor; for the sake of the multitudes he expounds it, and all delight in hearing it.
The devas, nāgas, ghosts, humans, and non-humans— From this point forth, they shall depart forever with no place of return.
The world from now on will have nothing to rely upon; I mourn my King in particular—on whom can he depend?
Together with Siṃhamati, we have lost our protection; we shall never again hear the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma teachings.
I would rather sacrifice my body and my life than remain alone in this world;
therefore, I now extinguish this cherished body so that, through this, my great vows may be further expanded.
I have planted roots of goodness before the Buddha, and my father, the King, has also constantly honored the Triple Gem;
by virtue of these merits, may both the King and I realize the Dharma-body.
In the presence of inconceivable Buddhas, I have made offerings and practiced all manner of wholesome deeds;
may all sentient beings universally share in this merit, and may my vows likewise never prove false.
When the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa and my body is cremated,
all those who hear of it or behold it in person shall all equally attain perfect enlightenment— not only those who have realized it through their present bodies.
If a person, whether awake or in a dream, should merely behold what I am doing now, they will certainly attain Buddhahood without doubt; it is not one who realizes it in their present body.
This cherished body of mine will ultimately perish; like a bubble on water, it is devoid of solidity.
May the various insects and beasts that devour me all swiftly attain the path to Bodhi.

Now I vow to practice with diligence; whether there be those who revile or slander me, or treat me with contempt, may I swiftly attain the state of a Tamer of Men (the Teacher), rather than merely being one who realizes it within this present body.
When I seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, should anyone look upon me with a heart of compassion, they shall swiftly attain Buddhahood within this world;
it is not merely those who have realized the truth in their present bodies.
If the vows I have now made and those yet to be uttered, for which I burn this body I hold dear,
are truly not in vain, may I once again behold the Buddha who has entered parinirvāṇa.
That I have now briefly beheld the World-Honored One—how is this different from the Teacher of Gods appearing once more in the world?
Though my body is now intensely scorched and withered, I still hope that while it remains alive, I may behold the Buddha.
The World-Honored One’s wisdom is without obstruction; he constantly turns the pure wheel through the three periods of time.
Just as in the past you extensively benefited all sentient beings, May I behold the Buddha arise from the fire;
If the Great Teacher who saves the world should briefly arise, He would be like the Honored One of Universal Vision with his former majestic power.
The Buddha, knowing the lion’s heart was sincere and earnest, rose briefly for his sake to display his supernormal powers;
he extensively manifested miraculous transformations for the world, causing immeasurable multitudes to grow weary of and loathe the body,
ultimately benefiting all sentient beings, before returning once more to cremate himself and enter the state of quiescence.
The great assembly, beholding the Buddha’s magnificent supernatural transformations, praised him with pure minds and sublime voices:
"The wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas is inconceivable; so too are their precepts and meditative concentrations.
Their wisdom and liberation are immeasurable, and their supernormal powers and transformations are likewise unfathomable."
Though already passed into parinirvāṇa, you can purify me; I now take refuge in your blazing body.
The World-Honored One’s majestic virtue is peerless, And his supernormal powers have reached the further shore.
Parinirvāṇa can cause one to feel weary of and detach from [saṃsāra]; I now take refuge in the Universal Eye’s vision.
Supreme and most excellent among all who possess compassion, Able to know the minds of others through one's own mind,
Who thoroughly heals sentient beings throughout boundless realms— I take refuge in the peerless Sugata.
Foremost among all physicians, you constantly bestow sublime medicines upon sentient beings;
able to eliminate the suffering of immeasurable ailments, I take refuge in you, the compassionate savior and protector.
By virtue of the merit gained from praising all roots of goodness, From reverently making offerings to all virtues,
And from relinquishing attachment to this body, I first vow to benefit all sentient beings.
"Aśūnyapratibhāsa!
At that time, the prince Siṃha adorned himself by making this great vow, and subsequently, amidst the increasing flames, he finally relinquished his life."

At that time, all those in the world—gods, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and even all persons and non-persons—having witnessed these events, all conceived a profound sense of weary detachment toward the world.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, after the prince had relinquished his body and life, he was immediately reborn in the Brahma Heaven as a Great Brahmā King, the most honored and most supreme among all the Brahmas, possessing great majestic virtue and endowed with great supernormal powers."
"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, after the prince had been born in the Brahma palace, he reflected to himself:
'From where did I come, having performed what roots of goodness, to be born here and obtain such merit, retribution, and great supernormal powers?'"
Having formed this thought, he then clearly and distinctly perceived and knew:
"In the human world, I was Prince Vīrya; I, together with my father the king, provided all manner of requisites to honor, revere, and praise the World-Honored One Ratnasaṃcaya."

"When the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, I immediately cremated my body within those blazing, fierce flames; having made a great vow and extolled the Buddha’s merits, by virtue of these roots of goodness, I am now born in this Brahma palace."

Nevertheless, I should now return to the human realm to comfort my father and repay the kindness of his birth; furthermore, I must make offerings at the site where the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha entered nirvāṇa and cremated his body.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, having formed this thought, the Great Brahmā King, together with his retinue of devas, vanished from that palace. Just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, he arrived in the human world and went to the place where the body of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnasaṃcaya had been cremated. There, he made offerings with celestial fragrances—namely, celestial powdered sandalwood, celestial gośīrṣa agallochum, tamālapatra, and other such incenses."
Furthermore, he scattered various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers—flowers as large as chariot wheels, like clouds filling the sky—as an offering.
After the Brahma-deva Siṃha had made this offering to the Buddha, he comforted his father, King Saṃpradīpta, saying:
"Great King, you should know that I am the Prince Siṃha who burned his body and lost his life; at that time, I was immediately reborn in the Great Brahma Heaven."
"May Your Majesty not again succumb to grief, sorrow, or distress; rather, you should rejoice and deeply celebrate your own good fortune.
Why is this? For Your Majesty has now attained the foremost of all great benefits."

Why is this so? The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. Yet you, O King, have already met the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; you have honored, revered, fulfilled, and made offerings to him. This is a rare and supreme great benefit.
Therefore, Great King!
From this day forward, you alone should single-mindedly receive and uphold this Dharma; your younger brother Siṃhamati should likewise receive and uphold this Dharma.
Furthermore, you should make offerings to the relics of the World-Honored One, disseminating them everywhere and extensively establishing stupas and temples;
I, too, shall always do likewise in my Brahma palace, upholding this wondrous Dharma and reverently honoring the relics.
Having spoken thus, he suddenly vanished.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, King Vīrya, having heard the voice of Brahmā, immediately went with his son Siṃhamati to the place where the relics of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnasaṃcaya were located. There they paid homage, prostrated, sang hymns, and offered praise; they brought all kinds of incense, all manner of flower garlands, and various musical instruments, as well as various types of banners, streamers, and precious canopies, to present as offerings."

Furthermore, in a short time, throughout those eighty-four thousand cities, he caused eighty-four thousand stupas to arise, made entirely of the seven precious jewels—each one yojana in height and each one krośa in width and length—extraordinary, majestic, radiant, and lovely, wherein the relics were enshrined so that all might offer them worship.

Furthermore, at each and every jeweled stupa, eighty-four thousand lamps were constantly lit; moreover, for each one, all kinds of famous incenses, all kinds of exquisite flowers and floral garlands, all banners and pennants, all precious parasols, and all musical sounds—drums, conchs, horns, shells, bells, chimes, and gongs—were fully provided without exception. Making such offerings, they upheld this Dharma.
“By virtue of these roots of goodness, that King Vīryarāja shall not be born in the evil realms for eighty-four thousand kalpas, and Siṃhamati shall likewise receive the same retribution;
the king’s chief queen, named Sumati, and his senior minister, named Akrodhana, shall also receive supreme retribution for eighty-four thousand kalpas.”

In this manner, throughout successive kalpas, that king made offerings to sixty thousand buddhas; in every birth he was always born as a universal monarch (cakravartin), ruling with the True Dharma and benefiting all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyatādarśin!
Not long after that Buddha Ratnaskandha had passed into parinirvāṇa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Samantaguhya-rāja appeared in the world."

For the sake of the world, he left his home to become a renunciant, demonstrated the practice of asceticism, proceeded to the Bodhi tree, and sat at the site of enlightenment; there, with the wisdom of a single thought, he severed ignorance and the habitual tendencies of afflictions, immediately realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, the Great Brahmā King Siṃha, observing with his divine eye, saw that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantaguptarāja had appeared in the world. He immediately descended again and stayed in mid-air, taking celestial incense and exquisite flowers and scattering them over the Buddha. Then, reaching the ground, he circumambulated him three times to the right, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and entreated the World-Honored One to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma."
Then that Brahma King Siṃha, standing before the Buddha, requested with a verse:
“World-Honored One, you should now expound the wondrous Dharma; we sentient beings are capable of hearing it.”
Wisdom now rises to crush the enemy; none in all the world can destroy it.
The Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Tamer, is fully endowed with the ten titles of the Truly Realized One.
The Great Teacher who benefits the world has now arisen; having spontaneously awakened to the wondrous Bodhi, his merit is perfected and he is supreme among men.
His noble wisdom was cultivated long ago; it did not begin only now.
World-Honored One, please manifest your wondrous voice; this great assembly now delights in hearing and receiving it.
Your great vow was originally for the sake of delivering the world, providing shelter and protection for those who have no refuge.
As your former vows have now been fulfilled, you have already reached the state of tranquil unconditionedness;
now, quickly open the gate of the Deathless, which can destroy the three bonds and deliver one from all afflictions.
When the Brahmā King had finished his petition with full detail, the Tathāgata silently granted his consent.
In an instant, the Buddha Samantagupta caused that Brahmā,
as well as the assembly of immeasurable billions of devas and humans, to experience supreme joy upon hearing the Sugata turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, having received this teaching, that Brahmā deity extensively prepared various offerings to repay his debt of gratitude;
thereupon, he further made a great vow:
"Now, before the World-Honored One Samantaguhya, I declare all the merits I have performed."
By virtue of these roots of goodness, in whatever place I may be born, may I always serve the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions.
Having made offerings to the Buddhas at my former site of enlightenment, I requested them to listen to their compassionate teachings for the benefit of sentient beings;
by reason of this slight merit, wherever I dwell, I vow to constantly sing praises before the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, saying: “Amoghadarśin!

At that time, the Prince Vīradatta, having offered his body as a virtuous root, was reborn in the Brahma palace. There, he successively made offerings to five thousand Buddhas, listened to the True Dharma, increased his roots of goodness, and constantly made vast and inconceivable vows.”
"Amoghadarśin!
You should know this now: was the King Anantavīrya at that time anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
Then the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where are those two sons of that king, Siṃha and Siṃhamati, located now?”
"Are these Buddhas being made offerings to in the present world,
or have they already passed into extinction and reside in other worlds?
The Buddha said:
"Aśvaghoṣa! You should know that the prince Siṃhamati at that time was none other than this present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya;
and the prince Siṃha at that time was you yourself, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa."

Because you made a great vow within the Buddha-dharma of that Tathāgata Ratnaskandha by sacrificing your body once, you have enabled thirty thousand multitudes of devas and humans to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; there is no doubt that they will ultimately realize great enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I contemplate the distant kalpas of the past, When there was a Buddha named Ratnaskandha, the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Self-awakened without a teacher, he appeared in the world, Able to benefit the devas, humans, and all classes of living beings."
Possessing the golden mark of a hundred merits, you manifest the gateway to the true meaning through a heart of compassion;
you reveal the path to enlightenment for all sentient beings and roar forth the teaching that can exhaust the source of all suffering.
Ratnarāśi stands preeminent, the most excellent among men;
accompanied by seventy-two billion sages and worthies—possessing the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations—he follows the Buddha into the city to beg for alms.
Today I am the Victorious King, possessed of boundless diligence and great majesty;
constantly accompanied by my two sons at my left and right, I have come to this high tower for a tour of observation.
From afar I beheld the Great Seer, the Tamer, surrounded by a multitude of bhikṣus;
at that moment, I and my son hurried down and rushed before the peerless, most excellent Honored One.
Having arrived at the presence of the Great Master, the Sugata, he prepared various kinds of exquisite offerings.
Prostrating at the feet of the Honored One, he spoke these words:
"I entreat the Tathāgata and the assembly of monks to accept my lifelong offering of robes, food, and all necessary requisites."
For eighty-four thousand years, these two sons maintained pure faith, seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
Once the Most Honored among Men had entered parinirvāṇa, they erected eighty-four thousand stupas, interspersed with various jewels and radiating wondrous light;
they did so solely for the sake of the remaining physical relics of the Human Jewel.
In each and every city, at the site of every jeweled stupa, He lit countless hundreds of thousands of lamps;
With incense, flowers, music, drums, bells, and chimes, That king offered such worship for the sake of the Buddha.
By planting such supreme roots of goodness, he successively encountered sixty thousand Buddhas;
he made offerings to them all and served them personally, seeking unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
"You, Aśūnyadarśin, do not doubt this further:
the sovereign who once ruled the great earth, that King of Profound Wisdom, was my very self; his name was Anantavīryabala."
Constantly making offerings with flowers and incense, you teach and transform all sentient beings;
lighting countless hundreds of thousands of lamps, you dispel the darkness of the world and create illumination.
Bestowing wealth and treasures never ceases, Listening to the True Dharma is likewise without weariness;
Vigorously practicing asceticism without momentary abandonment, All for the sake of realizing the unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa.
Before the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃcaya, you wrapped your body in cloth and set it ablaze;
like a lamp wick saturated with oil, in an instant the fire reached it and you were consumed by the flames.
At that time, though the fire of your body blazed with fierce flames, your fur remained unmoved and your spirit undaunted;
on the day that Jewel among Men entered parinirvāṇa, you personally acted thus for the sake of the world.
When such fierce fires were thus tormenting and pressing upon him, you still skillfully entreated him:
"May we behold the World-Honored One arise from the fire, and may his great compassion protect the world as he manifests his original form."
Only when my present aspiration is fulfilled shall I be able to relinquish my body and life as I wish;
yet even if I could but behold you for a moment as in the past, the merit thereby obtained would be inconceivable.
May all the vows I have made be fully realized;
If I am destined to attain Buddhahood in the future, I pray that I may behold the World-Honored One amidst the fierce flames.
The Buddha’s wisdom is pure and unobstructed, Equanimous and level throughout the three periods of time;
Illuminating the pure and sincere mind of the Lion, The Buddha manifests from the fire through his utmost sincerity.
Amoghadarśin!

Sustained by the power of this vow, the World-Protectors arise in response to a thought in an instant; because of this, they further make solemn vows of adornment—these inconceivable vows are truly immeasurable.
When the World-Honored One rose from that fire, everyone attained a mind of weary detachment;
with pure minds, they uttered words of praise:
"The Buddha's majesty is rare and difficult to fathom; his boundless marks and signs blaze forth like a great fire."
At that thought, the Dharma King suddenly arose; through the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifesting such supernatural transformations, thousands of beings attained liberation of mind.
"O Aśūnyadarśin, you who know the Lion, Out of great compassion, he has suddenly returned to his seat.
Because they witnessed this miraculous transformation of the World-Honored One, Thousands of beings have resolved to attain Bodhicitta."
Having brought benefit to the world through great compassion, he once again lay prostrate within a fierce fire;
the Lion then relinquished his body and, in a single thought-moment, was reborn in the realm of Mahābrahmā.
He immediately returned from the Brahma palace to the Buddha’s presence, making full offerings to the Honored One among Men;
holding exquisite celestial flowers and incense, he scattered them over the ground where that Buddha’s body had been pulverized.
Not long after that Honored One Ratnarāśi entered parinirvāṇa, there appeared another Teacher of Gods and Humans, Samantaguhya, who arose in the world for the benefit of the world.
Seated beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained the state of the Truly Real; this God among Gods was named the Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha).
Mahābrahmā the Heavenly King prepared an offering, Reverently prostrating before the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings;
He requested that the Wheel of Dharma be turned for the benefit of the world, And the Buddha, knowing his mind was pure, silently granted his consent.
Upon hearing the Dharma, the Brahma King was filled with great joy; his body attained peace and his mind became serene.
He further made extraordinary and great vows, planting inconceivable roots of manifold goodness.
In one kalpa, you encountered five thousand Buddhas, Whom you all served in person and honored with offerings;
The wise should harbor no further doubt: At that time, you were none other than Siṃha.
Amoghadarśin, you were my son at that time; later, you served the Buddha for five thousand years.
I clearly witnessed you burning your own body as you sought this unsurpassed path to Bodhi.
Furthermore, in the presence of immeasurable thousands of Buddhas, when their parinirvāṇa and śarīras were being enshrined,
you likewise burned immeasurable bodies you held dear, undergoing suffering yourself for the sake of the happiness of others.
I know that now and in other worlds, throughout immeasurable thousands of births,
whether a Buddha is present or has entered parinirvāṇa, you have always established this truthful speech.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of past lives, it was only through my supernormal power that I could know you,
Aśūnya! You have long since made this vow, and now its fruit has fully manifested.
Before the Great Teachers, the Buddhas, you have fully perfected inconceivable practices;
constantly singing praises of the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, you have cultivated great vows through the practice of austerities.
Now that I have obtained these verses in praise of the Great Dharma King, it is due to the accumulation of superior causes and conditions in the past;
furthermore, before the Buddha Samantaguhya-rāja, I grasped the most supreme and boundless vows.
You have now indeed obtained such a reward, having been graced by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, who manifested his majestic spiritual power. Then, in the midst of the assembly,
Amoghadarśin respectfully joined his palms and prostrated before the Buddha,
inquiring of the World-Honored One, the Teacher and Tamer of Men, concerning the matters of compassion and benefiting sentient beings:
"Great Sage!
What vow did I previously make, that I am now able to renounce immeasurable births?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will reveal a small portion; having received the holy teaching, I shall be able to understand."
“Emptiness! Regarding your deeds in the past, I shall now describe them to you in brief: In the presence of the Tathāgata Meghasvara, you already made such a vast vow:
‘When all Buddhas realize Bodhi, may I always attend upon and behold them.’”
Furthermore, before the Buddha Universal Eye of the Imperial Banner, he then made this great vow:
"If there should ever be a supreme guide in the world, may I immediately follow this same path."
"In the presence of the Tathāgata Sūryapradīpa, you also gave rise to supreme and wondrous vows of conduct.
You, Aśoṣadṛṣṭi, know this well: you constructed walkways made of various jewels, or established magnificent Buddha-vihāras, or erected extraordinary monasteries for the Saṃgha."
All those [offerings] were composed of the seven subtle treasures, and all requisites were presented to the Buddhas.
To the one honored among inconceivable multitudes, the Lion among Men, the Well-Born Buddha,
they brought seven-jeweled parasols and various implements, making offerings to the World-Transcending One, the God among Gods.
In the presence of that Tathāgata Universal Eye, he then further gave rise to sublime vows and practices,
extensively offering lamps and various provisions as offerings, presenting them to the Teacher of Gods and Humans in the world.
Having passed through immeasurable Buddhas, numbering more than a thousand million billion nayutas,
you have undertaken diligent hardships for yourself to bring peace to sentient beings, and have made those magnificent and vast vows.
I shall now declare the sincere vow you made before the Buddha Samantaguhya-rāja:
"If, through such practice, I am to attain Buddhahood, may the flowers I scatter fill the entire earth."
"In the presence of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound, you made this vow for the sake of the world:
'If there be any sentient beings who hear my name, may they all immediately attain the path of Buddhahood.'"
Furthermore, before the Buddha Śakraketu, he extensively raised offerings and made this vow:
"May all those by whom I am seen or heard, wherever they may be, all attain the path of Buddhahood."
At the time you offered seven precious jewels as a walking path for the Tathāgata Sūryapradīpa, and for the Buddha Amitatejovairocana, you made this vow:
"May I always offer sublime and wondrous adornments to these supreme sites; may my own buddha-field be just like this."
At the place of the Tathāgata Candrottara, you made this vow:
"May I obtain the foremost and most supreme celestial palace, wherein the Buddha, the Honored One, may dwell and travel to transform beings; may all sentient beings who enter it attain Buddhahood."
"When you bathed before the Sugata, you truly made this most sincere vow:
'If, during the intense heat of summer, may the bodies and minds of sentient beings be freed from the affliction of feverish distress.'"
At the time of the Buddha Aṅgīrasa, you also made such a superior vow:
"Throughout the long night of darkness, may I offer the light of lamps to dispel delusion."

If there are any sentient beings who eat my flesh at the place where I have sacrificed my body and life, they will all certainly attain Buddhahood without doubt; it is not merely those who witness it with their present bodies.

Whether in a state of awakening or within a dream, if there are sentient beings who hear my name, they will all attain Buddhahood without doubt; it is not that they must realize it in their present bodies.
When you were practicing with courageous diligence, those who harbored love or hatred toward your deeds shall all become Dharma Kings; it is not those who have attained realization in the present.
In your countless births throughout past eons, you have always aspired to seek awakening;
I now proclaim your true merits—you shall surely attain the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One in the future.
If there are birds, beasts, or any other beings, they will certainly attain Buddhahood without further doubt;
all those who have eaten the flesh of your body shall naturally realize the Dharma-body.
I know that you possess thousands of practices, all for the benefit of sentient beings;
yet if there were those who heard them and might give rise to doubt, I did not speak of them because the time had not yet come.
Whatever matters I have spoken concerning you all, if there are sentient beings who wish and delight to hear them, they shall each certainly attain Buddhahood without doubt;
it is not otherwise for those currently realized through their own bodies.
If anyone wishes to see the World-Honored Savior, who turns this pure and supreme Wheel of Dharma;
having heard it, they shall be able to shatter all suffering and affliction, and thus joyfully listen for the sake of realizing Bodhi.
If a person wishes to see the Buddhas of the three periods of time, And respectfully make offerings to this supreme field of merit,
To fully accumulate all manner of virtues, They must first receive and uphold this samādhi.
For the benefit of the world’s devas and humans, the World-Honored One, having proclaimed these matters,
descended from the Dharma-seat and walked slowly, returning at once to his own chamber to abide in stillness.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, Volume Two;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha,
Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.

Chapter Three: The Chapter on Supernatural Manifestations (Rddhipāda). At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Ānanda, as well as the devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brahmins, all had this thought:

"For what cause and by what condition has our World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having announced the name of this Dharma-gate of the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* amidst this great assembly of devas and humans—for the sake of the Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and those who are human and non-human—arisen from his seat and returned to his original dwelling to sit in silent stillness without yet providing an explanation?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin thought to himself:

"Now this great assembly of devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, as well as all the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others has gathered together, while our World-Honored One remains absorbed in meditative concentration at his original seat. I should now likewise manifest a small measure of supernatural power;
having manifested this power, I shall cause them to praise in various ways the World-Honored One’s meritorious deeds of great compassion."
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin had reflected thus, he immediately entered a samādhi.

By the power of this samādhi, he caused this trichiliocosm to become exquisitely adorned; everything therein was composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, musāragalva, coral, and pearl—and was thus embellished with these various jewels.
The ground is level and even, like the palm of a hand; the entire earth is composed entirely of such jewels.
Many *tāla* trees are interspersed in eightfold avenues, spread throughout the area.

Those various trees were magnificent and lovely: the *tāla* trees of gold had leaves and flowers of white silver; the *tāla* trees of silver had leaves and flowers of lapis lazuli; the *tāla* trees of lapis lazuli had leaves and flowers of crystal; the *tāla* trees of crystal had leaves and flowers of agate; the *tāla* trees of agate had leaves and flowers of musaragalva; the *tāla* trees of musaragalva had leaves and flowers of pearl; and the *tāla* trees of red pearl had leaves and flowers of gold.

In this manner, silk streamers and jeweled canopies were suspended everywhere; golden bells hung down, and precious nets covered all above. Banners and pennants were erected and displayed, all fashioned from various jewels.

Furthermore, with all kinds of exquisite adornments, they surrounded the dwelling place of the World-Honored One on every side. For the most part, these were lovely varieties of flowers—namely, utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers—and such blossoms filled this world entirely.
Thus, it was likewise perfectly adorned, pure, and sublime.

At that time, by the power of his samādhi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin further manifested such magnificent adornments, causing all the great assemblies in this trichiliocosm—including gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all others—to behold the transformation of a great lotus throne made of various jewels.

Each flower possesses immeasurable thousands of petals, pure and supple like the celestial robes of the Kācilindika devas; it enables all sentient beings to see and know one another, so that they may all sit together upon their respective flower-thrones.
