At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin again manifested such great supernormal powers within samādhi, causing the entire great earth of this trichiliocosm to quake in six ways—namely: shaking, shaking everywhere, shaking equally everywhere; surging, surging everywhere, surging equally everywhere; rising, rising everywhere, rising equally everywhere; trembling, trembling everywhere, trembling equally everywhere; roaring, roaring everywhere, roaring equally everywhere; and awakening, awakening everywhere, awakening equally everywhere. These six types each have three degrees, totaling eighteen signs. Thus it continued until the center surged while the edges subsided, and the edges surged while the center subsided.
It was just as when a round copper bowl from the kingdom of Magadha is placed upon a stone; it tilts and rolls about unpredictably, naturally producing sound.
In this same way, throughout this trichiliocosm, sounds are produced naturally without being struck or tapped; such is the nature of the event.
When this thunderous roar resounds, those sentient beings who awaken upon hearing the sound all experience the bliss of supreme and wondrous touch.
Just as the sentient beings in the Akṣobhya world to the east or the Land of Peace and Bliss to the west equally enjoy such happiness,
so too do they find peace upon hearing this sound.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin abided in samādhi, his mind became increasingly pure and free from defilement; it was compliant and supple, far removed from coarseness and wildness, tranquil and unchanging, profoundly moistened, and universally bringing peace and happiness.

Thereafter, he again performed such a supernatural feat that a rain of blazing fire fell throughout the void of this trichiliocosm; yet it did not cause the destruction of the bodies or minds of sentient beings, and those beings who were touched by the fire all attained this subtle and supreme bliss.
Just as a bhikṣu who has entered the fire-samādhi remains serene and blissful, so too do sentient beings touched by the fire feel joy.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, through the power of samādhi, further performed such a great feat of supernatural power that this trichiliocosm rained down fine powdered sandalwood incense; its subtle fragrance pervaded the entire trichiliocosm.
If those sentient beings who hear this fragrance all attain such supreme and preeminent bliss.

It is just as when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, received the prediction of enlightenment before the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara and attained inconceivable, rare, and wondrous bliss;
at that time, the inconceivable bliss that pervaded the bodies and minds of all sentient beings upon hearing the exquisite celestial fragrance was likewise so.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, who was among the assembly, had this thought:
"By what cause and condition has such an inconceivable and rare magnificence suddenly appeared?"
"By whom has this great supernormal manifestation been brought about?
Yet our World-Honored One is currently resting in his chamber in tranquil seclusion; it could not be he.
Could such great supernatural power possibly be produced by any among us, the great assembly of Śrāvakas?"
Is this the work of the many great beings in this assembly, who are like dragons and elephants?

Or could it not be Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Trailokyavijaya Bodhisattva, and even Amoghadarśin and others; or perhaps some other great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, endowed with majestic radiance, who have manifested this event?
At that time, having thought thus, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have heard the Blessed One often say this:"
"Among my disciples, Maudgalyāyana is the foremost in supernormal powers.
Now that this auspicious sign has appeared, could it not be the doing of one of great virtue?
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to Ānanda:
"Virtuous one!
This auspicious omen is extraordinary; it is not something I could have produced."

Why is this? I recall that once, at a certain time, I took this trichiliocosm and placed it entirely within my mouth; yet at that time, not even a single sentient being experienced a thought of alarm or fear, nor did they perceive any sensation of coming or going.
“Ānanda! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, while dwelling in the Brahma palace, I uttered a great sound that pervaded this trichiliocosm. Ānanda!”

I further recalled that in the past, in the presence of the World-Honored One, I let out a lion’s roar, saying: "One could place Mount Sumeru within one's mouth and pass through a kalpa, or less than a kalpa; such is permanence."
“Ānanda! Furthermore, I recall that in the past I went to the world of Gāndharva; there I uttered a sound that reached this entire world, so that all were able to hear and know it. Ānanda!”
Furthermore, I recall that in the past, while my body was dwelling here in this Jambudvīpa realm, I was able to move from afar the Mahā-vijaya Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. "Ānanda!

Furthermore, I recall that in the past I went to where the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda resided; though those nāgas were thus blazing with great venom, I then subdued them and caused them to abide in the precepts and goodness.
I also once humbled the evil Māra Pāpīyān.

“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, I went to the east and dwelt in that third-order thousandfold world system. There was a great city there named Ratnadvāra (Jewel Gate), where there were sixty trillion households. Within each and every one of those sixty trillion households, I manifested the body of myself as Maudgalyāyana, expounding for those sentient beings the teachings on the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self of all phenomena, causing them all to dwell securely in this True Dharma.”
“Ānanda! Although I was able to perform transformations in the past, I have never before seen such a miraculous manifestation as this;
how was it performed? Ānanda!”

Now, as I sit upon this great lotus throne, I behold the infinite and boundless Buddha-lands of the ten directions; those whose name is the same as my World-Honored One, Śākyamuni, have all returned to their respective abodes and sit in silent stillness. I perceive those Buddha-lands just as I perceive this Sahā world.
"Ānanda!
Previously, I too used my divine eye to observe thoroughly the causes and conditions of this transformation, yet in the end I did not know from where it originated.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"As for the four bases of psychic power I have accomplished, who of a similar class could possibly compare with them?
Only the World-Honored One, the Teacher of Gods and Humans; how could the supernatural powers of others ever equal mine?"
I once swallowed this buddha-field, yet the sentient beings of the great earth were unaware of it;
I have also ascended to the palaces of the Brahma-heaven, filling this world with a single voice;
and I have even devoured Mount Sumeru before the World-Honored One, as if for an entire kalpa.
I again sent forth a great sound from the realm of fire, so that it might be heard throughout this buddha-field;
I also shook the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, where he sat amidst a host of celestial maidens;
I also went to the abode of Nanda and subjugated such a great venomous dragon.
I further recall that in the past I performed a miraculous transformation, remaining here while manifesting in the eastern direction;
I caused sixty trillion households to each perceive my body before them.

Ānanda! Regarding the transformations I now behold, I have never before witnessed such great supernormal power; I can only give rise to a heart of profound wonder, for this supernormal power was not wrought by me.
I now dwell upon a great lotus throne, And see sentient beings likewise seated within flowers;
Furthermore, I behold the Buddhas, Kings of Great Majesty, Surveying the entirety of the worlds in the ten directions.
This was surely wrought by the World-Honored One of Sovereign Power, or performed by a Great Being;
such extraordinary and great spiritual transformations have never been seen since antiquity, but are now beheld for the first time.
At that time, when the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had uttered such a lion’s roar, ten thousand devas and humans within that great assembly attained the pure eye regarding all phenomena.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I have personally heard such words from the Buddha:..."
"Among all my śrāvaka great disciples, Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom.
Could it be that this present miraculous transformation is the work of that Great Virtuous One?
Then Śāriputra said to Ānanda: “Ānanda!
This auspicious omen is extraordinary and beyond my reach.”

Why is this? I recall that for twenty years since I began, I have diligently practiced *vipaśyanā*, observing with a single mind to seek the true reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*), yet I was ultimately unable to know their limits.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, I recall that in the past I took a single *kāṣāya* robe and placed it upon the ground. At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana—the foremost among the senior elders—possessed such majestic power (*vibhūti*) that he was unable to pick it up, nor even lift it off the ground; how then could one say he ‘held it aloft with his hands’?”

“Ānanda! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, I stood before the World-Honored One and let out a lion’s roar, as well as before all the great śrāvakas who were endowed with supernormal powers—both those in training and those beyond training—as well as devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and even the entire assembly of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others.”

At that time, the non-Buddhist Pāṭikaputta came to where I was; after contending with me regarding the entry into various meditative absorptions (dhyāna), he further desired to compete with me in concealing his body and vying for the lion’s roar.
At that time, I established the resolve of a man and performed the deeds of a man, thereby accomplishing such inconceivable wonders as these:

Except for the World-Honored One, who possesses all-knowing vision, and Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and those others who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*); except for those Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas who have accomplished the profound *dharmakṣānti*; except for those Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas who have attained the Samudrareṇu-samādhi; except for those Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas who have attained the Susaṃsthita-samādhi; and except for those Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas who have attained the Sarvabuddhapratyakṣa-samādhi—apart from such great Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas, if any other Tathāgatas, World-Honored Ones, or great Śrāvaka disciples were to come and ask me about the matter of concealing my body, or even if non-Buddhists such as Pāṭie-p'o-shê (Pārśva) and others were to further ask me where I abide when my body has vanished.

Ānanda! When I perform such a great supernormal transformation, none of the śrāvakas or even pratyekabuddhas can know where my body is; and when I speak, they hear my voice in the void but ultimately cannot know where my body is.
“Ānanda! I have always practiced the conduct of a great man with diligent effort, and I have likewise accomplished the tasks of one possessed of great wisdom. Ānanda!”
"My mind follows my conduct; it is not that I follow the movement of my mind. "Ānanda!
I now know for myself that my body is seated upon a great lotus throne, and I also see that the entire assembly of devas and humans are all seated upon those same great lotus thrones."

Ānanda! I further see that in all those worlds of the ten directions—immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable—there are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, all sitting beneath Bodhi trees at their sites of enlightenment, having attained equal and perfect awakening. They are fully endowed with immeasurable, boundless power of great majestic virtue, surrounded by the respectful attendance of the great assemblies of devas. The Great Brahmā King requests them to turn the wheel of Dharma, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If he should turn the wheel of Dharma, we shall follow him in accordance. "Ānanda!
I heard this sound; I saw this event."

“Ānanda! It is so, it is so;
just as the Elder Subhūti has just now roared the lion’s roar, you should uphold it in this way.”

At that time, when those gods, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, asuras, and others had seen and heard this, the hair on their bodies stood on end; they conceived a sense of rare wonder and attained what they had never experienced before, saying:
"How truly rare! Indeed, we have never before witnessed such a great event."

If even the disciples of the World-Honored One possess such supreme and wondrous supernatural powers and great majestic might, how much more so the samādhis, supernatural powers, and spheres of realization belonging to the Buddhas—how could they ever be fathomed or described?

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, seeing that the gods, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas of the world had conceived a sense of wonder, spoke these verses to further clarify this meaning:
“I abide in the gates of meditative concentration and liberation; The samādhi of non-contention is my foremost attainment.
In the past, in the presence of the World-Honored One, I manifested boundless supernormal powers.”
I turn the earth of the three thousandfold world system, causing it all to enter within a single pore;
like a potter’s wheel, it turns without end, yet sentient beings remain at ease, unaware of their movement.
In the past, while dwelling before the Tathāgata, I caused the various mountains and the great earth to disperse;
yet those sentient beings suffered no harm, for I dwelt within such a gateway of supernormal power.
With this world and its sentient beings, I place them all within my palm and enter through the crown of my head;
Even when I descend back down, they remain unaware— All of these are my supernatural powers.
I once entered meditative absorption and beheld sixty thousand World-Honored Ones in the eastern direction;
likewise in the south, west, and north, there were no fewer than sixty thousand Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, in the four intermediate directions, as well as above and below, the Buddhas likewise numbered sixty thousand.
With a golden body possessing the marks of equanimity, I scatter celestial incense everywhere.
May all sentient beings come to know and see him, each saying,
"I have a Subhūti who also presides over this realm as the Muni’s honored one, foremost among the śrāvakas in dhyāna."
"I have now uttered this lion’s roar; if those in the assembly have any doubts, they should ask the Buddha.
The Buddha raised his voice and admonished them, saying: "So it is, Ānanda!"
You should uphold this:
"I have extinguished the notion of sentient beings and the notion of a self; even the notion of a Buddha has been eliminated without remainder.
My practice of non-contention and emptiness is peerless; I truly abide in this samādhi."
Chapter Four: Maitreya’s Supernatural Powers, Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya had this thought:

"Now, the World-Honored One’s great assembly of Śrāvaka disciples—possessing great majestic virtue and endowed with supernatural powers—each have individually proclaimed their lion’s roars. Just as I do now, I too should manifest a small portion of a bodhisattva’s supernatural deeds before this great assembly of devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas throughout all the worlds."
At that time, after Maitreya Bodhisattva had reflected thus, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"I recall that once, in the early morning, having dressed and taken my bowl, I went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
'World-Honored One!'"
"I now wish to enter this city of Rājagṛha to seek food in accordance with the Dharma.
Having said this, he immediately set out.
"Ānanda!..."
On that day, I again had this thought:
"Whichever family first offers me food today, I shall first cause that person to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and only thereafter will I accept their food."
"Ānanda! Having reflected thus, I immediately entered the great city to beg for alms in sequence. Arriving at the house of a prominent Brahmin family, I stood silently beneath its gate."
“Ānanda! At that time, the brahmin of great lineage who was giving alms knew that I had come seeking food; seeing me standing there in silence, he immediately addressed me, saying:
‘Welcome, Ajita!’”
"Noble Ānanda! For what reason have you deigned to come here today?
Whatever you may require, please accept my food."
"Ānanda! I then said to that brāhmaṇa: 'Great Brāhmaṇa!'"
"If you can now plant roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, only then shall I accept your offering of food.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
At that time, the brahmin replied to me, saying:

"If you, O virtuous one, can now take this portion of food and offer it universally to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, only then shall I resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and diligently cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva with all my might."
"Why is this? It is because I, too, have previously planted all those roots of goodness under the various Tathāgatas.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
I then spoke again to the brahmin, saying: "Great Brahmin!

If you can now certainly establish this resolve, I shall accept this food and distribute it as offerings to Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; of this there is no doubt."
Then the brahmin spoke to me again, saying:
"Noble Ajita! Simply accept my food and distribute it as offerings to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; I shall then make a vow and act according to that vow."
"Ānanda! I then spoke again to that brahmin, saying: 'Great Brahmin!'"
"If you can now truly make such a vow and act according to that vow, I shall take your food and distribute it as an offering to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Ānanda!
That brahmin entreated me for alms-giving up to three times, and I likewise earnestly urged him to resolve his mind [upon the path]. Ānanda!
Having thus engaged in this reciprocal exchange and mutual agreement with that brahmin, I then said to him:
“Great Brahmin! As you have said, bring the food quickly; I shall distribute it for you to make offerings to as many World-Honored Ones as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
“Ānanda! [the Buddha continued.]
When the brahmin heard my words, he immediately offered me food;
having accepted it, I then, before his very eyes, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, distributed it as an offering to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Ānanda! At that time, after I had distributed that food as an offering to the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I returned to the house of that brahmin."

“Ānanda! At that time, when the brahmin saw such unimpeded supernormal powers of mine, his mind was struck with wonder and amazement, and the hairs on his body all stood on end. Thereafter, he rejoiced immeasurably and leaped for joy; he immediately took various kinds of excellent food and drink and offered them to me, urging me to eat my fill.”
Having accepted it at that time, I ate it to my heart's content.

Only then did that brahmin take all manner of precious jewels, all kinds of incense, all varieties of flowers, all flower garlands, and all exquisite, superior necklaces and ornaments, and follow me to the place where the World-Honored One was. With palms joined in reverence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately before the Buddha gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making this vow:
"May all sentient beings who hear of the roots of goodness from my gift of this morsel of food immediately abide in the stage of non-retrogression."
“World-Honored One!

If this vow of mine shall surely be fulfilled and I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, by virtue of these roots of goodness, may I also, at the time I attain Bodhi in the future, have such immeasurable and boundless assemblies of śrāvakas, all of whom are pure Mahā-arahats, no different from those of the present.”
If this vow of mine is true and not false, by this causal condition, let the entire great earth of this trichiliocosm tremble in six ways.
“When that great brahmin made this vow, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, at that very moment, the entire earth within this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.”
“Ānanda! If there are any among this assembly—whether gods or humans—who have conceived doubts regarding this matter of mine, they should inquire of the World-Honored One when he emerges.”
Ānanda! Even before I had attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I already possessed such great power of majestic virtue and reached the further shore of all supernormal powers.

“Ānanda! I recall that in the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
At that time, before that Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I attained all these bodhisattva *buddhānusmṛti-samādhis*;
having attained these samādhis, all the Buddhas throughout the various directions who were currently preaching the Dharma—those World-Honored Ones—constantly appeared before me.

Furthermore, having attained this gate of samādhi, throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas, I have used these supernormal powers to teach and transform immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them all to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as the great brāhmaṇa in the city of Rājagṛha does now.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, in the presence of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Padmottara, I used a single supernatural power to teach and mature three hundred trillion beings, causing them all to abide in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Ānanda! Furthermore, I once received a samādhi called ‘Universal Radiance’ from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Supreme and Non-retrogressive Conduct.
Having attained this samādhi, I taught and matured sixty-eight thousand devas of the desire realm, causing them all to resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Ānanda! You should know this:
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess inconceivable great supernormal powers that have reached the foremost perfection.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"I once, in the early morning, having adjusted my robes and bowl, Inquired of the Teacher Śākyamuni regarding his teachings on clarity and conduct;
Thereupon, prostrating, I took my leave of the Tathāgata:"
“World-Honored One!
I am now about to seek food.
Thus did the Great Master instruct me.
"Go now, and always keep in mind the benefit of sentient beings; after my parinirvāṇa, you shall become a Buddha, with all various merits fully perfected. Ānanda!
At that time, I thought to myself:
"I do not yet know where I shall go for my morning meal; in whose house shall I first receive food?
I ought to instruct them so that they may abide in Bodhi."
While I was wandering for alms, I encountered someone; I then met a brahmin of great lineage, who with a heart of reverence exclaimed: "Welcome!"
"How rare it is that you have come from afar, Ajita!
I now regret my own tardiness in welcoming you, O Benevolent One. I pray only that you will sit at once and accept my food;
the wondrous Dharma of the Great Being is inconceivable, and I shall offer you exquisite provisions."
I then said to that brahmin:
"If you can first resolve to attain bodhicitta for the benefit of the great assembly of devas and humans, only then will I accept your food."
That brāhmaṇa further challenged me:
"If you, Ajita, can now [offer] this provision of mine to as many Honored Ones as there are sands in the Ganges, then I shall resolve upon bodhicitta."
I then gave my word to that brahmin:
"Be careful not to retreat from Bodhi; by making offerings of you to the Buddhas, I shall ensure that your body ultimately attains the Great Fruit."
Then the brahmin made this further solemn vow:
"I pray that you may offer these to all the Tathāgatas; if the Victorious Buddhas, the Most Honorable Ones, should accept them, I shall practice for enlightenment without any doubt."
That brahmin believed my words; with sincere and utmost devotion, he accepted my food.
I took that offering and presented it to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, enabling the brahmin to behold them in an instant.
Having witnessed my great supernormal powers, they were either struck with awe or filled with joy;

they increased their offerings of exquisite food until they had finished making their offerings to me, and upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, they immediately resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
When the brahmin had thus resolved his mind, he further made vast and inconceivable vows:
"If there be any bodhisattvas who hear this, they shall swiftly attain Buddhahood within this world."
In the past, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I attained this subtle and supreme samādhi;
That bodhisattva named "Mindfulness of All Buddhas" Is able to bestow wondrous bliss beyond measure.
Formerly, in the presence of the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, when I received this supreme Samādhi of Mindfulness, I ascended and beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it was through their majestic power that I was able to see them.
If a person abides in this samādhi, they can manifest boundless miraculous transformations;
all that they have done throughout hundreds of koṭis of kalpas is solely for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Because I attained samādhi in the presence of the Buddha Padmottara,
I manifested supernatural powers to satisfy seventy thousand sentient beings, all of whom, through me, came to abide in the path to bodhi.
Furthermore, before the Most Supreme Tathāgata, I diligently cultivated the pure conduct;
the samādhi I attained was truly sublime, capable of bestowing profound bliss beyond measure.
In the presence of the Buddha Most Supreme Conduct, I received a samādhi named Universal Radiance;
during the time of the Buddha Moonlight, I dwelt in sublime dhyāna; before the Buddha Kāśyapa, I attained profound concentration.
Ānanda! Such great supernormal powers were all achieved in the past; by the sovereign power of these supernormal powers, I have seen all the Tathāgatas whom I have cultivated.
If one wishes to behold all the World-Honored Ones, Wishes to turn the unsurpassed, wondrous Wheel of Dharma,
And wishes to pull sentient beings out from the sea of suffering, That person should study this sublime samādhi.

At that time, when the Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, asuras, and all the world heard the lion’s roar of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, they were all greatly delighted; they conceived a sense of wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Chapter Five: Praising the Buddha’s Sublime Voice and Supreme Eloquence, Part One of the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin beheld the great assembly—consisting of devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others—and experienced what he had never known before. He conceived a sense of wonder and marvel; at times he was struck with awe and fear, such that the hairs on his body all stood on end.
Seeing this matter, he became single-mindedly composed; having arisen from samādhi, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Virtuous One!
Excellent, most excellent!"
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are most rare, most rare indeed. Why is this?
Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess great loving-kindness and great compassion, and are endowed with immeasurable virtues and merits.

“Ānanda! When all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas realize such Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do so because they awaken to the fact that all dharmas are without arising, they see that all dharmas are without activity, and they know that all dharmas are ungraspable. Thereafter, in the Deer Park at the Abode of the Ancient Sages in the city of Vārāṇasī, they turn the unsurpassed, wondrous Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects. Yet this Wheel of Dharma has never before been seen in any world—whether among Brahmās, Māras, devas, humans, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—as being able to be turned in accordance with the Dharma by anyone else.”
"What is meant by the 'three turnings of the wheel of Dharma,' and why is it further called the 'twelve aspects'?
They are as follows:"

"This is suffering, this is its origin, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering"; furthermore, "this suffering has been fully known, this origin has been abandoned, this cessation has been realized, and this path has been cultivated"—these constitute the three turnings. These three turnings are thus designated as the twelve aspects.

"Furthermore, this constitutes the eightfold noble path; herein there are immeasurable words, immeasurable phrases and names, immeasurable sounds and voices, immeasurable meanings and intentions, and immeasurable explanations. Nevertheless, these meanings are taught for the sake of revelation, for the sake of discussion, for the sake of analysis, for the sake of manifesting profound meaning, for the sake of easy understanding, and for the sake of completeness."
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
For this reason, I say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are most rare; the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess great compassion and are fully endowed with merit.”

Once the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they subsequently teach for the sake of the assembly of voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*) by means of teaching within the dharma that is without teaching, by means of speech within the dharma that is without speech, by means of signs within the dharma that is without signs, and by instructing them to realize that dharma within the state of non-realization.

Although there are no words to be spoken and no characteristics to be apprehended, all the wise have already awakened to it, all the virtuous and noble persons have likewise attained realization of it, and all the Arhats have attained liberation from that beginningless cycle of birth and death.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is as if there were someone who, holding a single bundle of grass, said:
'I wish to dam the great current of the Ganges River. "
"What do you think?
Would such a person be acting appropriately?
Ānanda replied:
"No, Great Being! Why is this so?
"What that person has done did not originally exist in the world;
why discuss whether it should have been so or not? Ānanda, Puṇyaprasava said: "It is so, Ānanda!"

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of his śrāvakas, further proclaims with words that which is beyond words, and explains through names and signs that which is devoid of names and signs; such is the nature of this matter.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Suppose there were a person who originally had no mouth or tongue, yet wished to produce a single sound that would be heard and known throughout all worlds.
What do you think?"
"Is the deed performed by that person appropriate? Ānanda replied, "No."
"O Mahāsattva! Why is this?
That which is created by such a person does not fundamentally exist in the world; how then can one discuss whether it is so or not?"
Amoghadarśin said: “It is so, Ānanda!

For the sake of the śrāvakas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise employs speech to proclaim within that which is beyond speech, and uses names and signs to explain that which is without names and signs.”
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Suppose there were a person who, holding a colored brush in hand, attempted to paint or write characters upon empty space.
What do you think?"
"Can what that person has done be accomplished? Ānanda replied, "No."
"O Mahāsattva!
Since that person's actions do not even exist in the world, why ask whether they are accomplished or not?
Akṣayamati replied:

"In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of his śrāvakas, proclaims within the ineffable Dharma by means of further words, and explains the nameless and signless Dharma by means of names and signs; such is the nature of this matter."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like a person who, lacking hands, feet, incantations, or skills, yet loudly proclaims:
'I am able to carry the King of Mountains, Sumeru.'"
"What do you think?
Can that person’s undertaking be accomplished?
Ānanda replied:
"No, Great Being!
Since that which this person has done does not exist in the world, how can one ask whether it is so or not?"
Amoghadarśin said: "It is so, Ānanda!

For the sake of the śrāvakas, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims within the wordless Dharma by means of words, and explains the nameless and signless Dharma by means of names and signs; the meaning is likewise."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

It is as if there were someone who, having reached the shore of the great ocean, might take up a single plank, or hold a small raft, or intend to wade across, or intend to swim across, employing various skillful means and saying these words:
'I shall cross the great ocean and ascend to the other shore.'"
"What do you think?
Is the action of that person appropriate?
Ānanda replied:
"No, Great Being! Such a thing has never existed in all the worlds; how can one say 'yes' or 'no'?"
Amoghadarśin said: "So it is, Ānanda!

For the sake of the śrāvakas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, within that which is beyond verbal expression, further proclaims by means of words; and regarding dharmas that are without names or characteristics, he explains them by means of names and characteristics. Such is their meaning."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The great compassion of all Buddhas is inconceivable; With the light of their pity, they constantly illumine all things.
Throughout immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, The Perfectly Awakened Ones have realized such a profound Dharma-gate."
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena has no place of birth; Through the gathering of causes and conditions, they come and go in emptiness.
Though the Unsurpassed Teacher skillfully proclaims this, Their self-nature is eternally quiescent.
The True Dharma of all Buddhas is difficult to measure; out of loving-kindness, the World-Honored One has proclaimed it.
Being able to reveal such a Dharma difficult to see, he benefits all devas and humans in the world.

The ineffable Dharma is difficult to encounter and hear; the Hero of Ten Powers is able to expound it extensively, revealing the supreme path of cool tranquility and bringing peace and security to the multitudes of gods and humans in the world.
The World-Honored One skillfully expounds the dharma of signlessness; Without a teacher, he naturally attained awakening.
He destroys all heterodox paths, Yet the ignorant and foolish do not know this reality-limit.
The ocean of the Buddhas' wisdom is difficult to fathom; they proclaim the Dharma-realm without end.
All śrāvakas have likewise realized it; they reveal its inconceivable transformations.
"Just as a person might take grass and stuff it into the Ganges, O Venerable One—
I consider that not difficult;
but for the Fully Awakened One to turn that wheel of non-arising, I hold this matter to be more difficult than that."
If someone were to take a five-colored brush in hand and paint all manner of variegated colors upon empty space;
and were to place words within that which is beyond speech—I hold this task to be more difficult than that.
If a person has neither hands nor feet, yet seeks to carry Mount Sumeru across the great ocean;
to turn the wheel of Dharma within the signless reality—this, I say, is more difficult than that.
If a person were without a tongue and without a mouth, yet could utter a single word that pervades worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and could cause realization within the dharma of non-realization— I say that this matter is more difficult than that.
At that time, the Venerable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable One!

The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are truly rare and marvelous; throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they have awakened to and thoroughly mastered all dharmas, reaching the ultimate further shore, and are thus titled Buddhas, World-Honored Ones."

Nevertheless, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, in accordance with the differences in the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions of sentient beings, naturally emit a subtle and perfect voice that universally proclaims various gateways of phrases. That is to say:
if there are sentient beings who delight in practicing generosity, the Tathāgata then praises and explains the dānapāramitā (perfection of giving), and they likewise think:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma of giving for me."
When there are sentient beings who delight in cultivating the prohibitive precepts, the Tathāgata then praises and explains the *śīlapāramitā* for them, and they further give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma of the precepts for me."
At times, when sentient beings delight in practicing patience, the Tathāgata then praises and expounds the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience), and they too give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma of patience for my sake."
At times, when sentient beings delight in practicing diligence, the Tathāgata then praises and expounds the *vīryapāramitā*, and they also give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One proclaims diligence."

If at times sentient beings delight in practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the Tathāgata then praises and expounds the *dhyānapāramitā* for them, and they likewise give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma of meditation for my sake."
At times, when sentient beings delight in seeking wisdom, the Tathāgata then praises and expounds the Prajñāpāramitā for them, and they too give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One is proclaiming wisdom for my sake."
At times, when sentient beings delight in seeking liberation, the Tathāgata then praises and expounds upon liberation for them; they, too, give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed liberation for my sake."

At times, when sentient beings delight in cultivating the knowledge and vision of liberation, the Tathāgata then praises and explains the knowledge and vision of liberation to them, and they also give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One proclaims the knowledge and vision of liberation for my sake."
If at times there are sentient beings who delight in being born in the heavens, the Tathāgata then praises and speaks of birth in the heavens for them, and they too form this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed for me the way to be born in the heavens."

If there are sentient beings who delight in cultivating the contemplation of impermanence, the Tathāgata then praises and expounds upon impermanence for them, and they likewise give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the teaching of impermanence for my sake."
If there are sentient beings who delight in practicing asceticism, the Tathāgata then praises and explains various sufferings to them, and they also form this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma of suffering for my sake."
There are sentient beings who delight in cultivating non-self; for them, the Tathāgata praises and explains non-self, and they also form this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma of non-self for me."
If there are sentient beings who delight in cultivating emptiness and stillness, the Tathāgata then praises and expounds the Dharma of emptiness for them, and they also give rise to this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the Dharma of emptiness for me."
If there are sentient beings who delight in cultivating the meditation on impurity, the Tathāgata then praises and explains impurity for them, and they too form this thought:
"The World-Honored One has proclaimed the teaching of impurity for me."
There are sentient beings who desire to be reborn in heaven; for them, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for rebirth in heaven, and they also form this thought:
"The World-Honored One has taught me the Dharma for rebirth in heaven."
"Venerable One!
Even unto those sentient beings who delight in various teachings, the Tathāgata teaches them various teachings, and they too form this thought:
'The World-Honored One has taught various teachings for my sake.'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the perfect voice, Which issues spontaneously according to the various classes of sentient beings.
Whatever their inclinations and whatever they wish to hear, The Tathāgata accords with them and brings it forth.”
If there are sentient beings who delight in giving, the Tathāgata then praises the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā);
if there are sentient beings who delight in observing the precepts, the Tathāgata further praises ethical discipline (śīla);
if there are sentient beings who delight in patience, the Tathāgata then praises forbearance (kṣānti).
If there are sentient beings who delight in diligence, the Tathāgata praises *vīrya* for them;
If there are sentient beings who delight in samādhi, the Tathāgata then praises meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) for them;
If those sentient beings delight in wisdom, the Tathāgata then praises *prajñā* for them.
If those sentient beings delight in liberation, the Tathāgata likewise praises liberation for them;
if those sentient beings cultivate impermanence, he causes them to hear that Dharma of impermanence;
if they delight in hearing about suffering and impurity, he likewise causes them to hear the sounds of suffering and impurity.
If they delight in hearing of emptiness and selflessness, the Teacher of the World praises emptiness and stillness with inconceivable sounds;
if they delight in hearing of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, the Master of the World speaks of the Pratyekabuddhas with wondrous tones;
or if they delight in hearing of the Buddha Vehicle, the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings praises the path to Bodhi.
Even those who have been born in celestial palaces, within their sounds likewise manifest the matter of being born in heaven.
Such wondrous sounds are inconceivable; they appear in accordance with the karmic responses of various classes of beings.
Once they have heard this pure sound, who would not proceed upon the path to Bodhi?
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are extraordinary and rare; the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to possess such blazing roots of goodness.”

Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, from long ago, have been able to make offerings to immeasurable, boundless Tathāgatas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges; furthermore, they have constantly practiced giving, patience, and diligence—namely, relinquishing their bodies, lives, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains—and performed various ascetic practices that are difficult to perform, thereby subduing body and mind, only then to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having realized awakening, one is then able to fully possess immeasurable eloquence to teach the Dharma to others.
What is eloquence? It refers to inconceivable eloquence, unsurpassed eloquence, unexcelled eloquence, and non-attachment.
eloquence; eloquence of wondrous liberation; unobstructed eloquence; eloquence of skillful synthesis;
corresponding eloquence; blazing eloquence; eloquence that requires no questioning;
anticipatory eloquence; eloquence of manifesting signs; eloquence of signlessness; eloquence of profound silence; [and] non-...
the eloquence that is free from timidity; the eloquence that removes anger; the eloquence adorned with various kinds of phonemes;
the eloquence adorned with various kinds of phrases; the eloquence adorned with meanings and phrases; the eloquence adorned with profound phrases; the eloquence that manifests profound meanings;
the eloquence that reveals the profound as shallow and easy to understand; and the absence of...
The eloquence of boundless analogies, the eloquence of swift agility, the eloquence of skillfully resolving doubts, the eloquence of achieving the limitless, the eloquence of inquiry,
the eloquence of answering extensively for brief questions, the eloquence of benefiting others, the eloquence of being irreproachable,
the eloquence of skillful deliberation, the eloquence of being free from impediment, and the eloquence of being without shame.
He possesses the eloquence of being free from humiliation; he is fully accomplished in the eloquence that is free from slander;
he is fully accomplished in the eloquence praised by the wise; he is fully accomplished in the eloquence of a fearless mind; he is fully accomplished in the eloquence that is not narrow or inferior;
he is fully accomplished in the eloquence of unerring phrasing; he is fully accomplished in the eloquence of non-forgetfulness; and he is fully accomplished in the absence of error.

The eloquence of being fully endowed with the power to preach the Dharma according to the inclinations of others; the eloquence of being fully endowed with the knowledge of others' sincere intentions to preach for them;

the eloquence of being fully endowed with the ability to reveal and develop teachings free from defilement; the eloquence of being fully endowed with the ability to preach through the adornment of sounds and phrases;
the eloquence of being fully endowed with the ability to preach concerning the past; and the eloquence of being fully endowed with the ability to preach concerning the future.
He possesses eloquence capable of explaining the present; he possesses noble eloquence;
he possesses the sublime knowledge of the realization of non-arising; and he possesses eloquence capable of bringing joy to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin reiterated this meaning and spoke in verse:
"Making offerings to the Most Victorious Honored One, In numbers beyond measure and boundless,
One can realize the Unsurpassed Way, The Great Teacher of the World."
Having extensively gathered all roots of goodness, you have attained that inconceivable eloquence—
unhindered, unimpeded, immeasurable, and boundless.
You who harmonize the meaning of liberation, O Honored One, Supreme and Unsurpassed Person.
He skillfully expounds the severing of the net of doubt, able to resolve every inquiry.
With various profound and esoteric teachings, as well as numerous parables, he possesses fully adorned eloquence; his wondrous voice is immeasurable.
Pure and in perfect accord, they dwell securely in the definitive Dharma;
inconceivable and indestructible, they possess no heart of fear.
With wondrous voice and wisdom concurrent, they are neither startled nor harmed.
With verses of unerring adornment, one dwells in peace and bliss without forgetfulness.
Unconfused regarding the various directions, free from dregs, one brings the mind to purity;
with respect to the past, the future, and the present, there is no obstruction.
The turning of the wheel is equal for both ordinary beings and sages; eloquence does not arise from elsewhere.
Heard simultaneously by those near and far, the Buddha’s voice issues forth as he speaks.
The volume of the ocean water may be measured, and the drops on a hair-tip may be counted, but the Buddha’s voice cannot be fathomed.
The great renown of all Buddhas and their eloquence are difficult to reach the limit of;
The limits of space may be exhausted, and Mount Sumeru may be easily weighed,
But the unsurpassed Teacher of gods and humans— his eloquence is profound and unfathomable.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Four: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Five: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
From the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha’s Sublime Voice and Supreme Eloquence," Part Two. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Ānanda!..."

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the voice of Great Brahmā; they possess the voice of the Great Lion; they possess the voice of the Great Hero, clear and resonant; they possess the voice of the Great Dragon King; they possess the voice of the Great Wondrous Drum; they possess the voice of the Great Wondrous Song; they possess the excellent and beautiful voice; they possess the voice of the Great Wind; they possess the voice of the Great Cloud; they possess the voice of the Great Thunder, and so forth.

“Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the voice of great goodness, the inconceivable voice, the immeasurable voice, the boundless voice, the incalculable voice, the perfect voice, the unimpeded voice, and the voice of the kalaviṅka bird.”

“Ānanda! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess voices that are perfect; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are realizable; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are knowable; the Tathāgatas possess voices of profound wisdom; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are indestructible and pure; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are stainless; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are beyond reproach; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are not hoarse or broken; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are exquisite; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are supremely exquisite; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are flawless; the Tathāgatas possess voices that are free from timidity; and the Tathāgatas possess voices endowed with all virtues.”

“Ānanda! When the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas emit their voices, if they wish for a single sound to pervade one Buddha-world, it can pervade it; if they wish to pervade two Buddha-worlds, or three, or four, or five, or ten, even up to hundreds of thousands of worlds, or even up to billions of nayutas, or even up to immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, and incalculable worlds, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, likewise emits such immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, incalculable, and inconceivable distinct sounds, which completely fill all those worlds, causing all sentient beings who hear the voice of the Tathāgata to think thus:”
"Now the World-Honored One has turned such a wheel of Dharma for me alone."
“Ānanda! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess such inconceivable voices as these. Ānanda!”
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess such a voice and such benefits.
"Venerable Ānanda!
It is, for example, as the orb of the sun provides great benefit to all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa who possess eyes."
What is its benefit?
It is that its radiance illuminates all things.
Thus it is, Ānanda!

Wherever the pure wheel of sound of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas reaches, it is able to preach the Dharma according to the needs of all sentient beings who possess the faculty of faith, thereby bringing about great benefit; its significance is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like the fifteenth night of the autumn month, when the lunar disc is pure and full; those people of Jambudvīpa who behold it are filled with joy."
In this way, Ānanda!

The perfected wheel of sound of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas can serve as the light for the sounds of all dharmas; those who hear it rejoice and obtain great benefit, and its meaning is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

It is like the great ocean, whose waters are of a single uniform taste, eternally abiding in profound stillness, difficult to enter and difficult to cross; yet within it there are many various rare treasures, which are able to provide great benefit to all sentient beings—whether humans or non-humans."
Thus it is, Ānanda!

The perfect voices of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are equal, of a single flavor, and profoundly serene; they are difficult to enter and difficult to fathom, yet they are subtle and wondrous, capable of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings—their meaning is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

It is like the great earth, which supports all mountains and forests, rivers and seas, royal capitals, great cities, and human settlements; it can also cause various kinds of crops, roots, stalks, flowers, and fruits to grow, thereby benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings."
In this way, Ānanda!

The universal wheel of sound of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas sustains all things so that they may not be destroyed; furthermore, it can cause the roots of goodness and the flowers and fruits of merit of sentient beings to grow, thereby benefiting the world—the meaning is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like space, which accommodates all things and enables sentient beings to perform various activities, travel, and dwell, thereby providing great benefit.
In this way, Ānanda!

The vast wheel of sound of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas pervades everything; it enables sentient beings to accomplish much and ensures that their enjoyment, coming, and going are without exception beneficial—their significance is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like the Pārijātaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; when its flowers bloom, they cause all the Trāyastriṃśa gods to give rise to joy and experience much pleasant happiness."
In this way, Ānanda!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas manifest the wheel of sound, able to open the gate of ambrosia for all, causing all sentient beings to equally realize eternal bliss; the meaning is likewise so.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One possesses the truly virtuous voice of Great Brahmā, the wondrous lion’s roar, and the bellow of a bull-king;
his supreme dragon’s cry fills the world, a vessel of majestic and resonant manly sound.”
The vast and majestic sounds of clouds, thunder, and wind— Inconceivable and all immeasurable—they circulate through the boundless realms of the ten directions;
Reaching everywhere without obstruction, they are heard by all.
The voice of the Tathāgata is perfectly complete; nothing in the world can obstruct its sound.
It is like the call of the kalaviṅka bird—what is heard is pure, elegant, and most subtle.
The Sage does not hope for recompense but brings joy to sentient beings; he teaches that one may realize this most supreme sound.
This profound verse of liberation is peerless, and nothing in the world can destroy it.
Unbroken and flawless, with a subtle and wondrous sound, Issuing forth in continuous, uninterrupted harmony,
Protecting the world without end, Possessing the voice of all perfected virtues.
The voice of the Subduer of Men is as he wishes; its sound pervades the three realms.
All those sentient beings feel joy in their hearts, each saying, "He proclaims this wondrous voice for me."
If one wishes for the sound to fill a single world-system, or two, three, four, or five;
or ten, twenty, up to fifty; or hundreds, thousands, millions, and billions, exceeding even those numbers;
or if it should exceed the sands of the Ganges—[the Bodhisattva] is able to fill all such lands.
Causing those sentient beings to have no divergent thoughts, they all form this thought: "It is only for me.
Just as when the solar disc appears, it can act as the guiding light for Jambudvīpa;
Thus the World-Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Humans, With the light of the Dharma’s sound illuminates the world.
Like the autumn moon amidst the host of stars, Its orb is full, uniquely bright and pure;
He brings great benefit to Jambudvīpa, And all sentient beings who behold him rejoice.
The World-Honored One’s voice is like this full moon, Inconceivable, pure, and supreme in the world;
Those who hear it never tire of it, Bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
Just as the waters of the great ocean are serene, Profound, vast, boundless, and difficult to fathom its bottom,
From within which various extraordinary jewels constantly emerge, Bringing benefit to all the worlds;
So too are these Buddhas of great renown, Whose voices are deep and far-reaching, likewise difficult to exhaust.
Constantly teaching and realizing that pure sound, it bestows indestructible universal bliss.
Just as the great earths throughout these three thousandfold worlds can support all diverse classes of sentient beings,
so too does the voice of the Buddhas universally sustain all, bringing about every benefit for the multitude.
Just as space can contain all things, And birds and all living beings find benefit therein;
So too does the Honored One with Perfect Feet widely receive sounds, Constantly benefiting sentient beings with supreme goodness.
Just as the *Citraratha* tree of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven brings joy to those gods when its flowers bloom,
so too do the nectar-like voices of all Buddhas bring ultimate benefit to sentient beings.
Venerable Sir, were I to praise his voice for a full eon, or even for a hundred eons, I could never reach its limit throughout every lifetime; such is the inconceivable voice of the Buddha.

Even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were each to sing praises at will with their voices for all eternity, they could never produce even a small fraction [of its excellence]; such is the inconceivable nature of the Buddha’s voice.
Even if all sentient beings, whether moving or staying, were at once to become Buddhas, the teachings spoken by those Buddhas would never be exhausted;
such is the inconceivable nature of the Buddha’s voice.
The World-Honored One possesses such wondrous voices, Fully adorned and peerless;
if anyone can give rise to a joyful heart, They shall never have fear of the evil realms.
The Buddha’s voice is thus inconceivable, Supremely subtle and beyond compare;
If there are bodhisattvas who attain this joy, Before long they shall become Kings of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the Four Great Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Suyāma the King of Devas,
Tuṣita the King of Devas, Nirmāṇarati the King of Devas, Paranirmita-vaśavartin the King of Devas, the Prince Mañjuśrī— the son of Māra—
and Mahābrahmā the Lord of the Sahā World, up to the Śuddhāvāsa [Devas], [all came].
The Celestial King, along with all other deities of great majesty and power, as well as immeasurable sons of the gods within the realms of desire and form,
having heard the sound of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin praising the meritorious qualities of the World-Honored One,
all conceived a heart of reverence toward Amoghadarśin and rejoiced.
Overjoyed and unable to contain themselves, they all scattered and suspended upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin divine,
exquisite sandalwood powder, celestial flowers and garlands, celestial fine garments, jeweled parasols, banners,
and pennants of various colors and ornate embroidery.

At that time, among the assembly were sixty trillion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devas from the realms of desire and form; hearing the description of the Tathāgata’s merits of voice, they resolved to attain it and gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, planting various roots of goodness.
Furthermore, there were five thousand bhikṣus who donned the armor of diligence and planted various roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Additionally, seven hundred million bhikṣuṇīs gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made great vows of resolve.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of upāsakas who each rose from their precious lotus seats and went directly to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin was;

additionally, two billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of women each untied the various jewels and necklaces from their own bodies and scattered them into the air, remaining suspended above the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, all of them planting roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Chapter Six: Praising the Tathāgata’s Merits, Part of the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are most rare and marvelous, because they are fully endowed with the merits of all Tathāgatas; they are fully endowed with the descent from heaven,
fully endowed with the entry into the womb, fully endowed with the abiding in the womb, fully endowed with the emergence from the womb,
fully endowed with birth from a mother, fully endowed with roots of goodness, and fully endowed with the various marks.
Because of the perfection of the feet, the perfection of the secondary marks, the perfection of adornments, the perfection of renunciation,
the perfection of entering meditative absorption, the perfection of great meditative absorption, the perfection of the profound mind, the perfection of the sincere mind,
the perfection of true faith, the perfection of fearlessness, and the perfection of the aggregate of ethical discipline.

Because of being fully endowed with [the aggregate of morality], because of being fully endowed with the aggregate of concentration, because of being fully endowed with the aggregate of wisdom, because of being fully endowed with the aggregate of liberation,

because of being fully endowed with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, because of being fully endowed with the various supernormal powers, because of being fully endowed with realized knowledge,
because of having reached the supreme further shore of all realization and knowledge, and because of having reached great compassion...
Because it is the one shore; because it has reached the supreme shore of compassion and great compassion; because it has reached the supreme shore of joy and great joy;
because it has reached the supreme shore of equanimity and great equanimity; because it has reached the supreme shore of the most excellent and peerless state;
because it has reached the supreme shore of all modes of conduct; because it has reached the various supernormal powers.
Because it is the foremost *pāramitā*; because it has reached the foremost *pāramitā* of non-obstruction regarding all phenomena;
because it has reached the foremost *pāramitā* of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*);

because it has reached the foremost *pāramitā* of benefiting through all paths of guidance; because it has reached the foremost *pāramitā* of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; [and] because it has reached all...
Because they have reached the supreme further shore of dhyāna, vimokṣa, and samāpatti;

because they have reached the supreme further shore of non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, non-arrogance, non-negligence, non-envy, and non-malice, having abandoned all faults and attained liberation from the five paths, reaching the four fearlessnesses; thus [they] cause one...
Because all sentient beings plant various roots of goodness, receive the retribution of their karma, and are taught and inspired to reach the foremost shore (*pāramitā*),
they cause all sentient beings’ aggregates of ethical conduct (*śīla-skandha*) to be unbroken,
unimpaired, unturbid, and unmixed; thus they fulfill the aspirations of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*), remaining inviolate and praised by the wise.
Regarding his transgressions, none among all the worlds— whether devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras,
śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas— are able to rightfully reprove him or unjustly disparage him.

“Ānanda! The merits of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are so preeminent that among all classes of sentient beings in the world, there is not even one who can measure or proclaim even a small portion of the Tathāgata’s merits, such as his ethical discipline. Where, then, could anyone possibly surpass him?”
“Ānanda! From this day forward, you all should contemplate in this way: ‘This realm of space is thus vast; these four directions are thus expansive. I fully know their limits and boundaries;
yet the merits of the Buddhas are immeasurable.’”
In this way, Ānanda!

All the aggregates of morality, all the aggregates of concentration, all the aggregates of wisdom, as well as the aggregates of liberation and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—belonging to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—and even all their modes of conduct, supernormal powers, and unimpeded benefits, cannot be fully described, cannot be displayed, cannot be known, and cannot be entered.
Why is this so? Ānanda!
All the merits possessed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are without limit.

Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess immeasurable conduct of precepts, immeasurable conduct of concentration, immeasurable conduct of wisdom, immeasurable conduct of liberation, and immeasurable knowledge and vision of liberation; indeed, they possess all immeasurable merits, which are entirely equal.
"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are fully endowed with such qualities as these.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"When the World-Honored One descended from heaven and entered the womb, he dwelt there in the inconceivable; his emergence was likewise so.
His birthplace is most excellent, his mother peerless, and his supreme virtues are foremost among all."
The body is endowed with the thirty-two marks, And adorned by the perfection of all the secondary characteristics;
The inconceivable deeds performed by all Buddhas Are entirely the result of long cultivation and accumulation over vast eons.
Supreme among humans, he seeks to leave the household life; He achieves the great samādhi of meditative concentration;
With a correct mind and pure faith, he is steadfast; There is no skillful means he does not know.
Fully endowed with both ethical conduct and meditative concentration, His wisdom is perfected and beyond compare;
He has likewise attained the knowledge and vision of liberation, And reached the further shore of supernormal powers and majestic virtue.
Able to extinguish blazing suffering and rescue sentient beings, Compassion and loving-kindness are the foremost essential practices;
Joyful relinquishment is likewise a wondrous practice of equanimity— This is what all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have realized for themselves.
Body and speech are always in accord with the movements of the mind; His conduct follows wisdom, beyond the reach of thought.
His majestic demeanor is peerless, transcending the world; The Dharma King’s spiritual power has reached the further shore.
Through the samādhi of non-contention, he perceives phenomena as they truly are; he clearly discerns what is possible and what is impossible.
His meditative concentrations and liberations are unfathomable, and he is universally able to benefit all sentient beings.
Samādhi and wisdom, śamatha and vipaśyanā are thus perfected; with pervasive radiance, they awaken the mind to extinguish defilements.
Free from greed, anger, and all transgressions, they have well-mastered liberation and fearlessness.
Their conduct of precepts is neither broken nor weakened; Free from turbidity and unmixed with defilement, it is utterly pure.
Though many beings provoke them, they feel no anger or vexation; Seeking no karmic reward, they are praised by the wise.
Without fault within and without reproach without, even by means of gods, humans, Brahmā, Māra, or even śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, none can find cause for censure; he is eternally pure.
The realm of empty space may yet be exhausted, And the limits of all directions may be reached;
But who could fathom the pure conduct of the Unsurpassed Tamer, the Teacher of Gods and Humans?
The great ocean might be drunk dry with the mouth, and likewise the boundless mass of waters;
the radiance of the Buddhas cannot be fathomed, and who could reach the limit of their pure conduct?
Mount Sumeru may be blown apart by the breath of one’s mouth, and the great and small Iron Ring Mountains likewise;
yet the wondrous conduct of the Buddhas cannot be known, and the depths of their pure ethical discipline are difficult to fathom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin thought to himself:
"Now, it would be truly excellent if the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to manifest his majestic spiritual power and grace this assembly with his presence."
Now, for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, I shall also inquire of the World-Honored One regarding the subtle and wondrous dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi.
The Tathāgata has previously revealed its name; now he should expound this Dharma for his disciples and clarify its underlying principles.
World-Honored One!
"Would it not be better to dwell in the peace of meditative absorption?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akāśagupta had such a thought, by the Buddha's supernatural power, caused the great earth of this trichiliocosm assembly to quake in six ways at that very moment—namely, shaking, surging, rising, trembling, roaring, and awakening—and thus it was endowed with eighteen modes of movement, up to surging and subsiding.
After it had shaken in this manner, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, again employed his supernatural power to emit a great radiance that illuminated this trichiliocosm.

When that light emerged, it caused all the celestial palaces of the constellations, the palace of the Moon Devaputra, the palace of the Sun Devaputra, and indeed all the light from the palaces of the various heavens in the desire realm to vanish and cease to appear. Furthermore, the majestic splendor of all the Brahma palaces—immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—was completely eclipsed; even all the celestial palaces of the form realm failed to appear because they were overwhelmed by the Buddha’s light.
When all the other lights had vanished, only the divine light of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, remained most radiant.

At that time, the World-Honored One, his heart permeated by great compassion and desiring to bring benefit to all sentient beings, arose from his meditative concentration. He proceeded with calm and measured steps toward the great assembly; having circled and surveyed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati and the others, all the gods and humans of this world—including Brahmā, Māra, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras—encountered the Buddha’s radiance and each rose from their respective lotus seats to approach the Buddha. Bowing with palms joined, they paid homage to the World-Honored One and then each withdrew to their seats.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin saw from afar that the physical marks of the World-Honored One were distinct, his appearance was upright, majestic, and extraordinary; his faculties were as tranquil as a tamed elephant king, and his mind was as clear and bright as limpid water. Seeing him come from that direction, fully endowed with all attributes and perfected in all-knowledge, he felt profound joy.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!

Observe how the World-Honored One has arisen from meditative concentration; as the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, comes forth from his quiet chamber, he will surely expound the foremost truth of sincerity, which is ultimately free from falsehood."

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is one who speaks wondrously, one who speaks truly, one who speaks in accordance with reality, one who speaks as it is, one whose words do not differ from the truth, and one who speaks excellently.
With a mind of skillful reflection, they constantly perform virtuous deeds; their physical actions are faultless, their verbal actions are faultless,
and their mental actions are faultless, such that all merits are fully perfected— namely, because they are perfected in the supreme,
foremost aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), perfected in the supreme, foremost aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*), and perfected in the supreme...
Because it is the foremost aggregate of true wisdom; because it is fully endowed with the most supreme and foremost aggregate of liberation;
because it is fully endowed with the most supreme and foremost aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; because it is fully endowed with the most supreme and foremost deportment;
because it is fully endowed with the most supreme and foremost supernormal powers; and because it is fully endowed with the most supreme and foremost benefit.
Because he is endowed with the most supreme, foremost, and inconceivable eloquence;
because he is endowed with the most supreme, foremost, and accomplished [attainments]; because he is endowed with the most supreme, foremost, and subtle [qualities];

because he is endowed with the most supreme, foremost, and celestial descent; because he is endowed with the most supreme, foremost, and entry into the womb; and because he is endowed with the most supreme, foremost...
Because of dwelling in the womb; because of being endowed with the most supreme and foremost birth and lineage;
because of being endowed with the most supreme and foremost perfection of merit; because of being endowed with the most supreme and foremost inconceivable primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*);
because of being endowed with the most supreme and foremost inconceivable secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*); and because of being endowed with the most supreme and foremost past...

Because of their karma; because they are endowed with the most supreme and foremost roots of goodness; because they are endowed with the most supreme and foremost perfection of the arousal of the bodhicitta;
because they are endowed with faith; because they are endowed with the destruction of afflictions;

because they are endowed with the great destruction of afflictions; because they are endowed with the renunciation of the household life; because they are endowed with knowledge of the five kinds... [and so forth].
That is to say: because he is fully endowed with the foremost body of precepts; because he is fully endowed with the foremost body of concentration;

because he is fully endowed with the foremost body of wisdom; because he is fully endowed with the foremost body of liberation; because he is fully endowed with the foremost body of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
because he has reached the further shore of the foremost supernormal powers; because he has reached the further shore of the foremost [unconditioned]...
Because other wisdoms have realized the further shore; because they have reached the further shore of the supreme discernment of phenomena (*dharma*);
because they have reached the further shore of the supreme discernment of meanings (*artha*); because they have reached the further shore of the supreme discernment of eloquence (*pratibhāna*);
because they have reached the further shore of the supreme tranquility of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and because they have reached the further shore of the supreme clarity and penetration.
Therefore, he has reached the further shore of the foremost faculty of wisdom and the path of enlightenment;
he has reached the further shore of the foremost loving-kindness and great loving-kindness; he has reached the further shore of the foremost compassion and great compassion;
he has reached the further shore of the foremost sympathetic joy and great sympathetic joy; and he has reached the further shore of the foremost equanimity and great equanimity.
Therefore, because he has reached the supreme, inconceivable perfection of majestic deportment;
because he has reached the supreme perfection of shame and modesty; because he has reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all phenomena;
because he has reached the supreme perfection of unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past; [and] because he has reached the supreme [perfection] regarding the future...
Because he has reached the unimpeded perfection of knowledge and vision regarding the present; because he has reached the supreme perfection of knowledge and vision regarding the present;
because he has reached the supreme perfection of bodily action that accords with wisdom;
because he has reached the supreme perfection of verbal action that accords with wisdom; because he has reached the supreme perfection of mental action that accords with wisdom...
Because he has reached the further shore of wisdom. "Ānanda!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in a single thought-moment, is able to fully know the mental activities of all sentient beings—their thoughts, whether wholesome or unwholesome, pure or defiled, and so forth."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like the great ocean, for the mass of their pure precepts is bottomless."
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like Mount Sumeru, for their mass of samādhi is unshakable.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like space, for their mass of wisdom is without limit.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like space, for they gather in all sentient beings without obstruction.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like the orb of the sun, for they produce the light of the Dharma for all the world.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like a great mass of fire, for they burn away the fuel of all the afflictions of sentient beings.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like rivers, like reservoirs, like lakes, and like springs, for they wash away the impurities of birth, old age, sickness, and death in sentient beings.
Venerable Ānanda!
