The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like skilled physicians, for they are able to cure all sentient beings of the suffering of various epidemics and diseases.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like great clouds and rain, for they are able to moisten and nourish sentient beings who have become withered by means of the water of the Dharma.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like lion kings, for they are able to shatter the great pride of all sentient beings.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like great ships, for they are able to ferry sentient beings across the river of birth and death.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like Nārāyaṇa, for they are able to subdue all the great powers of the world.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like the udumbara flower, for they are difficult to encounter throughout all the worlds.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like the flowers of the pārijātaka tree, for they possess the thirty-two marks of a great man which are lovely and delightful.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like parents, for they are able to bestow peace, happiness, and benefit upon all sentient beings.
Venerable Ānanda!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, act for the sake of benefit and act for the sake of peace and happiness, for they are able to cause all sentient beings to find stable dwelling.
"Venerable Ānanda!
If someone were to say:
'When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he possesses immeasurable eloquence.'"
To speak in this manner is what is called "skillfully speaking of the Tathāgata.
That the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world possesses inconceivable eloquence is what is meant by "skillfully speaking."
Venerable Ānanda! To speak briefly: when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there is boundless eloquence;

when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there is unimpeded eloquence; when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there is eloquence free from attachment; when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there is eloquence of supreme liberation; when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there is eloquence that accords with meaning, eloquence corresponding to meaning, eloquence that is subtle and pure, eloquence of skillful questioning, eloquence without being questioned, superior eloquence, unsurpassed eloquence, eloquence of loving-kindness, great eloquence of loving-kindness, eloquence of compassion, great eloquence of compassion, eloquence of sympathetic joy, great eloquence of sympathetic joy, eloquence of equanimity, great eloquence of equanimity, and the eloquence of the Buddha’s appearance in the world for the benefit of beings.
"Venerable Ānanda!
If someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata appears in the world fully endowed with the benefit of all sentient beings.'"
"This is what is called speaking well of the Tathāgata.
Venerable Ānanda!
If someone were to speak correctly:"
"By means of eloquence regarding identical meanings, he benefits sentient beings; this is the Tathāgata appearing in the world.
Furthermore, it says:

"If one says that his eloquence for benefiting others is for the sake of all sentient beings attaining benefit, and that he causes them to be fully endowed with correct speech and sound—this is the Tathāgata appearing in the world."
"Such a person may also be called one who speaks well of the Tathāgata.
Venerable Ānanda!
If a person were to say:"

"For those beings who have no refuge, no support, no rescue, no protection, and no compassion, the Tathāgata appears in the world as their refuge, their support, their rescue, their protection, and their compassionate one."
"This is what is called 'skillfully expounding the Tathāgata.
Venerable Ānanda!

Even if I were to spend an entire kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, singing praises of the eloquence and merit of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, for such a long duration, I would never reach even a single fraction of it."

Furthermore, even if one were to expound upon the merits of the Tathāgata’s eloquence for immeasurable eons—merits belonging to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—one would ultimately never reach even a small fraction of its limit.
"Venerable Ānanda!
Suppose there were a person who was old, sick, emaciated, and frail, who went into a great assembly and spoke these words:
'O people, you should know:'"
"Though I am advanced in years and crushed by illness, I can still take a great ocean and dry it up instantly with a single drop from the tip of a hair.
Although this person has never possessed supernatural powers or incantations, he is able to speak such resolute and bold words.
Venerable sir,
what do you think?
Is the meaning of that person's words to be trusted?
Ānanda replied, “No, Great Being!”
Amoghadarśin spoke again:
"Venerable One!
Regarding those words of that person, all the devas and humans in the world have indeed marveled at how rare and extraordinary this matter is."
"Could one who is thus distressed take all the water of the great ocean with the tip of a hair?
Would such a thought occur to him? Ānanda replied, "No."
"O Mahāsattva! 'It is so, Venerable One!
This matter is fundamentally non-existent; upon what could one rely to place faith?'"
"I now praise and describe the merit of the eloquence of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, yet I cannot reach even a small fraction of its limit;
such is the nature of this matter. Venerable Ānanda!
Let us set this matter aside for a moment."

Even if the Buddha were to now praise and describe his own merits down to the finest hair-fiber, he could not finish doing so even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas, let alone anyone else.
"Venerable Ānanda!
Let this matter rest for now.
I shall now further explain: suppose all sentient beings throughout the great earth—of various kinds—"

Whether they have feet, no feet, two feet, four feet, or even many feet; whether they have form or are formless; whether they possess perception, lack perception, or are neither possessing nor lacking perception—regarding all such sentient beings in this world and throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, even if they were all to simultaneously attain Buddhahood, those World-Honored Ones, though speaking for immeasurable kalpas, would never exhaustively praise the merit of even a single hair-pore of a Buddha.
"Venerable Ānanda!
You should know that all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, possess such inconceivable and perfected merits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Venerable One, behold the Dharma King arrive; he is worthy of offerings by all the world.
His merit and majestic radiance are most brilliantly manifest, and his fulfillment of omniscience is unshakable.”
The Buddha’s supreme and wondrous words are truly spoken; they are truthful speech, consistent with reality, and free from contradiction.
He skillfully expounds the noble Dharma with authentic knowledge, and his body, speech, and mind are likewise free from fault.
With a mind free of divergent thoughts and severed from discrimination, his ethical conduct is supreme and his samādhi profound;
his wisdom and liberation far surpass all others, and his knowledge and vision of liberation are beyond compare.
His majestic deportment is perfectly complete and inconceivable;
his supreme supernormal powers and knowledge of reality bring immeasurable benefit to the world, and his eloquence and wondrous conduct are likewise peerless.
Descending from heaven, he was born as a king of elephants and oxen; entering the womb, he achieved preeminence in the world;
his dwelling in the womb was extraordinary and peerless; his birth into a noble family was endowed with a mother of high station.
He has perfected all the faculties, foremost among them; his supreme marks are complete and inconceivable.
Endowed with every exquisite feature, he is most magnificently adorned; all is clear and distinct for the world to behold.
Fully endowed with a sincere mind and pure faith, Through meditative concentration, they remove defilements and possess great majesty;
Relinquishing worldly desires, they delight in leaving the home-life, And upon accomplishing Bodhi, they attain five kinds [of qualities].
Having already crossed to the further shore of the foremost supernormal powers, his wisdom is unimpeded and boundless;
together with śamatha and vipaśyanā, the Dharma King has attained mastery through thorough penetration.
The waters of the great ocean are vast and deep, yet they might perhaps be measured by the tip of a hair;
But the pure precepts of the Tamer of Men cannot be known, even after passing through kalpas as vast as space.
Though Mount Sumeru is firm, it may still be moved, And cast by hand as far as the Brahma palace;
But when the Buddhas first abide in meditative concentration, There is already nothing that can disturb or unsettle them.
Space may have its boundaries discovered, and the four directions may also have their limits known;
yet one can never perceive the realm of Perfect Enlightenment through conceptualization or discrimination of "this" and "that."
Venerable One!
Though the great earth is vast and wide, it can be measured entirely with a finger;
yet the mind and consciousness of the Honored One among Men, who has abandoned all afflictions, cannot be exhausted.
Just as the light of the sun’s orb dispels all darkness, And one perceives all good and evil as if seeing forms;
So too does the Sovereign Teacher of the World Able to shatter the vast, black clouds of ignorance.
Just as the autumn moon emerges from thick clouds, all sentient beings who see it rejoice;
the Dharma King’s light of wisdom is like the full moon—beholding such wondrous color, there is none who does not find delight.
Like a bright lamp in the long night of profound stillness, you act as a guide for all who possess eyes;
the wise ones of the world can dispel darkness, constantly illuminating sentient beings with the light of the Dharma.

The Sovereign Honored One who can set forth the torch of Dharma, the Great Teacher of gods and humans acting for the sake of others, has extinguished all realms of existence; therefore, he is called the Buddha, King of Radiance.
Noble wisdom is like rivers and springs, Able to wash away the dust of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
Like a great king of physicians dispensing excellent medicine, The Tamer is able to eliminate the manifold sufferings of disease;
Just as a dragon king sends down a great rain, It is able to fill all the great earths.
The Buddhas practice compassion in this way, Fulfilling all who delight in the Dharma.
When the Great Lion King roars his thunderous cry, He subdues all the evil beasts of the world;
The World-Honored One speaks with such certainty, Shattering the pride and arrogance of the heterodox.
Like a great ship that constantly travels back and forth, ferrying across all who come and go;
so do the Buddhas circulate everywhere, pulling out those who are perpetually submerged in the four currents.
The udumbara flower is rare in the world; it is most difficult to see here in Jambudvīpa.
The World-Honored One, the Lord of Gods and Men, is the most difficult among the difficult to encounter—the refuge for all the world.
Just as when the flowers of the Pāri tree appear, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven are filled with great delight;
so too, when one endowed with the marks and signs of greatness arises in the world, all sentient beings who behold him are filled with joy.
The World-Honored One’s spiritual transformations are inexhaustible;
as I now proclaim them, by extolling the Buddha’s myriad virtues, I ultimately bring benefit to all sentient beings.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Five: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Six: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.

Chapter Seven: The Buddha Performs Supernatural Powers. At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden hand from within his *kāṣāya* robe and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin. He then manifested the mark of the broad and long tongue and addressed the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, you, Amoghadarśin!
"It is well that you are now able to thus extol and proclaim the true merits of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha for the sake of all sentient beings.
Anagatadarśin!..."
If someone were to say:
"When the sentient beings of the world are without protection or refuge, there will certainly appear within them one capable of providing protection and refuge to act as their savior."
"Aśūnyapratibhāna!
You should know that this is indeed a skillful exposition of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!"
Furthermore, it is said:

"When the sentient beings of the world have no place of refuge, at that time there will surely appear in the world an inconceivable eloquence and immeasurable eloquence, which can serve as a great refuge for sentient beings."
"Amitābha! You should know that this is indeed a well-spoken discourse on the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Amitābha!"
Furthermore, if it is said:

"When sentient beings in the world mostly engage in conduct of greed, mostly engage in conduct of hatred, and mostly engage in conduct of delusion, at that time there will surely appear a Great Teacher in the world who is free from desire, hatred, and delusion, in order to eliminate these three poisons."
"Amitābha! You should know that this is precisely what is called 'skillfully expounding the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Amitābha!"
Furthermore, it is said:

"When the sentient beings of the world are full of stinginess and full of jealousy, at that time there must surely arise a Great Teacher who has distanced himself from stinginess and jealousy and delights in practicing generosity, appearing for the purpose of destroying stinginess and jealousy."
“Amoghadarśin! You should know that this is precisely what is called ‘skillfully teaching the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Amoghadarśin!”
Furthermore, if it is said:

"When the beings of the world lack the conduct of shame, remorse, and modesty, at that time there must surely appear a Great Teacher of shame and remorse in the world to eliminate that lack of shame and modesty."
"Aśūnyapratibhāna!
You should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking well.
Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!"
Furthermore, it is said:

"When sentient beings in the world frequently practice arrogance and haughtiness, there will surely appear in the world a Great Teacher of harmony, respect, gentleness, and flexibility to eliminate such arrogance."
"Aśūnyapratibhāna!
You should know that this is precisely what is called 'skillfully teaching the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!"
Furthermore, it is said:

"When the sentient beings of the world lack compassion, are unable to rejoice in giving, frequently practice anger, and possess defiled, poisonous minds—at such a time, there will surely appear in the world a Teacher who has severed the poison of anger, who is fully endowed with the four immeasurables, and who teaches the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion for the sake of great benefit."
"Amitābha! You should know that this is precisely what is called 'skillfully teaching the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Amitābha!"
Furthermore, it is said:

"When the world abounds in evil and there are no virtuous beings, a Great Teacher arises who can provide such benefit as to instruct those capable of generating roots of goodness, and cause those who already possess roots of goodness to increase and expand them."
"Aśūnyapratibhāna!
You should know that he is one who speaks well of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!"
Furthermore, it is said:

"In this world of the five turbidities, where the illnesses of sentient beings increase, there is a Great Being who is able to perform acts of benefit, guiding them with the Dharma of transcendence to bring peace and happiness to all beings."
"Amoghadarśin! You should know that these words refer to me. Why is this so? Because..."
“I have now appeared in this world of the five turbidities to proclaim the sublime Dharma, sever the stains of heterodoxy, and bring great benefit to all sentient beings.

At that time, as the World-Honored One stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin with his hand, he immediately employed his supernatural power to cause this great assembly, in a single thought-moment, to see all the present Buddha-lands of the east—immeasurable, boundless, unspeakable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* in number. Within those lands, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones who had not yet entered parinirvāṇa, as well as all the realms of those sentient beings, were all manifested before them. They also heard the voices of those Buddhas preaching the Dharma, and they saw those lands adorned with various kinds of pure and magnificent arrays.

In this manner, even all the Buddha-lands and every realm throughout the ten directions—south, west, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—became clearly manifest before him, as if he were looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand.

Furthermore, when the World-Honored One stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin with his hand, through the Buddha’s spiritual power and the causal conditions of Amoghadarśin’s original vows, in a single thought-moment he saw the past Buddhas—immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, and incalculable—who had entered nirvāṇa throughout the ten directions, as well as the pure adornments of their lands, all clearly and distinctly visible as if looking at the palm of one's own hand.
Moreover, by the power of the Buddha, he also saw the future Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their pure lands fully endowed with adornments.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, through the power of his original vows and sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, beheld all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as the pure and magnificent adornments of their respective Buddha-fields. To further proclaim this meaning, he rose from his seat, maintained perfect dignified deportment, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke in verse:
"The waters contained within the trichiliocosm, If one wished to measure them, they could all be known;
But for the Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Whose conduct and precepts are so profound and far-reaching—who can fathom them?"
Mount Sumeru, so high, broad, and most majestic, The frail, aged, and sickly could blow apart with their breath;
Yet when the World-Honored One first enters meditative concentration, It is difficult to fathom even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
The limits of space might be measured by one's feet, And the boundaries of the four directions might likewise be traversed;
But for the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One, His wisdom is profoundly deep, without source or bottom.
Space is equal and unobstructed, yet it may be stirred by violent winds;
the Tathāgata’s fundamental nature is free from afflictions—where, then, could the poisons of greed, anger, and delusion dwell?
Just as the orb of the sun, perfectly full, abides in the sky with pure radiance pervading the world;
so too does this one of the lineage of Arhat-sages shine brilliantly among this assembly of devas.
Furthermore, like the autumn moon joined with the constellation Mṛgaśiras, its majestic radiance transcends the world and outshines the multitude of stars;
so too does the Great Dharma King, like the full moon, blaze forth uniquely above gods and humans.
Just as the udumbara flower is exceedingly rare, appearing only once in a great while and not manifesting in every age;
so too does the Teacher of Gods among Gods, the Tamer of Men, appear only at certain times, manifesting according to the aspirations of sentient beings.
The World-Honored One’s wondrous hand has rubbed the crown of my head;
adorned with golden hues and the marks of a hundred blessings, he is indestructible and fully endowed [with all attributes]. Such is the benefit he brings.
The Bhagavat’s mantra and his words of truth, as the Dharma King among men who turns the wheel of the True Dharma,
pervade the worlds of the ten directions, bringing immense benefit and complete mastery.

When the World-Honored One stroked my head with his hand, I beheld the Supreme Persons of the ten directions, as numerous as the grains of sand spoken of in the Ganges River; the multitude of rishis of great majestic virtue was even more so.
When the Great Muni honored me by placing his hand upon me, I immediately saw all the Buddhas, such as Amitābha.
Even more numerous than the grains of sand counted in the Ganges River are those most excellent among men;
I have seen and known them, awakened by the Tathāgata’s own hands of loving-kindness, in the world of Sukhāvatī.
There, the Arhat, the Honored One among two-legged beings, Akṣobhya, brings benefit through the light of his great compassion.
Having been touched by the World-Honored One’s divine hand, I beheld all the Honored Ones who have attained parinirvāṇa throughout the world—
those who, in a single thought-moment, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and who have subdued their faculties through great compassion;
when the World-Honored One stroked me with his hand, I also beheld the former vows of Maitreya.
Just as all future events will be, they are clearly understood and free from further doubt.
I have already seen the Buddhas of the past; it is likewise so for those of the future and the present.
As for all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, their supernormal powers and virtuous might are difficult to describe.
When the World-Honored One stroked me with his hand, I saw everywhere throughout the ten directions the Saviors of the World, as well as the pure buddha-fields of all the Buddhas;
because of this, I further gave rise to the most supreme vow.
The supernatural powers of all Buddhas are inconceivable; their precepts, concentration, and wisdom are likewise so.
All other meritorious virtues are beyond description; I only pray that you will constantly instruct and guide me as you do now.
When the Tathāgata reached down and touched me, I immediately beheld the various stūpas and temples of the ten directions,
made of myriad jewels and golden in color like the sands of the Ganges, complete with all manner of subtle and wondrous offerings.
All Buddhas possess great renown, their various marks and signs filling the ten directions;
with hundreds of thousands of musical sounds they are honored, and I see all those lands in this very way.
In that land there are further stūpas of the Buddhas, Interspersed with golden threads and precious crystal;
Towering more than one yojana high, They are all upright, majestic, and adorned in this manner.
Furthermore, he beholds the great and venerable stupas and temples, exquisitely adorned with various precious gems;
some are situated in the midst of space, where celestial flowers are constantly scattered upon them.
I further beheld those supreme stupas, surging forth to a height of twelve yojanas;
they were called "Kindled Lamps" by those Buddhas, their radiance illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
When the World-Honored One stroked my head with his hand, I beheld ineffable, wondrous stupas;
each of those Buddhas possessed great renown, and all within them were the powers of the Tathāgata.
When the World-Honored One stroked the crown of my head with his hand, I was thereby able to see all the Buddha-fields.
Some there were burning their bodies, others undergoing humiliation; the various types of practices are beyond description.
Each one, within their own field, cultivated asceticism without ceasing day or night, as if trying to extinguish a blazing fire.
With courageous and vast vows they deliver sentient beings, all for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi.
I have also beheld the lands of the ten directions, where various bodhisattvas constantly exert themselves,
gouging flesh from their own bodies to light many lamps, all for the sake of the radiance of bodhi.
I further beheld a pure body, constantly standing before all Buddhas;
even after those World-Honored Ones had entered nirvana, it remained for the sake of seeking the great virtue of Bodhi.
I further saw those who act for the sake of the Dharma, pouring fragrant oil over their bodies to light lamps;
though they afflict their bodies and concentrate their minds throughout the ten directions, they never fix their hearts on wealth, food, or similar things.
I further behold various noble men who constantly relinquish their heads, eyes, bodies, hands, wives, children,
royal thrones, and kingdoms and cities, with the resolve to enable all living beings to attain peace and happiness.
As I see it without exception, it cannot be expressed in words;
my knowledge and vision are most supreme, for through the Buddha’s majestic power, I have observed all things.
Through the majestic power and sustaining grace of the World-Honored One, I have been enabled to see this rare and wondrous event;
to the Auspicious One, the Foremost among Gods, the God among Gods, I now take refuge as the Most Supreme.

Chapter Eight: The Extensive Inquiry upon Seeing Boundless Buddhas, from the Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Now this entire assembly of devas and humans, having seen that the World-Honored One has long remained in meditative concentration and remains silent without speaking, all feel a deep longing and yearning; they only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to take this seat.

At that time, having heard that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin had made his request on behalf of that great assembly of devas and humans, the World-Honored One sat upright with right mindfulness and granted his consent in silence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, having received this silent consent, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I now wish to ask a question; if the Holy One will grant me leave, I shall venture to speak.
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:

"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall answer whatever you ask, severing your doubts and gladdening your heart; this shall be witnessed by gods, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas alike."
Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what samādhi should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate?”
Which samādhis should one draw near to?
Which samādhis should one practice?
Having thus contemplated, drawn near to, and practiced these samādhis, what phenomena does the bodhisattva directly perceive that brings about peace and happiness?
How should one attain being like the great ocean, by virtue of receiving and retaining extensive learning?
How should one attain being like Mount Sumeru, by virtue of the mind of enlightenment remaining steadfast and unshakable?
How shall one attain being like the Great Iron Ring Mountains, such that all the heterodox arguments of external paths cannot shake them?
How shall one attain being like space, such that there is no obstruction among any phenomena?
How should one attain being like space, because the mind is free from attachment?
How should one attain being like the solar disc, because it dispels all the darkness of ignorance?
How shall one obtain that which is like the lunar disk, because the pure dharmas are perfected?
How shall one obtain that which is like the circle of a lamp, because of the light of the Dharma-activity?
How shall one obtain that which is like a great torch, because all aggregates of sensation are extinguished?
How shall one obtain that which is like a mass of fire, so as to incinerate all afflictions?
How shall one obtain that which is like rivers, ponds, and springs, so that all sentient beings may enjoy it according to their wishes?
How shall one become like a great ship, so that all sentient beings may cross to the other shore?
How shall one become like a bridge, so as not to sink into the afflictions of birth and death?
How shall one be able to subdue all adversaries and destroy the armies of Māra and all forms of arrogance?
How shall one be like the Pārijātaka tree, opening the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment for all sentient beings in every direction, with its fragrant breeze wafting everywhere?
How shall one attain that which is as rare and difficult to find as the udumbara flower?
How shall one attain that which is like the King of Medicine, who equally cures the sickness and suffering of all sentient beings?
How shall I come to be like a great king of physicians, giving rise to a heart of great compassion out of pity for sentient beings?
How shall I come to be like a sandalwood tree, removing all burning afflictions and providing refreshing coolness?
How shall one become like a great rain cloud, showering the rain of Dharma equally so that all are satisfied?
How shall one become like a vessel of honey, able to fully expound the Dharma of a single flavor?
How shall one attain the lion’s roar, so as to be able to grant fearlessness to all sentient beings?
How shall one become like parents, equally bestowing peace, happiness, and benefit upon all sentient beings?
How shall one come to see the true Dharma, reaching the further shore of suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality?
How shall one come to explain the profound intent, reaching the further shore of the ultimate meaning?
How shall one attain the eloquence for skillfully expounding the Dharma, reaching the further shore of being able to discern it?
How shall one attain skillfulness in expounding the Dharma, reaching the further shore of being fully endowed with expedient means?
How should one distinguish the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), by virtue of skillfully knowing the dharma of syllables and phrases?
How should one attain right intention and right practice, by being fully endowed with contentment?
How shall one come to govern the great assembly with fearlessness?
How shall one come to expound the meaning of reality as it is, thereby entering the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
How shall one come to be like the great ocean, wherein all phenomena are of a single flavor?
How should one attain the state of being like a great mountain, because the samādhi is tranquil and cannot be shaken?
How should one attain the state of being like a door-sill—or as it is also called, the banner of Śakra—because the bodhicitta is unshakable and irreversible?
How shall one obtain firm strength through the perfection of one's resolve?
How shall one obtain perfect deportment by refraining from hollow flattery?
How shall one obtain a handsome body by joyfully preaching the Dharma for others?
How shall one obtain the most exquisite and supreme physical marks?
How shall one obtain nobility, being born into a great lineage?
How shall one become a Great Dharma King through the merit and blessings of one's reward?
How shall one attain the perfection of immeasurable eloquence?
How shall one attain the eloquence that is free from attachment?
How shall one attain the eloquence that is unerring?
How should one discern various names, phrases, and eloquence?
How should one attain inconceivable eloquence?
How should one attain boundless eloquence?
How should one attain the eloquence of liberation?
How should one attain the eloquence of synonymous meaning, which is also called "accomplishment"?
How should one attain the eloquence of following the intended meaning of others?
How should one gradually attain the eloquence of intimacy?
How should one attain the eloquence of answering what is asked?
How should one attain the eloquence of speaking spontaneously without being asked?
How shall one attain unimpaired eloquence?
How shall one attain non-regressive eloquence?
How shall one attain the eloquence of various explanations through profound phrases and syllables?
How shall one attain the boundless and limitless eloquence of illustration?
How shall one attain the complete possession of the Brahma-voice even before having realized great Bodhi?
How shall one obtain the foremost and most subtle voice?
How shall one obtain the voice of the kalaviṅka bird?
How shall one obtain the voice of the lion king?
How shall one obtain the voice of a great dragon king?
How shall one obtain the voice of a great bull king?
How shall one obtain the voice of a great bell or drum?
How shall one obtain a voice of supreme and wondrous song and praise?
How shall one obtain the sound of musical strings?
How shall one obtain a voice that is plaintive, pure, and beautiful?
How shall one obtain the voice that resounds like wind, clouds, and thunder?
How shall one obtain the voice of profound and majestic eloquence?
How shall one obtain the voice of true and perfect eloquence, adorned with all exquisite speech, letters, and phrases?
How shall one obtain the voice that is profoundly deep and capable of great skillful exposition?
How shall one obtain the voice of eloquence through various parables?
How shall one obtain the voice that receives the most supreme offerings from all worlds?
How shall one obtain the voice of eloquence for debating with others?
How shall one obtain the voice that has reached the further shore of supernormal powers?
How shall one obtain the voice of the non-forgetfulness of the Dharma?
How shall one obtain the voice that never lacks the sound of wholesome dharmas?
How shall one obtain the voice praised by others for its perfection in the practice of all roots of goodness?
In this way, everything shall be fully possessed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, having raised such questions as these, spoke in verse to further proclaim this meaning:

“Endowed with the golden hue and the marks of a hundred merits, Able to awaken to the single Dharma for boundless benefit— I now ask concerning your most supreme merit: Which samādhi should be contemplated first?”
The Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom is peerless; how could there be anyone in the world who surpasses it?
I now entreat the Honored One: what meditative concentration should I practice, so that the merit obtained may be inconceivable?
Great Master of Gods and Humans, Supreme Tamer!
Contemplating this samādhi, what are its merits?
How should a bodhisattva practice it so as to be able to bring peace and happiness to all?
How does one naturally become an ocean of great learning?
How does one guard the resolute mind and dwell in the realm of the Buddhas' virtues?
How is it that, like the Great Iron Ring Mountains, one harbors no heart of resentment within, yet is able to subdue all those of external paths?
How is it that one is unimpeded like space?
How does one further attain mastery over the mind?
How is one like the sun and likewise like the moon?
How is it that you share the same torch and are like a lamp?
How do you provide illumination for the multitude?
And why must one further contemplate samādhi?
How does one liberate oneself from all afflictions?
How can one cross to the far shore of birth and death?
How does one resolve the mind within the wheel of suffering to transcend alone the three realms, peerless and unequaled?
Why is it that the Pārijātaka tree, adorned with the wondrous marks and signs of a Great Man, does not appear?
Why is it that the courageous and heroic one, like the Udumbara flower, does not manifest in the world?
How is it that one gives medicine without expecting recompense?
The Good Physician, the Savior from Suffering, the Tamer of Men, Can eliminate the various fevers of sentient beings; Abiding securely in pure precepts, they attain refreshing coolness.
How shall one obtain the Dharma-treasure, And cross to the other shore through immeasurable merit?
How is this profound and subtle Dharma Like the sweet taste of honey, unsurpassed in its excellence?
How does one obtain this lion’s roar, which causes sentient beings to be free from fear?
How does one benefit others equally as parents do, attaining that profound and inconceivable bliss?
How can one attain sublime eloquence and practice the path of great renown toward enlightenment?
How does one expound that most excellent way?
And how does one obtain unimpeded wisdom?
How does one become skillful in means regarding the meaning?
How does one excellently know the characteristics of all phenomena?
How does one discern the bodies of names and phrases?
What are mundane phenomena and what are supramundane?
What is right mindfulness and what is right practice?
What is contentment and what is thorough reflection?
How is it that one's great learning is like the great ocean?
How does one praise the Buddha’s true virtues?
How does one speak of those sentient beings, [showing] that the root of birth and death is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
How is it that all phenomena are without distinction, Just as the great ocean is of one and the same saltiness?
How is it that they are as immovable as a mountain, With a non-retrogressive mind like a door-sill?
How is it that you have no other activities but focus your single mind on seeking unsurpassed, great bodhi?
How is it that you are fully endowed with all dignified deportments, your physical form so upright and majestic that all who see you rejoice?
How can one always be born into a great noble family, and also receive the vast mass of merit of the Dharma King?
How can one attain that immeasurable eloquence, such that all one’s speech cannot be fathomed by the world?
How are the meanings of words and phrases so profound and subtle?
I now ask this of the Protector of the World:
How does one attain the unsurpassed and rare excellence, and how does one draw near to true eloquence without forgetfulness?
How is it that the nature of the faculties is called "concordant"? Whether asked or unasked, how does this correspond?

How is it that one who has not yet realized [the goal] possesses the Brahma-voice—its sound so pure and subtle, like the lovely song of the kalaviṅka bird, the voice of great wisdom and heroic prowess heard afar?
How is it that you have the voice of a lion and a great dragon, yet further attain the deep and weighty roar of a bull-king?
How is it that the World-Honored One has attained the music of strings, fully possessing the sounds of all various instruments?
How does one obtain that sweet-toned voice, constantly proclaiming what brings joy to all?
How is it that the sound of one's merit remains unimpaired, emerging like the wind or like a rolling thunderclap?
How do you produce various kinds of analogies and sounds, Able to proclaim all profound teachings?
How do you utter these excellent words and voices?
And how do you never forget any of the dharmas?
How does one obtain the recollection of past lives while still in the midst of existence?
How are those various supernormal powers cultivated?
How does one practice without weariness, thoroughly knowing all wholesome dharmas?
Such are these inconceivable dharmas, naturally revolving throughout the ten directions;
O World-Honored One!
I have no further doubts regarding them, and for this reason I now inquire about the place of refuge.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin had thus questioned him with earnest and profound respect, he immediately used his supernormal powers to ascend into the air. There, in mid-air, he spontaneously manifested a celestial jewel-canopy, exquisitely adorned and composed of the seven treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, musaragalva, and pearl—complete with all such various precious ornaments.

From within that jeweled canopy, various kinds of flowers rained down; those many flowers circled three times to the right and came to rest upon the Buddha’s head. Then, from amidst those flowers, they praised him in verse:
“We take refuge in the Great Tamer, the Supreme Man, The Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among two-legged beings.
Among all the worlds of devas and humans, Who could possibly be compared to you?”
Sentient beings in the long night of darkness, Deluded and inverted, have fallen onto deviant paths;
The Most Honored One of Supreme Wisdom, the Eye of the World, Is able to cause them to return once more to the level and upright path.
Having lost the seeds of the pure dharmas, sentient beings have their hearts scorched within by afflictions;
the Supreme Honored One is like a parent to the world, able to cause them to dwell securely in the realm of pure dharmas.
The loss of the sublime Dharma deeply harms humanity; future generations will surely face cause for dread.
You, Most Honored One, have accomplished the practice of great compassion and serve as the true guide for all sentient beings.
All sentient beings lack virtuous benefit, have no protection, and no savior;
O Teacher of the World, whose great compassion is rare, may the World-Honored One truly act as their protector and refuge.

At that time, after these verses had been spoken from within the flower, the flower reached the feet of the Tathāgata; in an instant, it flew away and traveled throughout the trichiliocosm, scattering as offerings before all the Buddhas.

From within that jeweled canopy, moreover, there emerged a ball of sandalwood powder as large as a chariot wheel; upon reaching the body of the Tathāgata, it suddenly vanished, yet the exquisite fragrance of that sandalwood filled the trichiliocosm.
All sentient beings who smell this fragrance shall experience supreme and wondrous bliss, just as a bodhisattva enters the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin had manifested such supernatural feats, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How shall these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain such wisdom—namely, great wisdom, swift wisdom, nimble wisdom, fierce and sharp wisdom, signless wisdom, skillful-entry wisdom, profound wisdom, vast and universal wisdom, fearless wisdom, and perfect wisdom?
Furthermore, how does one obtain incalculable and immeasurable roots of sublime goodness—namely:
roots of goodness in which the mind is like a vajra, because it penetrates all phenomena;
and roots of goodness in which the mind is as soft as kālinjara cloth, because it is capable of performing actions?
The root of goodness of a mind like the great ocean is that it gathers all clusters of precepts;
the root of goodness of a mind like a level stone is that it sustains all undertakings;
the root of goodness of a mind like the king of mountains is that it gives rise to all wholesome dharmas.
The root of goodness of a mind like the great earth, because it sustains the activities of sentient beings;
the root of goodness of attaining a mind that does not follow others, because it remains far removed from unrighteous instruction;
the root of goodness of attaining a mind that practices well, because all dharmas are securely established therein.

One attains the roots of goodness of indestructible faith because one has no doubt regarding the spheres of activity of all Tathāgatas; one dwells in a single world yet naturally and universally beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions, hears those Buddhas proclaim the sublime Dharma, further beholds the great assemblies of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, and observes the pure adornments of the Buddha-fields, having no doubt whatsoever regarding such matters as their enjoyments;
and so on, until one embraces the roots of goodness of certainty, benefiting oneself and others at all times.
“World-Honored One!
Just as I do now, it is truly for my own benefit and also out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings that I inquire of the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!”
I now further inquire of the Tathāgata for the sake of expanding the pure faith of sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
I now further inquire of the Tathāgata for the sake of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may become fully endowed with inconceivable roots of goodness.
World-Honored One!
It is also for the sake of these great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, who are clad in the armor of great diligence and vast vows, that I question the Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, within the cycle of birth and death, exert great diligence for the sake of all sentient beings, yet do not grasp at the mark of a sentient being. Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas deliver all sentient beings throughout the long night of the afflictions of birth and death, they truly do not dwell upon the conceptualization of birth, death, or affliction.”
“World-Honored One!
It is for the sake of such sentient beings that I inquire of the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!”
When there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice loving-kindness and compassion, they harbor no resentment whatsoever toward sentient beings.

Even if sentient beings should revile, abuse, lash, beat, or otherwise inflict various forms of suffering and oppression upon them, such bodhisattvas never retaliate against those beings; they do not give rise to thoughts of aversion, do not forsake their original vows, and remain free from discriminatory or distracting thoughts, single-mindedly cultivating great loving-kindness and great compassion.
"Bhagavān!
It is for the sake of those bodhisattvas who abide thus in the Mahāyāna that I inquire of the Tathāgata. Bhagavān!"

There are certain bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, for the sake of sentient beings, desire to relinquish their own happiness and all articles of pleasure, and desire to undergo all manner of blazing, intense suffering, giving rise to this thought:
"How shall I cause all sentient beings to attain the most supreme happiness, and how shall I cause all sentient beings to attain the great light of the Dharma?"
“World-Honored One!
When those bodhisattvas reflect in this way, there is no thing—whether internal or external—that they do not give away, that does not benefit others, or that does not bring abundance.”
“World-Honored One!
It is for the sake of such bodhisattvas that I inquire of the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!”
When there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who don such armor of diligence, they give rise to this thought:

"I shall now, for the sake of each and every sentient being, remain in the great hells throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction as naturally as inhalation and exhalation; yet I shall not regard this as suffering, nor shall I ever retreat from the mind of enlightenment."
"World-Honored One!
It is for the sake of these bodhisattvas that I further question the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!"
There are certain bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having donned such armor of diligence, give rise to this thought:
"I shall now, for the sake of all sentient beings, undertake all manner of tasks and servile labors, attending to them in various ways without regarding it as suffering."
Thus, some become slaves, some become servants, some become attendants, and some become disciples.
I should act in this manner, even by assuming various forms of kinship, to bring sentient beings to maturity.
"World-Honored One!
I further inquire of the Tathāgata for the sake of these bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One!"

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, for the sake of all sentient beings, give rise to great courage and vigor, practicing various ascetic austerities. They sacrifice their bodies, hands, feet, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains; at times they have their limbs severed joint by joint and their bones broken and marrow extracted, yet they do not regard this as suffering and never grow weary or indolent, instead continuing to blaze forth with even greater intensity in the quest for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“World-Honored One!
It is for the sake of such bodhisattvas that I have requested this of the World-Honored One.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin had thus questioned him, in order to reiterate this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"I ask the Celestial Teacher about supreme wisdom: how is that great wisdom accomplished?
How does one attain swift wisdom and agility, as well as sharp wisdom, intelligence, and the power of thorough penetration?"
By what cause is that profound wisdom attained?
Proclaim for me the wisdom that exhausts the boundless; this vast and universal omniscience is the supreme quest for enlightenment.
How may one attain fearlessness?
Please explain to me how to be fully endowed with skillful means.
How does one attain the vajra-mind, so as to be free from doubt regarding all phenomena?
How does one attain this supple mind, with precepts as clear and pure as the ocean?
How does one become as immovable as a mountain, adorned by the resolute vow for enlightenment?
How does one practice so as not to follow others, But dwell with clear understanding of the meaning?
How does one attain indestructible faith, Free from further doubt regarding the deeds of all Buddhas?
How does one attain that wisdom of recollecting births, Abiding in a single realm yet manifesting in the ten directions,
Universally beholding all Buddhas and hearing their Dharma, And clearly perceiving the great assemblies as well?
Without their bodies leaving a single land, they are able to make offerings to the Honored Ones of the ten directions—
with exquisite flowers, various incenses, and unguents, as well as all other inconceivable requisites.
With their minds dwelling in this land without other distractions, their bodies manifest throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions.
I have personally attended upon and served those Buddhas, all through the power of their boundless supernormal faculties.

Now, for the sake of practicing compassion, I invite you who dwell in shame and remorse, who practice for the benefit of others rather than seeking self-interest; it is for this reason that I invite you of great renown.
All those who have resolved their minds to seek the Buddha-wisdom, whose roots of goodness have matured in an inconceivable way—
how should such a samādhi be cultivated?
For their sake, I ask the Unattached One.
Donning this armor of patience for the sake of sentient beings, [thinking]:
"I must uproot all their heavy sufferings," they have already abandoned the notion of a "sentient being"; for this reason, they inquire about the truth of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Those who constantly abide in a mind of equanimity, observing all sentient beings without discriminatory thought,
and who are always able to accomplish compassion— for their sake, I ask the Tathāgata.
"What dharma should be practiced therein to swiftly attain such inconceivable [realization],
with the merit obtained being boundless?
For their sake, I entreat the Tamer."

The courageous person clad in the armor of the great vow, for the sake of a single sentient being, would endure the suffering of flames within the great hells throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
how excellent it is that they bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings!
They know neither sleep nor fatigue; there is nothing, internal or external, that they do not give away.
To those who thus embrace all sentient beings, I now inquire for their sake, O Universal Observer.
Reproached, humiliated, and beaten with verbal abuse; their bodies subjected to the suffering of various forms of oppression;
becoming slaves and servants for others—all these result from having invited the World-Honored One [to their homes].
Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of heads, He was able to give away whenever anyone came seeking them;
When he gave away his heads, he felt supreme joy, For the sake of seeking unsurpassed, wondrous Bodhi.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he further gave away His hands, his feet, and the rest of his limbs.
To rescue and liberate sentient beings who have lost their way, To eliminate birth and death and restore them to the correct path;
Furthermore, to bestow wives, concubines, sons, and daughters, As well as the seven treasures, pearls, jade, gold, and silver,
And even to relinquish exquisite utensils of all kinds— It is for their sake that I question the Tathāgata.
Relinquishing body, life, and wealth without weariness, listening to the Dharma through the long night without fatigue,
with a mind always in tranquil extinction practicing the dhūtas— for these reasons, I question the Perfectly Awakened One.
Constantly binding my mind to truthful and sublime speech, I immediately distance myself upon hearing coarse and vulgar words;
harboring no resentment toward others, it is for their sake that I consult the Sovereign.
Constantly regarding sentient beings with a compassionate heart, as parents love an only child,
and practicing equanimity toward both enemies and kin, I therefore entreat the King of Men on their behalf.
Such virtues as these now exist, which I have today proclaimed;
yet for those among the assembly who may not yet possess them, I likewise inquire of the Buddha on their behalf.
“World-Honored One!

I now possess roots of goodness; at the very moment I first posed this question, I have already attained them. By virtue of these merits of the Bodhisattva, may I swiftly realize the King of Samādhis of Quiescence.”
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Chapter Six: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Chapter Seven: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: Praising the Characteristics of Samādhi. At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Amoghadarśin!”

In the past, you were able to make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; under those Buddhas, you planted various roots of goodness and fully practiced the perfections (pāramitās). Having accomplished all that was to be done regarding all dharmas, you have constantly acted as an uninvited friend to those multitudes of sentient beings.
I ask the World-Honored One about this great meaning for the sake of those sentient beings who practice great compassion and have perfected right faith;
I ask the World-Honored One about this great meaning for the sake of those sentient beings who don the great armor;
I ask the World-Honored One about this great meaning for the sake of those sentient beings whose great bodhicitta is immovable and non-regressive.
For the sake of those sentient beings whose minds possess indestructible faith, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning;
for the sake of inspiring in all sentient beings vast and great vows as their adornment, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning;
for the sake of those sentient beings who possess inconceivable roots of goodness, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning.
For the sake of those sentient beings who don the inconceivable armor, I ask the World-Honored One about this great meaning;
for the sake of those sentient beings who transcend the triple world, I ask the World-Honored One about this great meaning;
for the sake of those sentient beings who are dedicated to the true meaning, I ask the World-Honored One about this great meaning.
For the sake of those sentient beings who accord with great wisdom, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning;
for the sake of those sentient beings who delight in the practice of the profound Dharma, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning;
for the sake of those sentient beings who value generosity, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning.
For the sake of providing a profound re-exposition for all sentient beings, I ask the World-Honored One about such a great meaning;
for the sake of all sentient beings who are able to relinquish both internal and external bodies and wealth, I ask the World-Honored One about such a great meaning;
for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to accomplish the supreme and unsurpassed aggregate of precepts, I ask the World-Honored One about such a great meaning.
For the sake of those sentient beings who are endowed with profound patience, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning;
for the sake of those sentient beings who are courageous and diligent, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning;
for the sake of those sentient beings who have attained profound meditative concentration, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning.
For the sake of those sentient beings who possess profound and weighty wisdom, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning;
for the sake of skillfully gathering all sentient beings through the expedient means of material resources, I inquire of the World-Honored One regarding such a great meaning.

"Furthermore, for the sake of those sentient beings whose minds are like adamant; for the sake of those sentient beings whose minds are like a door-bolt, neither moving nor turning; for the sake of those sentient beings whose minds are like pure water, free from dust and grime; for the sake of those sentient beings whose minds are like the kācilindika cloth; for the sake of those sentient beings who delight in entering into profound meanings; for the sake of those sentient beings who revere the True Dharma; for the sake of those sentient beings who can cast off burdens and bear them; for the sake of those sentient beings who do not begrudge their own bodies or lives; and for the sake of those sentient beings who do not delight in any conditioned phenomena of the world—I ask the Tathāgata about such a great meaning."
“Amoghadarśin! It is only you who, at this time, are able to pose such a question to the Tathāgata on behalf of these great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, saying:
“Amoghadarśin! You should listen attentively and reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail and with full analysis.”
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
As I have received your holy teaching, I shall receive it with single-minded attention.”
The Buddha said, "Aśūnyadarśin!
There is a bodhisattva samādhi called 'Mindfulness of All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. You should draw near to, cultivate, observe, and contemplate such a samādhi."
Having cultivated, observed, and contemplated this samādhi, one then attains the expansion and accomplishment of the practice of the Dharma that brings manifest happiness;
one then attains the expansion of the wholesome root of non-attachment;
one then attains the expansion of the wholesome root of non-hatred; and one then attains the expansion of the wholesome root of non-delusion.
Because they have attained the fullness of shame and remorse, they achieve the accomplishment of supernormal powers; because they achieve these, they attain the perfection of all Buddha-dharmas;
because they attain this, they attain the purification of all Buddha-lands; because they attain this, they attain the perfection of descending from heaven for birth;
because they attain this, they attain the perfection of entering the womb; because they attain this, they attain the purity of remaining in the womb.
Because of being complete, one attains the perfection of a mother’s birth; because of being complete, one attains the perfection of a family’s birth;
because of being complete, one attains the perfection of the subtle purity of the sense faculties;
because of being complete, one attains the perfection of the marks of a Great Man; because of being complete, one attains the perfection of the various secondary characteristics.
Because of the perfection of attaining [the fruits], one then attains the perfection of supreme tranquility; because of that, one attains the perfection of great tranquility;
because of that, one attains the perfection of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); because of that, one attains the perfection of acting as a refuge for all sentient beings;
because of that, one attains the perfection of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*); and because of that, one attains the world...
Because they are fully endowed with supramundane dharmas; because they attain the full endowment of the dwelling place of all dharmas;
because they attain the full endowment of knowing supramundane dharmas through skillful means; because they attain the full endowment of skillfully penetrating all dharmas;
and because they attain the full endowment of skillfully knowing the characteristics of phenomena regarding the past limit and the future limit.
...then one attains the perfection of skillful adornment of words, phrases, and meanings; then one attains the perfection of wisdom;
then one attains the perfection of subtle supernormal powers; then one attains the perfection of skillfully transforming the mind;
then one attains the perfection of skillfully instructing others; then one attains [the perfection] for the sake of other sentient beings and...

Because he is endowed with the power of superiority over persons—whether white or black, high or low, full or deficient, increasing or decreasing—he then attains the perfection of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*);
because he is endowed with this, he then attains the perfection of the orientation toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) which has not yet been realized;
because he is endowed with this, he then attains the perfection of right practice (*samyak-pratipatti*); because he is endowed with this, he then attains the perfection of intention (*āśaya*).
Because of being complete in feet, one attains mastery; because of being complete, one attains the perfection of supernormal powers;
because of being complete, one attains the perfection of a noble and eminent family; because of being complete, one attains the perfection of a great lineage;

because of being complete, one attains the perfection of physical beauty; because of being complete, one attains the perfection of great majesty; because of being complete, one attains the perfection of great radiance.
Therefore, one attains the perfection of all meritorious qualities; therefore, one attains the perfection of great merit;
therefore, one attains the perfection of being a Great Man like a bull-king; therefore, one attains the perfection of a voice that causes others to rejoice;
therefore, one attains the perfection of a voice that causes others deep joy; and therefore, one attains the perfection of a subtle and wondrous voice.
Because they are complete, one attains the perfection of the Brahma-voice; because they are complete, one attains the perfection of appropriate eloquence;
because they are complete, one attains the perfection of non-contentious eloquence; because they are complete, one attains the perfection of unattached eloquence;
because they are complete, one attains the perfection of eloquence that accords with reality; and because they are complete, one attains the perfection of manifold eloquence.
...then one will attain the perfection of eloquence in all speech and sounds;

then one will attain the perfection of never being separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout one's births, and always reverently making offerings to them; then one will attain the perfection of being free from birth in the borderlands;
then one will attain the perfection of always being born in the central lands; and then one will attain the ability to travel extensively through all worlds.
Because one has fully accomplished the worship, service, and consultation with all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones;
because one has fully accomplished immeasurable and boundless merit; because one has fully accomplished the adornments of all bodhisattva merits;
and even because one has fully accomplished the adornment of the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse,
saying: "Aśūnyadarśin!..."
Any bodhisattva who is able to practice this Will behold all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
They shall immediately and swiftly attain the various supernormal powers, And by means of these, they shall further behold pure lands,
Thereby being able to take birth in a wondrously perfect manner, And likewise be perfectly endowed at the time of entering the womb.

When dwelling in the womb, there is no peer; born of a most pure and noble family, fully endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence—one should likewise cultivate those various dharmas of practice.
Having left home to renounce worldly desires, abandoning both human and celestial cravings, he seeks enlightenment for the sake of the world;
wherever he is born, there shall always be the nectar of immortality.
They also attain the various supernormal powers and the bases of psychic power, and they turn the wheel of wisdom to perfect that world;
these people of great virtue, possessing vast learning and dhāraṇī, perform their practices by means of this ocean of much hearing.
He presides over the great assembly with clear understanding of their meaning;
skillfully knowing the expedient teachings for sentient beings, he fully understands the spheres of practice of all dharmas, both mundane and supramundane.
The wise possess the perfection of knowledge; they remain far removed from all karma and the afflictions of delusion.
Having relinquished all conditioned phenomena, they constantly draw near to the unconditioned.
He constantly observes sentient beings with the divine eye, and further listens to the Dharma with the divine ear;
clearly knowing his past lives, he skillfully understands the thoughts of others.
Wandering with mastery through supernatural transformations, their minds skillfully turn according to causes;
attaining great renown as they travel through Buddha-lands, they are able to extensively benefit all worlds.
Clearly understanding what is possible and what is impossible, there is no phenomenon he does not know;
deeply illuminating both pure dharmas and defilements, he constantly cultivates the supreme samādhi.
Those who are able to attain the perfection of right practice, their wisdom is truly peerless;
possessing right reflection and great majestic power, they likewise abide securely in right cultivation.
Furthermore, they are born into great families and noble lineages; their appearance is dignified and upright, bringing joy to all who behold them.
Although they dwell amidst conditioned existence, the merit they have cultivated cannot be destroyed.

In every birth they constantly receive great merit; Coming and going, they often become kings among men, Or serve as Śakra, the Honored One of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, And at times become gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven or Brahmā Lords.
Every sound you utter is peerless: the sublime resonance of Brahmā, the lion’s roar, the beautiful voices of all dragons throughout their range, the great merit-sound of the bull-king’s bellow;
it encompasses the strains of stringed instruments and song, as exquisite and refined as the voice of the kalaviṅka bird.
Able to harmonize principles and meanings to bring joy to the multitude, it is because they have attained samādhi that this is so.
They produce refined, pure, and beautiful sounds; using many words of affection, they gladden all beings.
With deep, elegant, and wondrous tones, as well as skillful speech, their voices are ever-present and never cease.
His gait and movements are like those of a dragon king; He universally emits flashes of lightning that illuminate all things;
He sends down rain that saturates the great earth— This is called the merit of the dragon, difficult to measure.
In such places where these dragon-like humans roam, dwelling in this sublime samādhi and superior supernormal powers,
they manifest immeasurable and innumerable transformation bodies, making equal offerings before all Buddhas.
Verses, stanzas, parables, and various compositions, With elegant and correct phrasing and well-ordered principles— He constantly bestows such Dharma-joy upon sentient beings;
Because he has attained this supreme concentration, he is unimpeded.
Those born shall never be apart from the Buddhas, And shall likewise behold the Bodhisattvas and the Noble Sangha;
Constantly dwelling in places of benefit free from hardship, They shall accomplish samādhi that illumines the ten directions.
Desiring to consult with all Buddhas everywhere, or to be born in immeasurable,
inconceivable lands to manifest before and make offerings to all Buddhas— such is the accomplishment of samādhi.
Such merits are ineffable, transcending the realm of numbers and beyond all measure;
they arise eternally together with the perfect awakening at the tree of enlightenment—this is the meditative concentration praised by all Buddhas.

Chapter Ten: Right Contemplation, from the *Bodhisattva-nianfo-sanmei-fen* (The Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha). At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to achieve the Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi as taught by all the Buddhas, what dharmas should those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas approach and practice in order to be able to achieve this contemplative samādhi?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, saying: "Amoghadarśin!

If any Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas wish to achieve the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) taught by all Buddhas; wish to constantly behold all Buddhas, serve and make offerings to those World-Honored Ones; and wish to swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), they should abide in right mindfulness and remain far removed from deviant thoughts. They should sever the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) and contemplate non-self (anātman). They should contemplate this body as being like a mass of foam on water; they should contemplate this form (rūpa) as being as hollow as a plantain tree; they should contemplate this sensation (vedanā) as being like a bubble on the water; they should contemplate this perception (saṃjñā) as being like a mirage in the heat; they should contemplate these formations (saṃskāra) as being like clouds in the sky; and they should contemplate this consciousness (vijñāna) as being like a reflection in a mirror."

"If a bodhisattva wishes to enter this samādhi, they should conceive a sense of profound dread; they should mindfully remain far removed from censure and avoid being rebuked by others; they should mindfully eliminate shamelessness and lack of remorse while accomplishing shame and remorse; they should accomplish śamatha and vipaśyanā; they should remain far removed from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;
they should always maintain single-minded diligence and valor, eliminate indolence, and give rise to a vast mind."

Constantly mindfully observe the three gates of liberation; constantly mindfully give rise to the three kinds of right knowledge; constantly mindfully sever the three unwholesome roots; constantly mindfully accomplish the collection of all samādhis; constantly mindfully bring all sentient beings to fulfillment; and constantly mindfully preach the Dharma equally for all sentient beings.

One should contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness—namely, the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena—and one should reflect upon the defects of the four kinds of nutriment, namely, edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness; therein, one should cultivate the perception of impurity regarding these nutriments.

One should mindfully contemplate the four immeasurables—namely, cultivating great loving-kindness, practicing great compassion, abiding in great sympathetic joy, and being endowed with great equanimity—and one should mindfully contemplate the accomplishment of the various dhyānas without becoming attached to their flavor.
Furthermore, one should contemplate all phenomena and constantly keep in mind:
"I shall not begrudge my body nor preserve my life; I will relinquish both body and mind to embrace extensive learning."

Reflecting on such dharmas, one should protect them accordingly; one must not disparage the wealth of the Dharma of extensive learning, but should receive and uphold the teachings as they were heard according to their true meaning, giving rise to a heart of reverence toward all Buddhas.

"Furthermore, one should give rise to a sense of reverent respect toward the Dharma and the Saṃgha; associate with virtuous spiritual friends and distance oneself from evil companions; eliminate worldly and meaningless speech; remain unattached to worldly pleasures and not abandon secluded dwellings."
"Dwelling in all things, one gives rise to a mind of equanimity; toward all sentient beings, one has no sense of retreating or sinking, no mind of harm, and no envy or jealousy;
regarding all phenomena, one gives rise to a mind of discernment, commits no evil, and remains free from mental defilement, for no phenomenon can be found to have a fixed location."
Constantly seek out the most profound and vast sūtras; therein, always give rise to superior faith, and do not harbor suspicion or entertain divergent thoughts.
Such sūtras are supreme and expansive; you should constantly recite, uphold, and contemplate their exposition.
Why is this? Because this is the path and Dharma of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, which alone is capable of generating the Bodhi of the Buddhas.

"In future ages, you shall attain the immeasurable merits of those Buddhas; you should proclaim this Dharma for others according to the Law. Subdue arrogance, do not disturb right hearing, and revere, respect, and make offerings to this Dharma. Abandon all desires and seekings, cease all strife and contention, eliminate sleepiness, extinguish the net of doubt, eradicate delusion, and clearly recognize the view of self. Do not engage in frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), and stay far away from the Nirgranthas, those of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), those who live by their own means, and the proponents of the *Cārvāka* and *Pāṣaṇḍa* doctrines."

"One should always dwell well within the dānapāramitā, fulfill the śīlapāramitā, constantly mind the kṣāntipāramitā, not abandon the vīryapāramitā, sport in the dhyānapāramitā, and be fully endowed with the prajñāpāramitā, relinquishing body and life without a heart of attachment."

"Just as the nature of the four great elements cannot be altered, so too should one give rise to a mind of equanimity toward the earth element, and likewise toward the water, fire, and wind elements."

“He has perfected his physical actions and is diligent in mind; he has no fear for his livelihood, nor does he crave robes, food, medicinal requisites, bedding, dwellings, halls, or any material possessions. He delights in practicing the dhūta ascetic virtues and always abides in contentment; he seeks neither gain nor profit, nor does he pursue fame, for all attachments have been extinguished without remainder.”

"Contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness, sever the four inversions, do not dwell on the thorns of evil, forever cross over the four floods, cultivate the four bases of psychic power, and abide in the four modes of deportment."

One should possess the five faculties and further increase the five powers; one should extinguish the five hindrances, not employ the five passions, remain far removed from the five turbidities, and achieve the five liberations. Thus one attains entry into internal self-reflection upon the vast noble wisdom and correctly contemplates the five aggregates.

Not engaging with the six sense objects, subduing the six sense faculties, extinguishing the six consciousnesses, severing the six feelings, eliminating the six cravings, practicing the six foundations of mindfulness and the six factors of wisdom, one constantly seeks benefit within the six supernormal powers.

By cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, one penetrates the seven elements—the element of harming, the element of malice, the element of renunciation, the element of desire, the element of form, the element of formlessness, and the element of cessation—thereby eliminating the seven underlying tendencies and the seven stations of consciousness.

One should abandon the eight forms of indolence, eliminate the eight kinds of false speech, clearly understand the causes of the eight worldly dharmas, attain the eight types of noble awakening, realize the eight liberations, and cultivate the eightfold noble path.

One should draw near to, contemplate, extensively analyze, and single-mindedly cultivate the removal of the nine abodes of sentient beings; extinguish the nine kinds of pride; abandon the nine afflictions; constantly reflect upon the nine kinds of joyful dharmas; and draw near to and practice the nine successive meditative attainments.
He never thinks of committing the ten kinds of evil deeds, but diligently practices the ten paths of wholesome action and constantly seeks the wisdom of the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
“Aśūnyadarśin!
I shall now briefly explain for you the various great benefits to be obtained from this Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha:
if there is a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who should practice and study this Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, practicing in this manner is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness;

one who contemplates this will not regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, shall fulfill all those Buddha-dharmas, and will even be able to act as a great refuge for all sentient beings, causing them to achieve the unsurpassed knowledge of all modes (anuttara-sarvajñā).
"Aśūnyadarśin! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess great wisdom, they are able to contemplate;
this is not something that śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can observe."

"Aśūnyadarśin! If a person, with regard to this Buddha-remembrance samādhi, at any time draws near to it, contemplates it, practices it, or upholds it, or recites it, or writes it down, or teaches others to write it down, or teaches others to recite, uphold, and study it, or even develops it slightly."

Whether one explains it or is able to proclaim it extensively, although they may experience hardship and fatigue for a short time, what they have done will never be in vain; they will certainly obtain the fruit of their reward and attain great benefit.
