"Aśūnyadarśin! Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas uphold the Dharma for the sake of others, they will swiftly attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will certainly become buddhas in a future world."

"Aśūnyadarśin! You should know that this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* comprehensively encompasses all dharmas; therefore, it is not within the realm of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"If there are people who hear this teaching even for a moment, they shall certainly attain Buddhahood in the future; of this there is no doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If a person wishes to cultivate this samādhi, They will be able to keep all Tathāgatas in mind."
Having contemplated this Dharma-gate, one should distance oneself from all that is contrary to the Dharma;
one should also distance oneself from shamelessness and lack of remorse, and destroy both the views of nihilism and eternalism.
Furthermore, one should abide in the three gates of emptiness and mindfully cultivate the wisdom of liberation with diligence.
Having uprooted the three unwholesome roots, one should likewise contemplate the three wholesome foundations;
if one knows how to observe the three bases of feeling, attaining this sublime concentration will not be difficult.
If a person seeks the supreme samādhi, they should first maintain the precepts and subsequently cultivate wisdom;
naturally they will remain far removed from all false views, as well as from frivolous discourse and idle talk.
They should sequentially contemplate that all sensations are suffering, and thereafter observe the mind of arising and ceasing.
When a person contemplates samādhi, they should deeply reflect upon supramundane matters;
once all doubts regarding all phenomena are entirely eliminated, attaining this samādhi will be exceedingly easy.
One should also be well-versed in the four foundations of mindfulness;

first, one should contemplate that the body does not abide even for a moment, constantly seeking liberation and meditative concentration. If one does not cherish life, how could one begrudge the body?
One should not, on account of extensive learning, treat others with contempt; how could one ever slander the True Dharma?
Having heard the True Dharma, one should be able to contemplate it, upholding what one recites day and night.
One should revere all Buddhas and deeply honor the Dharma, serving the Sangha community without daring to be disrespectful.
One should always be mindful of the kindness of virtuous friends, stay far away from all evil companions,
and never sit or rise together with wicked people, except when they are preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly.
For the sake of seeking supreme enlightenment, never abandon the *āraṇya*;
all sentient beings are equal, so do not make distinctions among phenomena.

Seeking the true limit of reality of those dharmas, with a mind unattached amidst the characteristics of all phenomena, one can completely eliminate all thoughts of contempt; before long, one will surely attain this samādhi.
Clearly recognize the view of self and doubt, and likewise remain vigilant against all frivolity;
do not give rise to thoughts of evil desire, and you should extinguish strife and sloth.
If one does not study the teachings of those external paths, all such frivolous disputations will naturally vanish;
by simply being able to accord with the words of the Buddha’s Dharma, one may obtain this samādhi in an instant.
Constantly practicing generosity, as well as ethical discipline and patience, Vigorously exerting effort without weariness,
Always abiding in meditative concentration and wisdom, One naturally attains the practice of this samādhi.
One who can give away their head and eyes without attachment or fear, and who never hesitates to relinquish other possessions,
will proceed toward enlightenment without hardship and shall also swiftly attain this tranquil meditative concentration.
If one can maintain the mind like the great earth, And likewise like water, fire, and wind,
Furthermore equal to space, without limit or shore, That person will swiftly attain this meditative concentration.
If one possesses sincerity of body, speech, and mind, and does not covet food, clothing, or wealth,
being free from any desire for material requisites, one can thus cultivate and realize this samādhi.
One should always maintain focused mindfulness of the four right efforts, And likewise accomplish those bases of spiritual power.
One must swiftly distance oneself from perverted conceptions, First severing the thorns of the afflictions.
One should contemplate blocking the rivers of the four floods, And consider drying up all thirst and craving.
Fully endowed with the five faculties and the five powers, Tearing asunder and destroying the garment of the five hindrances,
Not harboring the five kinds of sensual desires, One should likewise abandon the delusions and deceptions within the mind.
Furthermore, one should aspire to seek the five liberations, contemplate the samādhi of the five bodies,
and swiftly observe and understand the locus of the five aggregates.
One should distance oneself from those who are not respectful and prudent, and likewise diminish the six bases of contact.
One correctly contemplates the mind within the six bases of sensation, Constantly mindful of severing the six kinds of craving;
Furthermore, one accomplishes the world through the six supernormal powers, And also cultivates the six recollections along with clear knowledge.
Diligently seek the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven noble riches; one must certainly abandon those states of doubt and uncertainty.
If one desires to attain samādhi constantly in this manner, one will gradually disperse and extinguish all afflictions, remaining forever far removed from the seven stations of consciousness.
These eight perversions shall likewise be uprooted; if one can abide in the Eightfold Noble Path, one will surely and swiftly realize this profound concentration.

Constantly abiding in the practices of the eight great beings, and further delighting the mind with the eight liberations, unstained by the eight worldly dharmas and detached from the world, the attainment of supreme wisdom will not be far off.
Free from ill will toward others, one should first eliminate these nine kinds of pride;
by contemplating the nine dharmas that are the roots of joy, one attains those nine successive stages of dhyāna.
Cut off these ten unwholesome causes of evil; One should cultivate the ten kinds of goodness of the wise.
If one can practice these ten powers, Attaining this samādhi will ultimately be without difficulty.
One should mindfully uphold all wholesome dharmas and relinquish unwholesome conditions for various evils;
by diligently seeking that right mindfulness before and after [practice], how could it take long to realize this samādhi?
Once one has dwelled in such a samādhi, One shall turn the inconceivable power of wisdom,
Universally beholding the golden bodies of all Buddhas, And wherever one is born, shall always hear the True Dharma.
If you wish to see those World-Honored Ones— those who have already entered parinirvāṇa, those currently present,
and all those compassionate ones of the future— you should contemplate this supreme samādhi.

Chapter Eleven: Contemplating Samādhi. Part One of the Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to accomplish the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) taught by all Buddhas, how should they contemplate so as to attain stable abiding?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, saying: “Amoghadarśin!

If any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to accomplish this samādhi, they should first maintain right mindfulness of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past; next, they should mindfully contemplate all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the present; and finally, they should mindfully contemplate all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future.”
He thus reflects that all these Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpannas, Sugatas, Lokavidas, Anuttaras,

Puruṣadamyasārathis, Śāstṛs of gods and humans, Buddhas, and World-Honored Ones throughout the worlds of the ten directions and the three periods of time have descended from heaven and attained [enlightenment].
Namely: the perfection of entering the womb, the perfection of abiding in the womb, the perfection of emerging from the womb, the perfection of renouncing the world,
the perfection of all virtues, the perfection of the faculties, the perfection of the primary marks, the perfection of the secondary characteristics, the perfection of adornments,
the perfection of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
The accomplishment of [the fruits], the accomplishment of liberation, the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the accomplishment of the four fearlessnesses and great compassion,
the accomplishment of joy and equanimity, the accomplishment of shame and remorse, the accomplishment of dignified deportment, the accomplishment of all practices,
the accomplishment of śamatha, the accomplishment of vipaśyanā, and the accomplishment of clear knowledge and liberation.
Furthermore, there is the accomplishment of the gates of liberation, the accomplishment of the four foundations of mindfulness,
the accomplishment of the four right efforts, the accomplishment of the four bases of power, the accomplishment of the five faculties, the accomplishment of the five powers,
the accomplishment of the factors of enlightenment, the accomplishment of the noble eightfold path, the accomplishment of past causes and conditions, and the accomplishment of the twin miracles.
The accomplishment of the various teachings, the accomplishment of the great universal teachings, the accomplishment of the aggregate of ethical discipline,
the accomplishment of all samādhis, the accomplishment of unimpeded benefit,
the accomplishment of unimpeded benefit for others, the accomplishment of all wholesome dharmas, the accomplishment of pure form, and the accomplishment of a pure mind.
“...the accomplishment of pure wisdom, the accomplishment of the sense bases, and the accomplishment of a golden body endowed with a hundred merits.
At that time, having contemplated such marks of the Tathāgatas, that bodhisattva should further constantly reflect:
‘Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have minds free from agitation and should likewise abide in a mind of non-attachment.’”
Once the mind is free from attachment, he should further reflect in this way:
"In this context, what is called 'Tathāgata'?
Is it that form itself which is the Tathāgata?"
Is it that the Tathāgata is apart from form?
If one takes the dharma of form to be the Tathāgata, then since all sentient beings possess the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), all sentient beings would be Tathāgatas.
If one takes that which is apart from form to be the Tathāgata, then being apart from form is a dharma without causes or conditions; how can a dharma without causes or conditions be the Tathāgata?
"Having thus contemplated and understood form, the Bodhisattva next contemplates sensation (*vedanā*).
At that time, he further reflects:
'Is it precisely this sensation that is the Tathāgata?'"
Is it that the Tathāgata is apart from sensation?
If the Dharma of sensation itself were the Tathāgata, then since all sentient beings possess the aggregate of sensation, all sentient beings would be Tathāgatas.

If the Tathāgata were apart from the Dharma of sensation, then being apart from sensation would constitute a dharma without causes and conditions; how could such a dharma without conditions be the Tathāgata?
"Having thus observed form and sensation, and so on up to observing consciousness in the same way,
that bodhisattva further reflects:
'If these aggregates are not the Tathāgata, could those sense faculties possibly be the Tathāgata?'"
Having reflected thus, he first contemplates the eye:
"Is the Tathāgata the eye itself?
Or is the Tathāgata apart from the eye?"
If that very eye were the Tathāgata, then all sentient beings possess this eye, and thus all sentient beings would be the Tathāgata.
If the Tathāgata were apart from that eye, then being apart from the eye would constitute a non-conditioned dharma; how could that which is not a conditioned dharma be the Tathāgata?
“Having thus observed the eye, the Bodhisattva observes the ear, the nose, and so on, up to the mind, observing them in the same way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflects:
‘If there is no Tathāgata within these sense faculties, could there perhaps be a Tathāgata within those great elements?’”
Having reflected thus, he first contemplates the earth element:
"Is the Tathāgata identical to the earth element,
or is the Tathāgata distinct from the earth element?"
If the earth element itself were the Tathāgata, then since all internal and external phenomena belong to the earth, the earth element would thus be the Tathāgata.

If the Tathāgata were something apart from the earth element, then being apart from the earth would constitute a phenomenon without causes and conditions; how could such a phenomenon without conditions be the Tathāgata?
“Having thus observed the earth element, he likewise observes the water, fire, and wind elements in the same manner.
When that bodhisattva is able to engage in such right reflection, he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of form, nor does he observe the Tathāgata apart from form;

likewise, he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of feeling, nor apart from feeling; he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of perception, nor apart from perception; and so on, up to: he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of consciousness, nor apart from consciousness.”
"Furthermore, when he contemplates, he does not observe the Tathāgata with the eye, nor does he observe the Tathāgata apart from the eye;

likewise, he does not [observe] with the ear, nor apart from the ear; he does not [observe] with the nose, nor apart from the nose; and so on, up to: he does not observe the Tathāgata with the body or the mind, nor apart from the body or the mind—it is also thus."
Furthermore, when he contemplates, he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of form, nor does he observe the Tathāgata apart from form;

likewise, he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of form nor apart from form, nor by means of sound nor apart from sound, and so on, up to: he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of tangibles or mental phenomena (*dharmas*), nor apart from tangibles or mental phenomena—it is also thus.
Furthermore, when he contemplates, he does not observe the Tathāgata by means of earth, nor does he observe the Tathāgata apart from earth;
likewise, it is the same for water—not observing by means of water nor apart from water—and so on up to wind—not observing the Tathāgata by means of wind nor apart from wind.
"When that bodhisattva contemplates in this way, he is able to thoroughly penetrate and understand all those phenomena, clearly comprehending them without obstruction.
At that time, that bodhisattva should further reflect thus:
'In this regard, by what further true dharma can one attain that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?'"
Is bodhi attained by means of the body, or is it attained by means of the mind?

If it were attained by the body, then this present body is without sensation, without consciousness, dull, ignorant, and insentient—just like grass, trees, stones, or walls. Yet that bodhi is neither form nor body; it is not a conditioned formation, nor is it an attainment; it cannot be seen or heard, nor can it be touched or realized through contact.
This body is thus; how can it achieve the realization of bodhi?

If it were achieved by the mind, then this very mind is fundamentally formless and without characteristics; it cannot be seen or heard, cannot be touched or realized, and cannot be grasped, being like a magical illusion.
Bodhi is likewise: it possesses no mind and no sensory encounter; it cannot be seen or heard, and cannot be known or realized.
"If this mind is thus, how can it achieve the realization of bodhi? "Anavatapta!
This is what is meant by a Bodhisattva’s correct mindfulness and reflection: that one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* neither by means of body and mind, nor apart from body and mind."
The Buddha said:
“Aśūnyadarśin! That bodhisattva should always observe and contemplate in this manner.”
When one can contemplate all phenomena in this manner, one immediately comes to abide securely within the True Dharma; the mind becomes immutable and immovable.

It should be known that at such a time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva fulfills the dharmas of a Bodhisattva, naturally distances himself from unwholesome reflections, and swiftly accomplishes the true Dharma-realm of the equality of the perfectly awakened Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored Ones of the past and future, And all the All-Seeing Ones of the present—
By quieting the mind in empty stillness and practicing loving-kindness, One desires to behold the Buddhas without difficulty."
The great majestic radiance of the Buddhas of the past, Out of compassion for the world, bestowed equal happiness;
They are mindful of those among men who are like the white lotus, The Taming Men of Perfected Virtue.
Furthermore, by recollecting his descent into birth, his entry into the womb, his dwelling therein, and the excellence of his noble mother— all these being fully complete—
and by contemplating the various wondrous signs of that birth-family, it shall not be difficult to behold the Equally Awakened One.
He also contemplates their various excellent and sublime adornments, as well as their original vows and former practices;
the subtle words and wondrous meanings of their teachings in the beginning, middle, and end—all these belong to the Sugata’s body of liberation.
Abiding in the gates of liberation and making offerings, With right exertion and those four bases of power, One should attend to the faculties that are fully perfected;
The powers and the factors of enlightenment are likewise so.
If one contemplates the Buddhas, the Honored Ones of Liberation, before long one shall reach the supreme state of tranquility;
with thoughts for the benefit of all the world, the merit of their wholesome qualities is difficult to fathom.
With exquisite form and a pure mind, one further contemplates the World-Honored One’s various marks of excellence;
with a vajra-body and the signs of a hundred merits, one should know that the Tathāgata’s every thought is fulfilled.
How can one be named a Tathāgata within the Dharma?
It is precisely by observing the sphere of infinite space.
The Buddhas are neither form nor sensation; they are neither perception, mental formations, nor consciousness.
Such dharmas as these are not the Tathāgata; a person of right view and wisdom should also realize this.
Nor are the Buddhas apart from them; the "Arhat" and "Sugata" are but names.
The Buddhas are not the eye, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, nor the dharmas and so forth.
Nor is the Tathāgata apart from them; the adornment of perfect awakening is merely a name.
There is only the great name, but no true Buddha; apart from the name, where could there be a reality?
If a wise person knows that all things are but a combination of conditions, then attaining perfect enlightenment will not be difficult.

If one were to take the aggregates (skandhas) as the Tathāgata, then since all sentient beings possess these aggregates, all sentient beings would be Buddhas; for the aggregates are equal and shared by all.
One does not take form and so forth as the Buddhas, nor is the Tathāgata named apart from the aggregates;
through correct contemplation over immeasurable kalpas, inconceivable wisdom is finally accomplished.
The body is like grass, wood, and stone walls; bodhi is formless, quiescent, and without arising.
There is neither a rigid body nor grass and wood—how can one speak of realizing bodhi with the body?
This mind is signless and formless; awakening is neither mind nor has it any shape.
It can be realized through that which is neither body nor mind, yet it is not a non-realization—difficult to conceive.
This is the most supreme state of tranquility, wherein all non-Buddhists are utterly bewildered.
If one seeks right diligence in this Dharma, One shall surely and swiftly attain this samādhi.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi Section, Scroll Seven.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi.
The Eighth Fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
The Remainder of the Chapter on the Contemplation of Samādhi. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva realize and know the relinquishing of the view of self?
The Buddha said:
"Aśūnyadarśin! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain realization and knowledge, they are free from dwelling and attachment, thereby departing from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
In this way, although the bodhisattva is without dwelling or attachment, he is able to bring great benefit to all the beings in the world, including devas and humans."
"What is meant by 'benefiting'?

It refers to being a great illumination of the Dharma, lighting the great torch of the Dharma, blowing the great conch of the Dharma, beating the great drum of the Dharma, sounding the great kettledrum of the Dharma, boarding the great ship of the Dharma, and establishing the great bridge of the Dharma."

Now, as you wish to ferry all sentient beings across the torrential river of the four flows of birth and death and establish them on the unconditioned shore of nirvāṇa, you should immediately contemplate the fundamental nature of this body.
"Next, one should contemplate the impurity of the body:
it is foul and filthy, putrid and decaying, overflowing with boils, pus, excrement, and urine.
This body is impermanent; it does not remain still for even a moment."
It is subject to decay and withering, incapable of lasting long;
it deceives the childish, being precarious, fragile, and unsubstantial.
It is like a mass of froth on water, filled with maggots, where sinews and bones support one another as it moves along empty and burdened, serving no practical purpose.
Whether for a hundred years, a hundred thousand years, or even eighty thousand kalpas, though one may protect and nurture it with every kind of pleasure, it ultimately ends in decay and destruction.

Throughout this long night, this body is never free from afflictions nor does it emerge from perversion; it is constantly devoured by various evil birds and beasts, and it always travels together with those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. Coming and going through birth and death, it undergoes all manner of suffering and distress, or serves as a slave to perform various painful tasks. Constantly bound to others, it lacks autonomy; how, then, could that which is thus produced perceive suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path?
"Now this body of mine is merely empty, deceptive, and delusive; not a single dharma within it is solid.
For this reason, I should now take all these parts of my body and give them as a gift to all sentient beings:
if there are sentient beings who cherish their own bodies as precious, I shall for their sake relinquish both body and life."
If there are sentient beings who require my vital essence, I shall bestow that vital essence upon them;
if there are sentient beings who require my flesh, I shall offer my flesh to them.
Why is this? It would be better for me to give first so that they may obtain food, rather than withholding my gift and allowing them to eat on their own.
Now, by the roots of merit obtained through this pure-hearted giving, I vow to immediately eradicate the root of the view of self.
When that bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, he does not cling to the view of a self;

having extinguished the view of a self, he subsequently relinquishes his body for sentient beings to use—giving up his life-force for those who cherish their lives, bestowing vital energy upon those who require it, offering his flesh to those who need meat, and if there are sentient beings who require his labor, he immediately becomes a slave to serve their every command.

"Aśūnyadarśin! For these reasons, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abandon the view of self, do not abide in the view of self, and realize the nature of the view of self; thus, they are able to seek a firm body within this that is not firm."
“Āśūnyadarśin! It is like this:
suppose in a capital city, a town, or a village, many young boys or many young girls go out from their own homes to the riverbank and see a mass of water-foam.
They play with that foam together—namely, by breaking it apart, dividing it, and grinding it away until it is dispersed and nothing remains—and yet that mass of foam does not think:”
"Who can disperse me today?
Even though this froth is destroyed, it has no mind of resentment or anger.
"Emptiness-Seer! [This is how it is]."

In this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates his own body as impermanent and subject to destruction—like that mass of foam which cannot endure for long—one should know that such a person has attained this samādhi and will swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one can remain far removed from the view of self, There will be no place of dwelling or attachment whatsoever.
For the benefit of the world’s devas and humans, One shall realize the Great Bodhi so difficult to see."
If one grows weary of the body’s impurities—this seat of ulcers where pus and blood flow;
this body that decays and lacks solidity, impermanent, frail, and subject to destruction.
Abiding but briefly like an illusion, lacking any substantial reality; Like a mass of foam, empty and without truth;
Rearing it through the long night brings no ultimate benefit; That birds and dogs may devour it is most loathsome.
Though one provides for it with all manner of requisites, this body will inevitably meet with decay and destruction;
since one cannot attain a stable dharma, there is only suffering throughout immeasurable kalpas.
The sufferings of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts—hunger, thirst, and manifold afflictions—are ever ablaze;
the world’s urgent pressures exceed a hundred *rāva* hells, yet from the very beginning, one does not perceive them as they truly are.
Today my body is of its own accord empty and void; this impermanent form changes in an instant.
To all those sentient beings who eat meat, I am willing to serve as their vital essence and their servant.
I thought at that time, constantly speaking these words:
"Should there be those who wish to eat my flesh, or my vital essence and blood, for their sake I now relinquish them; let them freely devour this body of mine."
May all those with jewel-like bodies behold me relinquish this life;
I now dare not cherish my own body or life, wishing only to swiftly accomplish that samādhi.
Just as those bubbles are constantly breaking apart, I have never once given rise to a heart of anger or resentment;
now this body of mine is like a mass of foam—how could there be any occasion for the arising of hatred or enmity?
If one can contemplate the body as being like foam upon water, this person will certainly seek bodhi;
not only will they be able to serve the Honored Ones of the ten directions, but they shall also swiftly attain the supreme samādhi.

Chapter Twelve: Manifesting a Smile, from the *Bodhisattva-nien-fo-san-mei-fen* (The Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha). At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with serene composure.

Because such is the nature of the Dharma of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, at the moment of his smile, the World-Honored One emitted various rays of light from his mouth—namely blue, yellow, red, white, golden, and crystal-colored. These lights shone afar, ascending as high as the Brahma palace before returning downward, circling three times to the right and entering the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having witnessed this event, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed him in verse:
"The Most Victorious World-Honored One does not smile without cause; That you now manifest a smile must surely have a reason.
O Tamer of the World, you should explain it; For what cause and condition do you smile once more?"
With a vajra-colored body and a form of a hundred merits, you benefit all through the realization of suchness;
as the refuge for the entire world, what is the cause of this smile?
The World-Honored One is unsurpassed and peerless; where could there be anyone who might surpass him?
His merits are fully perfected and beyond reproach; for what reason does he now manifest this smile?
All the worlds turn toward You; O Tamer of Men, please now proclaim:
who today has attained great benefit, that the World-Honored One smiles without cause?
Who today shall receive the great throne?
Who today attains the true mass of merit?
Who today becomes the King of Peace and Security?
The World-Honored One is able to bring about this smile;
you who are the refuge for all the world, Great Teacher of gods and humans, should now speak.
If the Honored Buddha utters this wondrous sound, gods and humans will rejoice and the assembly of sages will offer praise.
After the Venerable Ānanda had posed this question, the Blessed One said to Ānanda: “Ānanda!

While I was explaining the meaning of this Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Right Mindfulness, thirty thousand people within this great assembly were distanced from dust and defilement and attained the pure Dharma-eye.”
Furthermore, eighty trillion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devaputras distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye;
furthermore, thirty thousand bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs attained the fruit of anāgāmin;
furthermore, thirty thousand bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās attained the dharma of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).

Furthermore, thirty thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; all of these shall attain equal and perfect enlightenment during the Star Constellation Eon (*tārakā-kalpa*), and they are precisely those who previously resolved their minds upon bodhicitta.

Additionally, there were ninety trillion nayutas of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwelt securely in bodhi without regression; all of these shall become Buddhas in the future. Those World-Honored Ones will have four kinds of titles:

some shall be titled "Radiance" (*Prabhāsa*), some "Vairocana," some "Śākyamuni," and some "Sun, Moon, and Jupiter"; such various names and titles as these shall appear in the world according to their respective buddha-fields.

Furthermore, there are ninety-two billion, one hundred thousand nayutas of sentient beings who have merely resolved their minds toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas; these individuals shall all realize the fruit of the śrāvaka in the future.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having known this matter, observed the ten directions with his pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans. Seeing ninety billion, one hundred thousand nayutas of Buddha-worlds, and because he was to perform such great benefit for them, he further uttered a sublime, vast, and wondrous sound that pervaded this trichiliocosm. Once all had heard it, the sound then reached all the sentient beings within those various Buddha-lands as well, so that they too heard it.

Thereafter, from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, he again emitted a great light named "Boundless Majesty. This light shone universally throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, causing immeasurable billions of nayutas of sentient beings to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*.

Furthermore, there were even more sentient beings than that number who resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they shall all in the future attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and subsequently, in those lands of the ten directions, they shall all achieve Buddhahood, appearing in the world with the title of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Durdharṣa (Invincible).
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Exceeding hundreds of thousands in number, without any reduction, The three types, thirty, and again ninety—
All such as these see Bodhi, For the sake of benefiting those who have resolved their minds."
Those ten thousand beings, as well as thirty thousand who had attained wisdom and pure vision, having heard this, contemplated the Perfectly Enlightened One correctly;
they were liberated from human existence and the various evil realms.
Furthermore, over eight hundred million nayutas of devas obtained the noble, pure eye.
Because they have heard the Tathāgata’s wondrous voice, The evil realms are forever extinguished without remainder;
They attain patience through thirty trillion *yojanas*, And upon generating the resolve for enlightenment, they immediately leave the three evil paths behind.
These beings shall all become Buddhas in the future, Just like the flourishing vegetation in the height of spring.
Furthermore, thirty trillion sentient beings rose from their seats and gave rise to the Great Mind;
by this majestic power they shall attain Buddhahood and benefit the world upon the great earth.
Additionally, sixty thousand sons of the gods all resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
They are all equal to the Honored One Maitreya, Having cultivated the causes of happiness, they shall realize the state of bliss.
For this reason and by these conditions, the Teacher of Gods and Humans Smiled for the sake of this vast matter;
I have now proclaimed the meaning of his smile— Ānanda, you should know the cause of this smile.

Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Supernatural Powers (Abhijñā), Part One of the Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

How should one know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having dwelled in a sense of shame and dread of blame and having distanced themselves from that lack of shame and dread of blame, will then attain this samādhi?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, saying: “Amoghadarśin!

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who constantly practices a sense of shame and remorse, yet while practicing such shame and remorse, this bodhisattva might still commit various kinds of evil deeds—namely:”

When engaging in misconduct of body, one immediately gives rise to shame and remorse; when engaging in misconduct of speech, one likewise gives rise to shame and remorse; when engaging in misconduct of mind, one likewise gives rise to shame and remorse. One gives rise to shame and remorse when giving rise to a jealous mind; one gives rise to shame and remorse when giving rise to a lazy mind. One gives rise to shame and remorse before the Tathāgatas; one gives rise to shame and remorse before the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; one gives rise to shame and remorse before all sentient beings who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle; one gives rise to shame and remorse before those of the Śrāvaka vehicle; one gives rise to shame and remorse before those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and one gives rise to shame and remorse before humans and devas.
What are shame and remorse?
They refer to constantly feeling ashamed before others and also feeling self-reproach for abiding in all unwholesome dharmas; therefore, one always possesses shame and remorse.

"Abiding in a sense of shame and dread of blame, one remains far removed from all lack of shame and lack of dread of blame; one eliminates what is unwholesome and contemplates wholesome matters. Bearing this heavy burden, one’s essential nature is pure, and one ultimately never commits an offense that others could slander."

Furthermore, this bodhisattva is always able to fulfill unimpaired physical action, fulfill unimpaired verbal action, and fulfill unimpaired mental action; having fulfilled these, they are then able to abide in this samādhi.

Abiding in this samādhi, they are never separated from seeing all Buddhas, never separated from hearing the sublime Dharma spoken by all Buddhas, and never separated from reverently making offerings to the entire Sangha of noble ones.
Having fulfilled such things, they are then able to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a great eon named Sukhāgata. Within that Sukhāgata eon, there was a third subsequent eon named Ratnolkā."
"Aśūnyadarśin! Within that kalpa there was another intermediate kalpa named Nine Adornments, and during that time it was called the Age of Many Defilements.

Furthermore, there was a kalpa named Thousand Years; within it there was a wheel-turning king named Sukṣetrajña, and that King Sukṣetrajña had planted roots of virtue in the past and possessed great majestic power."
“Āśūnya-darśin! At that time, the great city where King Sukalpa resided was named Viśuddha-puṣpa, which was filled with exquisite fragrances.
That city was sixty yojanas wide from east to west and seventy yojanas long from south to north; its walls were surrounded by twelve hundred tiers.”
The dimensions of that city are composed entirely of pure gold, adorned with various requisites and interspersed with the seven treasures. "Anagata-darśin!

If you now wish to know the exquisite splendor of the adornments of the fruits of King Sudarśana’s merit in the City of Pure Fragrant Flowers, it is no different from the Great City of Good Abiding belonging to King Anantavīrya as previously described."
"Aśūnyadarśin!

To the north of that city is an inner gate named Mālyadvāra (Flower-Garland Gate). Outside is a garden named Abhaya (Fearless), forty yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by groves of trees made of the seven precious substances."

There was a great pond, square and vast in dimension, measuring ten yojanas on each side, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities, like the Mandākinī Pond of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Surrounding that pond on all four sides were *tāla* trees made of various jewels—those *tāla* trees made of gold had silver flowers and fruit; those made of silver had *vaiḍūrya* flowers and fruit; and so on, up to the *tāla* trees made of pearl, which had gold flowers and fruit—just like those in the city of Supratiṣṭhita, exactly the same and without any difference.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One—named Aṅgiras (translated in the Sui language as 'Divided Flavor') Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, the Tathāgata Aṅgiras resided within the Abhayavana Grove, surrounded before and behind by a great assembly of ninety-nine billion nayutas of bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions;
all of whom had attained mastery, with their minds well-liberated and their wisdom well-liberated."
Having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, fully attained their own benefit, and being no more subject to future existence;
following the true teaching, they have reached the further shore.

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgiras entered the city of Pure Flower Fragrance at dawn, wearing his robes and carrying his alms bowl, surrounded on all sides by a great assembly of ninety-nine billion hundred thousand nayutas of śrāvakas."

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, King Sudarśanakāra, knowing that the World-Honored One had entered the city in the early morning, personally adorned himself and mounted a great, well-trained elephant named Nartaka. Accompanied by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas before and behind him, he departed from that city of Pure Flower Fragrance in order to welcome the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, King Sukṣetrajña, seeing from afar that the World-Honored One Aṅgiras was approaching along the road—his radiance and deportment sublime and distant like a mountain of gold, his faculties tranquil and his mind harmonious and serene, having reached the supreme shore of pliancy—just as a great dragon has subdued all things, as an elephant acts with mastery, and as a great lake is clear and transparent; having seen him thus, he descended from his vehicle and approached the World-Honored One. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha's feet, he circumambulated him three times to the right and addressed him, saying:
'I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept the offerings I have prepared for tomorrow morning.'"
"Furthermore, Aśūnya-darśin!
At that time, having heard such a request from King Sudarśanakṛt, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgirasas accepted the invitation in silence for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

When King Suvīkṣaṇakārin heard that the World-Honored One had granted his request, he immediately ordered the chief cook that very night to prepare various kinds of exquisite, delicious foods; there was nothing among all the delicacies of the human world that was not fully provided."

In the city of Pure Flower, the roads were leveled and smoothed, and the ground was adorned with various fragrant pastes. Precious banners were erected in every street and alleyway, and exquisite, renowned streamers were distributed everywhere, alongside an array of various vessels made of gold and precious gems.

Furthermore, he used exquisite gośīrṣa sandalwood to create perfumed water which he sprinkled over the ground; he also scattered various powdered incenses and various loose flowers over the Buddha as an offering.

Thereafter, before that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, they made offerings by burning various kinds of famous incense and piling up various kinds of flower garlands; they also made offerings with various songs, praises, verses, and Dharma words; furthermore, they made offerings with various sublime musical sounds and playthings.
Having performed such various offerings, that king then presented the most excellent food and drink as an offering to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.
"Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!

At that time, after King Sudarśana had extensively prepared such subtle, supreme, and most excellent provisions to fulfill his offerings to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgiras, he once again at another time arrayed his great procession and personally led immeasurable thousands of sentient beings to the Fearless Garden (Abhayavana) to go before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgiras. Having prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Now is precisely the right time; we only pray that you will bestow your compassion and perform what ought to be done. Furthermore, Anagamin!

At that time, after the Tathāgata Aṅgiras had heard King Sudarśanakṛt’s earnest entreaty, and knowing that all sentient beings were capable of receiving transformation, he then performed for them various supernatural powers as was appropriate.
Having manifested these supernatural powers, he and ninety-nine billion hundred-thousand nayutas of arhats ascended together into the void.
Abiding in the void, he immediately emitted ninety-nine billion hundred-thousand nayutas of rays of light that illuminated immeasurable worlds in the eastern direction;

likewise, he again emitted the same number of rays of light to illuminate the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir, pervading all ten directions in this very manner.

In each of those directions, there were ninety-nine billion hundred-thousand nayutas of great radiances. Each of those radiances manifested eighty billion hundred-thousand nayutas of great lotus thrones, and upon each of those lotus thrones sat a manifested Tathāgata. The physical dimensions, stature, and even all the various modes of deportment of those Tathāgatas were exactly like those of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgiras, without any difference whatsoever.
"Aśūnyadarśin!

Just as those emanated Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, each have immeasurable billions of nayutas of bhikṣu assemblies surrounding them in the void, so too does each have an emanated Śakra, Lord of Devas, and an emanated Brahmā—whose physical dimensions and size are exactly like those of this present Unsurpassed Brahmā and the Greatly Honored Śakra, Lord of Devas, without any difference whatsoever."

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, when that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgiras manifested such supernatural feats, in an instant all the musical instruments of the devas resounded spontaneously without being struck, and all manner of requisites appeared spontaneously without being made."
"Aśūnyatādarśana!

At that time, when the devas of the desire realm beheld the World-Honored One Aṅgiras manifesting such a great supernatural transformation, they immediately scattered upon the Buddha divine sandalwood, powdered incense, aloeswood, tagara, tamālapatra, ox-head sandalwood, black aloeswood, and so forth."
Furthermore, with various kinds of exquisite flowers—namely, kesa-ra flowers, mahā-kesa-ra flowers, and so forth—they scattered them as offerings over that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgīrasa.
"Furthermore, Aśūnya-darśin!
At that time, the World-Honored One Aṅgiras addressed King Sudarśanakāra, saying:
'Great King!'"
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
Great King!
All conditioned phenomena are suffering."
Great King!
All conditioned phenomena are without self.
Great King!
All conditioned phenomena abide only momentarily; they cannot remain for long.
Great King!
All conditioned phenomena are not solid; they are of a nature to disintegrate.
"Great King!
All conditioned phenomena are ablaze, like a fierce flame.
Great King!"
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are profound and abstruse, like a great pit of fire.
Great King!

You should even contemplate the relinquishing of all conditioned phenomena; you should give rise to deep revulsion and find no pleasure in them; you should contemplate detachment and ultimately aspire toward liberation.
“Āśūnyadarśin! At that time, King Sudarśanakārin, with single-minded devotion, joined his palms in reverence toward the Tathāgata Aṅgiras and praised him, saying: ‘So it is, so it is.’”
O Great Virtuous Sugata!
O Great Virtuous Bhagavān!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
"O Great Virtuous Blessed One!
All conditioned phenomena are suffering; all conditioned phenomena are without self.
O Great Virtuous Blessed One!"
"Just as the holy teachings state, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) should be kept at a distance, must be abandoned, and one should ultimately seek liberation from them. "O Amoghadarśin!"
At that time, the Tathāgata Aṅgiras taught such a Dharma to King Sudarśana, causing him to rejoice, to maintain focused mindfulness, and to practice accordingly;
having caused him to rejoice, to maintain focused mindfulness, and to practice accordingly, he then inspired him to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa!

At that time, the Tathāgata Aṅgiras, seeing that King Sudarśanakṛt had heard the Dharma with joy, had resolved his mind upon Bodhi, and that all sentient beings had received benefit, immediately rose up with his entire body together with a great assembly of ninety-nine billion hundred-thousand nayutas of Arhat bhikṣus. Traversing through the air on foot, he departed from the City of Pure Flowers and then descended once more. With his usual majestic deportment, surrounded by his retinue before and behind, he entered the Garden of Fearlessness."

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, when King Sukṣetradhara had personally witnessed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgiras manifesting such extensive miraculous powers, he gave rise to the bodhicitta and made this vow:

'May we, in future ages, all obtain such great supernormal wisdom; may we all likewise preside over great assemblies; and may we, in future ages, all deliver the Great Lion’s Roar before hosts of devas and humans, exactly as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgira does today, without any difference.'"

"O Aśūnya-darśin! At that time, when King Sudarśanakāra saw that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgirasas, together with the great assembly, returning through the air, the king immediately prepared his carriage and followed the Blessed One to their original dwelling place, and only then did he return."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

Later, at another time, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgīrasa, together with the great assembly, proceeded in due order until he reached the palace of King Sudarśana. Having arrived, he sat upon the prepared seat, and the community of bhikṣus also sat down in succession."

At that time, King Sudarśana, together with his ministers and their respective retinues, each surrounded by their own circles, as well as the citizens within the city and their families, likewise each surrounded by their own circles, all personally brought whatever food they possessed and offered it with their own hands to the World-Honored One Aṅgīrasa and the great assembly of his disciples, the śrāvakas.
The food was fragrant and delicious, replete with every flavor; he offered it to the Buddha and the assembly of monks according to their wishes, and all who partook were fully satisfied.

Thereafter, having further honored and venerated them with various exquisite incenses, various flower garlands, various garments, various precious jewels, all manner of requisites, and sublime music, he immediately summoned the prince on that very day, placed the celestial crown upon him, and invested him with the royal throne. Yet, casting aside the four continents and his kinsmen, and feeling a profound weariness toward birth and death, he requested the Buddha to allow him to leave the household life. Thereupon, in the presence of the World-Honored One, the Buddha Aṅgīrasa, he shaved off his beard and hair, and donned the dharma robes.

At that time, there were eighty-four trillion hundred thousand nayutas of people whose roots of goodness had already matured; they too, being deeply weary of the world, went forth from the king to lead the homeless life.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, once King Sudarśanakārin had gone forth, he adjusted his robes in the midst of the assembly, joined his palms in reverence, and then addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgīrasa, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
How does a bodhisattva practice and contemplate the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*?

How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva realize this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, so as to immediately abide in the stage of non-retrogression, swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and manifestly achieve all dharmas of merit?
"Āṣāḍhi! When the bhikṣu King Sudarśanakārin had thus questioned him, the Tathāgata Aṅgiras immediately addressed that royal bhikṣu, saying:
'Sudarśanakārin!'"

You should know that there are two dharmas which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva must fully cultivate; by doing so, one will immediately attain this Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi and be able to swiftly accomplish Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these two?
First, to have faith in all Tathāgatas and not give rise to opposition;
second, to have faith in what the Buddha has taught and not dare to slander or defame it.
He formed this thought:
"This is the vast realm of all Buddhas, inconceivable.
Well-observed, Kṛtaka!"
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attained this samādhi, is able to swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Sukṣetra-kāraka! [Listen well!]"
Furthermore, there are two dharmas which, when fully cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enable them to swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these two?
First is śamatha, second is vipaśyanā. Skillful in contemplative practice!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by fully cultivating these, attains this samādhi and can swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Sudṛśa! Furthermore, there are two dharmas which, when fully cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enable one to attain this samādhi and swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these two?
First, distancing oneself from the view of nihilism; second, eliminating the view of eternalism.
Good observer!
Is it because a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully practiced and cultivated this samādhi, is able to swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“Sudṛṣṭikāra! Furthermore, there are two dharmas which, when fully cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enable one to attain this samādhi and swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these two?
First, abiding in a sense of shame (*hrī*); second, cultivating a sense of remorse (*apatrāpya*).
Excellent observation, you who act!
"This is how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by fully cultivating and attaining this samādhi, can swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Anagha!"
When that Tathāgata had spoken thus, the bhikṣu King Suvibhaktakārin again addressed the Tathāgata Aṅgirasas, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having established themselves in a sense of shame and remorse, come to attain this buddhānusmṛti-samādhi?
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Aṅgiras addressed the bhikṣu Sudarśanakāra, saying: "Sudarśanakāra!"

If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas always practice a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) regarding all their actions—namely: giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse when committing physical misconduct; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse when committing verbal misconduct;

giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse when committing mental misconduct; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse when giving rise to envy; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse when giving rise to indolence; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse toward the Buddhas; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse toward the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse toward sentient beings who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse toward those of the Śrāvaka vehicle; giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse toward those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse toward gods and humans.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Eight: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Nine: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
The Remainder of the Chapter on Supernatural Powers: “What are shame and remorse?
They are defined as always feeling shame before others, and also feeling remorse within oneself for abiding in all unwholesome dharmas.”

Constantly practicing a sense of shame and dread of blame, they achieve such shame and dread; they remain far removed from unwholesome states, mindfully seeking what is wholesome, bearing their heavy burden upon themselves, possessing pure spiritual lineage, and remaining free from any transgression or violation.
“At that time, having heard the instructions from that Buddha, the bhikṣu King Well-Contemplated dwelt in a sense of shame and remorse.

To extinguish all unwholesome dharmas, he applied himself with diligent effort and aspiration, single-mindedly dedicating his efforts. He abided in all wholesome dharmas and brought them to fulfillment; reflecting upon them further and more extensively so as not to forget them, he concentrated his mind with single-minded devotion, abiding in right contemplation and penetrating deeply into the dharma-realm.”
In this way, monks, when observing the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one does not see a single dharma increase, nor does one see a single dharma decrease.
Having observed that dharmas are without increase or decrease, he should thus see all dharmas as having neither coming nor going;
he should thus see all dharmas as being without gain or loss; he should thus see them...
One should see all phenomena as being without arising or ceasing; one should see all phenomena as being without distinction;
one should see all phenomena as being without difference;
one should see all phenomena as arising from causes and conditions; one should see all phenomena as being like dreams. One should...
Thus they shall see all phenomena as like a mirage;
they shall see all phenomena as like a reflection in a mirror; they shall see all phenomena as like a shadow;
they shall see all phenomena as like an echo; they shall see all phenomena as like...
Like a magical illusion, they should thus see that all phenomena have no superiority or inferiority;
they should thus see that all phenomena are fundamentally without distinction of high or low; they should thus see that all phenomena cannot be accomplished;
they should thus see that all phenomena are originally unarisen; they should thus see.
"All dharmas have no place of arising; one should contemplate all dharmas as being entirely equal in this way.
'Akāśadarśin!'"
Once he has been able to perform such contemplation, he will also be able to practice accordingly, and before long he will be able to attain this samādhi.
"Aśūnyadarśin!
Once that bhikṣu, King Well-Observed Action, had attained this samādhi, he was immediately able to achieve unimpeded eloquence, explaining the meanings of all dharmas without end.
Furthermore, after sixty billion hundred thousand nayutas of kalpas had passed, that bhikṣu King Well-Contemplated Action then attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Aśvaghoṣa! You still harbor doubts regarding this matter; I shall explain it for you so that they may be severed and eliminated. Aśvaghoṣa!"

You should know that at that time, King Sudarśanakṛt, having renounced the four continents, the five sensory pleasures, and all worldly requisites, together with his assembly of eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* ministers and subjects, simultaneously went forth into homelessness, shaved off their hair and beards, and diligently practiced the path under the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One Aṅgīrasa; it was not some other person, and you should not view him as anyone else.
For what reason?
O Śūnyatādarśin!
You should know that the bhikṣu King Well-Contemplated of that time is none other than the present Tathāgata Padmottara.

Furthermore, at that time, King Sudarśanakṛt renounced all the articles of pleasure throughout the four continents and, together with a great assembly of eighty-four thousand billion nayutas of ministers and subjects, went forth to practice the Way under the Buddha Aṅgīrasa. Abiding in the practice of shame and remorse, he correctly contemplated all phenomena and focused his mind in contemplation; before long, he immediately realized this samādhi.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!
For these reasons, I now earnestly and with great gravity proclaim to you that the merit produced by this gate of samādhi is profoundly deep, vast, and inconceivable."

It should be known that it is not those who have failed to extensively plant supreme and wondrous roots of goodness who are able to hear this, nor those who can read, recite, receive, uphold, practice it, or even explain its meaning and principles to others.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

If there are good sons or good daughters who are able merely to hear of this samādhi with their ears, you should know that those good sons and good daughters are by no means of meager merit or those who have planted few roots of goodness. They are not ones who have planted roots of goodness under only one Tathāgata; nor are they ones who have planted roots of goodness under two, three, four, or five Tathāgatas; nor are they ones who have planted roots of goodness under ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even up to a hundred Tathāgatas; nor are they ones who have planted roots of goodness under two hundred, three hundred, or even up to thousands, tens of thousands, millions, or billions of Tathāgatas."

In this way, it is not even the case that one has planted roots of goodness under, nor thickly accumulated merit before, even as many as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Tathāgatas, nor even immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas and more than immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of such Tathāgatas, to obtain even a small portion of hearing the name of this King of Treasures Samādhi; how much less could one possibly write it down, read it, recite it, receive and uphold it, contemplate its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, or analyze and explain it for the sake of many people?
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

If any sons or daughters of good family merely hear of this Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, you should know that those sons and daughters of good family are not of meager merit nor have they planted few roots of goodness; you should know that those sons and daughters of good family are indeed those who are fully endowed with the Bodhisattva Vehicle."
Why is this? O Aśūnyadarśin!

If any person should hear this king of samādhis, you should know that such individuals will, by following its sequence, naturally realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), with the sole exception of those who have already exhausted all outflows (āsrava).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!
You abide in the practice of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Venerable World-Honored One!
Do they constantly realize this king of samādhis?
That Buddha replied:
"Aśūnyatādarśin! You have seen it thus; they too have realized this king of samādhis.
Furthermore, Aśūnyatādarśin!"

It is like a medicine called "True and Authentic. If this medicine is smeared upon a military drum and struck with a mallet during the heat of battle, then even those in the opposing ranks who have been wounded by poisoned arrows, swords, or spears will all be restored to health through the power of that medicine, becoming peaceful, secure, and free from affliction.
Thus it is, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who merely hear even a small portion of the name of this king of samādhis, they shall all, through the power and majesty of the renown of this samādhi, attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening—except for those who have exhausted their outflows and realized it through bodily witness.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, which is composed of four jewels; if any sentient beings come to its presence, they immediately take on its color."
Why is this? Because the majestic radiance of those mountains is all of one single color.
Thus it is, Akṣayamati!

If those sons or daughters of good family should even briefly hear the name of this Jewel Samādhi, they shall all, by the power of the majesty and glory of the name of this samādhi, spontaneously and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—except for those individuals who have exhausted their outflows and attained the stage of certainty.
Why is this? Aśūnyadarśin!
It is because this samādhi possesses inconceivable and supreme efficacy.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
It is like all great rivers, ponds, and streams, which all enter the great ocean and become of one salty taste; this is entirely due to the vast power and virtue of the great ocean."
Thus it is, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

If those sons of good family and daughters of good family can merely hear the name of this samādhi with their ears—even if they do not read it, recite it, receive it, uphold it, cultivate it, practice it, explain it to others, teach it to others, nor are able to analyze and expound it in detail—nevertheless, all those sons and daughters of good family shall successively achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? It is because the renown of this samādhi is supreme and because of its majestic power.
"Furthermore, Aśvaghoṣa! [The Buddha said:]..."
If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, at the time of speaking with sincerity and at the time of speaking well, are able to speak with sincerity and speak well, saying:
"The Dharma-gates of all Buddhas shall certainly be attained; they will be revealed, manifested, and made prominent, bringing vast benefit to all the worlds."
"This is called truthful speech; this is called well-spoken discourse.
'Emptiness-Seeing!

If those sons or daughters of good family can attain such truthful speech and well-spoken discourse, they will certainly obtain an immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable mass of great merit. How much more so the mass of merit obtained by those who can skillfully explain this Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi?"
"Aśūnyadarśin!

Suppose there were immeasurable and boundless Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who for immeasurable and boundless kalpas—exceeding the number of sands of the Ganges—practiced the perfection of giving without even a moment’s rest or cessation; if I were to speak of the merit they would obtain, it would be inconceivable."
I shall now explain this to you in further detail:

if there should be another bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to hear and receive this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, whether by reading and reciting it, upholding it, practicing even a small portion of it, or explaining even a small portion of it, the merit they obtain cannot be compared to, measured against, calculated, reckoned, or described in relation to the previous act of giving; how much more so for one who is able to hear and receive it in its entirety, practice it, and expound it?
"Can this mass of merit be measured?
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"I recall in the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One Aṅgīrasa."
The refuge of all worlds, endowed with great compassion, he proclaims the wondrous Dharma.
There is nothing seen by him that he does not know; he clearly understands both the past and the future, and is likewise able to penetrate the affairs of the present.
He perceives equally even the most subtle and hidden things, and thus awakens to them.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is inconceivable; out of compassion for sentient beings, they preach it for them.
Seeing all those sentient beings tormented by suffering, they give rise to a heart of great pity.
At that time, that Tathāgata had a retinue of ninety-nine billion śrāvakas, all of whom possessed mastery and had exhausted birth;
they all together surrounded the King of the True Dharma.
To the northeast of that city there is a grove, perfectly adorned and named Abhaya;
here dwells the Tathāgata, the Great Sage, together with a multitude of billions of Arhats.
That King Cakravartin, having carefully observed his duty, prepared his magnificent jeweled chariot and departed from the city;
surrounded by immeasurable ministers and subjects, all sentient beings were filled with love and joy.
The King beheld the World-Honored One’s mind in perfect tranquility, his body and speech pure and his faculties well-disciplined;
endowed with all sublime and wondrous deportment, King Suvīkṣaṇa’s reverence increased all the more.

The king then proceeded to where that Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the World-Honored One’s feet, and spoke to request the Buddha to accept his offerings; the World-Honored One consented by remaining silent.
Because the Tathāgata had consented to accept [the offering], the King immediately issued an edict to all the ministers and citizens within the city:
"Now you must prepare exquisite offerings; I wish to present them to the Buddha Aṅgīrasa."
When all matters were thus prepared, the King personally announced:
"I pray that you will compassionately look upon this moment; may the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, together with the noble Saṅgha, accept my humble meal today."

The Tathāgata Aṅgīrasa accepted the King’s invitation; this mass of great merit manifested vast supernatural powers, subsequently producing immeasurable billions of rays of light that universally illuminated all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
From each and every ray of light emerge immeasurable, hundreds of thousands of billions of great lotuses—
subtle, exquisite, and brilliant, bringing joy to all people— and they serve to awaken the roots of all virtues within sentient beings.
"You, Aśūnyadarśin, know that from each of these flowers there emerges a manifested form of a Tathāgata;
appearing before the eyes of those who gaze upon them, they proclaim throughout the ten directions this Dharma in unison:
'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and truly suffering.'"

Furthermore, it is said that selflessness is utterly frail and weak; in the end, all things are subject to destruction and lack solidity. Who, then, would say that a wise person gives rise to craving and delight?
All conditioned phenomena are like a fierce conflagration; their blazing heat and intense fervor are exceedingly difficult to withstand.
As the World-Honored One, Aṅgīrasa, thus proclaimed, the Buddha gave rise to profound renunciation for the sake of sentient beings.
When the devas beheld this great supernormal power, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played simultaneously;
fragrant flowers rained down spontaneously—how extraordinary, how rare, and inconceivable!
Because that king witnessed the Buddha’s miraculous transformations, he made immeasurable offerings;
regarding this Honored One most venerable throughout the four continents, he cast aside the five desires as if discarding a pair of sandals.
Before the Buddha, he shaved his hair and donned the kāṣāya; thereupon he inquired about the subtle and wondrous samādhi:
"Abiding in what supreme dharma can a man enter the gate of samādhi?"
Thus the World-Honored One Aṅgīrasa has said:
"Abiding in two dharmas and reflecting well upon them, one shall personally realize this subtle dhyāna and attain inconceivable, supreme bliss."
The King heard that Buddha’s words of truth, and with a heart of profound joy, he entered this samādhi;
constantly mindful of bodhi and honoring all Buddhas, he immediately received the honorific title "Supreme Lotus."
If one can faithfully accept the words of the Tathāgata and harbor no further doubt regarding this sūtra,
entering the profound Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s realm, one will naturally attain entry into this samādhi.
If one hears of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) without alarm or doubt, and likewise harbors no notions of self or person regarding phenomena,
diligently recollecting śamatha and vipaśyanā— one thus reflects deeply and attains supreme dhyāna.
Abiding in shame, remorse, and reverence, one should constantly cultivate all forms of right effort;
once one recognizes evil as it manifests and feels shame, how could it take long to realize the King of Samādhis?
Constantly observing all phenomena, one sees no increase, Nor does one personally perceive any decrease in phenomena;
Seeing all phenomena as like empty space— The wise Bodhisattva penetrates this truth.
All phenomena neither arise nor perish; Their original nature is pure and eternally serene.
Knowing all phenomena to be identical to dreams, one who sees thus attains samādhi;
therein they do not construct marks of distinction, seeing neither original cessation nor arising,
like a mirage or a reflection— one who can see thus attains samādhi.
The characteristics of phenomena are equal, without high or low, nor existence or non-existence, nor superiority or inferiority;
like echoes, shadows, illusions, and transformations—thus seeing people realize samādhi.
All phenomena are quiescent, without victory or defeat; one perceives neither external forms nor the internal mind.
There is no accomplishment, nor is there even a name; one who sees thus realizes samādhi.

A bhikṣu who contemplates with such single-minded diligence, constantly reflecting throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, having received the Honored One’s teaching upon his head in the presence of the Buddha, shall before long realize this samādhi.
When they realize this samādhi, they are already without deficiency regarding bodhi;
they also behold all Buddhas of the ten directions and perform offerings to the great assembly of beings who possess merit.
After passing through sixty billion hundreds of thousands,
nayuta kalpas of practicing all deeds and serving immeasurable Buddhas, he then realized that great Bodhi.
"You, Aśūnyadarśin, should now know:
who was that king at that time?
A wise person should not give rise to divergent views; he was none other than the Buddha Padmottara."
I now instruct you all, as well as all the devas and humans in every world:
if you wish to reach the ultimate source of all dharmas, you should contemplate and swiftly purify this samādhi.
You will surely gather a great mass of merit, incalculable and beyond measure.
If one wishes to attain wondrous bliss beyond conception, one must first purely cultivate this samādhi;
if one wishes to see all Buddhas— those of the present, the future, and the ten directions—
or seeks to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, one must likewise first practice this samādhi.
If you wish to perfect the various excellent marks, To be fully endowed with the supreme adornment of the secondary signs,
And seek rebirth in a pure family, You must first uphold this samādhi.
Aniruddha, if you see sentient beings Who desire to distance themselves from all evil realms,
Those who wish to fully know of those born in the lower realms Should constantly praise and recite this samādhi.
It is not by making offerings to a single Buddha, Nor to two, three, four, or five,
Nor even to hundreds of millions or nayutas of Buddhas, That one will come to hear this supreme samādhi.
Having made offerings to Buddhas beyond the count of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, in order to realize unsurpassed great bodhi,
and having attained all that the multitude desires, they are then able to hear this supreme samādhi;
having made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of Buddhas, they have long planted various roots of goodness in the past.
Only by constantly giving rise to a heart of joy and reverence can one preach this supreme samādhi;
having served immeasurable thousands of Buddhas— those supreme among gods who radiate light—
and practicing with diligent effort without weariness, one may then recite and praise this Samādhi Sūtra.
He beheld immeasurable billions of Buddhas, Whose boundless pure radiance was like the solar orb;
Having deeply cultivated all roots of goodness, Only then did he succeed in hearing this wondrous samādhi.
Furthermore, it is like a battlefield in this world where many suffer from poison;
yet if they happen to hear the sound of the medicinal drum, all poisons are eliminated and they attain peace and happiness.
If someone speaks of this samādhi, and those who happen to hear this supreme concentration, they shall realize awakening through the power of that samādhi—
not those who have already exhausted their outflows and attained the stage of certainty.
The merit of that concentration is equal to Mount Sumeru; when a person realizes it, there are no distinct marks.
Should one ever go to the place of that mountain, they would become identical in color to it, making them difficult to distinguish.
If a person hears the sound of this samādhi— superior among all concentrations like the great ocean—
by the power and majesty of this samādhi, they will realize bodhi without further doubt.
Just as all streams flow into the great ocean—whether large rivers, small streams, or ponds—they become of one identical taste, impossible to distinguish;
so too is that [Dharma-realm] without any marks of difference.
If a person hears this samādhi, they immediately bring to mind all Buddhas of the ten directions;
through the power of this samādhi, they attain perfect enlightenment—not by means of that person who has realized it through their own body.
If bodhisattvas were to practice only dāna for more than boundless eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—
making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions and extending down to all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm—
though the merit obtained from such extensive practice of giving over vast kalpas may be said to be great, [it would not equal the merit of upholding this Dharma].
It is still not as good as expounding the gateway of wondrous samādhi, Which gives rise to a single thought of loving-kindness that covers all beings.
This samādhi of skillful contemplation is like a compassionate mother; Its radiant manifestation of holy virtue is difficult to measure.
If a wise person can seek it with a single mind, They shall swiftly attain Buddhahood and possess sovereign mastery.

Chapter 14: On the Cultivation of Samādhi. Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha, Part One of Chapter Fourteen: On the Cultivation of Samādhi. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by being endowed with how many dharmas, will be able to enter this buddhānusmṛti-samādhi?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, saying: “Amoghadarśin!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with three dharmas, they are able to enter this buddhānusmṛti-samādhi.
What are these three?

First, being fully endowed with the root of goodness of non-attachment; second, being fully endowed with the root of goodness of non-hatred; third, being fully endowed with the root of goodness of non-delusion.
If one is able to be fully endowed with the three roots of goodness, one will immediately achieve the six pāramitās.
Because that bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the root of goodness of non-attachment, they constantly practice giving and thus fully accomplishes the dāna-pāramitā.
