In every birth, one shall always obtain abundant family wealth, be fully endowed with treasures and riches, have all necessities arrive at will, and be forever free from poverty. Possessing great majesty and power, one’s mind becomes vast and expansive, no longer narrow or inferior, naturally subduing that unwholesome root of greed.

Because they are fully endowed with all merits, no sentient being who sees them fails to revere them; whatever they say, everyone believes and practices. Without requiring great effort, they attain this samādhi and swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, because that bodhisattva harbors no malice, anger, or resentment toward any sentient beings among the devas and humans of all worlds, he is able to fulfill the wholesome root of non-anger and constantly abides in the śīla-pāramitā and kṣānti-pāramitā.

Having fully perfected the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), even when encountering verbal abuse, slander, flogging, beating, the severing of hands and feet, the gouging out of marrow, or the splitting of the skull—when all such sufferings come together in urgent distress—one remains without anger, resentment, malice, or hatred; thus, one eradicates the unwholesome root of aversion (*dveṣa-akuśalamūla*).

Having given rise to a mind of great compassion that pervades the entire realm of sentient beings, one will never be separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in any state of existence; whether dreaming or awake, one will always be at peace.
Devas will provide protection, such that weapons cannot harm, poison cannot affect, fire cannot burn, and water cannot drown.

One will always have an abundance of food, drink, medicine, clothing, bedding, and all manner of necessities. All those in the world—gods, humans, and sentient beings—who see one will praise them, and before long, they will be able to realize this samādhi and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, because that bodhisattva is able to fulfill the wholesome root of non-delusion, he has long cultivated *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and being perfected in skillful means (*upāya*), he is able to sever the unwholesome root of delusion. He achieves subtle and profound wisdom, clearly and distinctly understanding all phenomena, and remains unimpeded regarding the various gates of divergent doctrines; thus, when others pose difficult questions or challenges, he explains and resolves them without hesitation.
"Amoghadarśin!
These are the three dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enable one to realize this samādhi and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin, there are three further dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can enter samādhi and can also swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“What are these three?

First, observing all conditioned phenomena as impermanent and knowing them as they truly are; second, observing all conditioned phenomena as suffering and knowing them as they truly are; third, observing all phenomena as selfless and knowing them as they truly are.”
If a bodhisattva can contemplate in this way, they will be able to enter this samādhi before long. Āśūnyadarśin!
These are the three dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fulfill to realize this samādhi and also swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!
There are three further dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can enter samādhi and also swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"What are the three?

First, while the Tathāgata is present, one practices various offerings; or after his parinirvāṇa, one at times makes offerings to the relics of the Buddhas—whether with various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers, flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, burning of various famous incenses, lighting lamps, banners, canopies, precious stūpas, music, and so forth. Whether making these offerings oneself or encouraging others to do so, one constantly makes this vow:

'May whatever roots of goodness from these acts of offering and vows, wherever I am born, cause me to swiftly attain the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), and may I also realize and perfect Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"Second, whether the Buddha is present or has entered parinirvāṇa, one shall praise and proclaim the Tathāgata’s true merits:

whether they be morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, dignified deportment, supernormal powers, eloquence, the absence of strife, compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, or equanimity—and all other meritorious qualities of the World-Honored One—one shall constantly praise them. Furthermore, one shall make this vow:

'May the mass of merit and the virtues I obtain from praising the Buddhas from this day forward, by virtue of these roots of goodness, cause me to attain the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi and enable me to swiftly perfect the fruit of the unsurpassed path.'"
"Amoghadarśin!
These are the three dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the entry into samādhi and is also able to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess another three dharmas by which they will, before long, be able to accomplish samādhi and shall also swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
What are these three?

First, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear of the true merits of this samādhi from all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, or even at times merely hear the name of this samādhi, they immediately reflect to themselves:

"Just as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, when they originally practiced the bodhisattva path in their quest for Bodhi, all sought this very samādhi; therefore, upon hearing of this samādhi, I shall give rise to sympathetic joy."
For the sake of great enlightenment today, I too should diligently seek such a samādhi, so as to achieve and fulfill its great benefit.
Therefore, having now heard the name and the merits of this samādhi, I give rise to deep sympathetic joy.
This is called being fully endowed with the first method of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Second: "Just as all those future Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, when practicing the bodhisattva path in pursuit of enlightenment, cultivated this samādhi for the sake of great benefit."
"Therefore, having now heard this samādhi, I too give rise to sympathetic joy.
This is called the second fulfillment of the dharma of sympathetic joy. Third:

"As for all the present Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the ten directions who currently abide in the world—those who have transcended all realms of existence, uprooted the seeds of habituation, severed the flow of speech, distanced themselves from applied and sustained thought, realized profound concentration, and are endowed with great compassion—they too, when practicing as bodhisattvas in the past, heard this samādhi and gave rise to sympathetic joy in every instance."
"Now that I have obtained the hearing of this samādhi, why should I alone not give rise to sympathetic joy?
When he reflects thus, he gives rise to deep sympathetic joy; this is called being fully endowed with the third dharma of sympathetic joy.
"Amoghadarśin!

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva fully accomplishes the three kinds of sympathetic joy; may the merit and all roots of goodness thereby obtained be shared with all sentient beings so that they may together realize this samādhi, and may they also swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, Aśūnyatādarśin!
If any sons or daughters of good family should give rise to sympathetic joy toward this samādhi, the merit they obtain will be truly vast, immeasurable, boundless, and difficult to describe."
"I shall now cite various parables for you to reveal a small portion of the truth so that you may understand it. 'Anaviladarśana!

Suppose all the Ganges sands within this trichiliocosm were gathered into a single heap by someone; then, from that great heap of sand, one would take each individual grain and grind it into fine dust. Having done so, one would then take a single mote of dust from that pile and pass it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and further beyond immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, inconceivable, ineffable, and unfathomable worlds equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, only then placing that single mote of dust down.'"
In this manner, one continues in succession until all the sands and dust particles used to calculate all worlds have been completely distributed.
Āśūnyatādarśin! What do you think?
"Suppose those people of the world were able to know even a small portion of the number of worlds;
would they be capable of it? Abhaya said, "No."
“World-Honored One!
“Aśūnyapratibhāna!
Let this matter rest for now.”

Suppose there were a master mathematician in this world, foremost in intelligence and wisdom; could he, by exhausting all his intellectual power and skill in calculation, weigh, examine, and further count and know the number of worlds?
Amoghadarśin said,
“No, World-Honored One.”
"No, World-Honored One!
As I see it now, there are only the Venerable Śāriputra and those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the stage of non-retrogression who might perhaps have a slight resemblance."
The Buddha said,

“Aśūnyadarśin! If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the aforementioned number of worlds filled to the brim with the seven treasures and other various requisites, were to use them to make offerings to all sentient beings;”
"Amoghadarśin! What do you think?
Is the merit obtained by that person through such offerings and the practice of giving not indeed great?"
Amoghadarśin said: "Very many,
World-Honored One!"
“Immeasurable,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"Aśūnyadarśin! I shall tell you further:

although those sons and daughters of good family may possess vast merit from offering all manner of vessels filled with the seven treasures to all sentient beings throughout all worlds, it still does not equal the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family who, upon hearing the name of this King of Samādhis Jewel, give rise to the three kinds of sympathetic joy and vow to dedicate [the merit] toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this so? Aśūnyadarśin!
It is because those three kinds [of qualities] arise from extensive learning, and that extensive learning originates from correct exposition.
"Amoghadarśin!
Because it is correctly taught by him, it is able to give rise to all roots of goodness; this is precisely this samādhi.
What samādhi is it that can give rise to all roots of goodness?"
This refers precisely to this Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, it can give rise to all roots of goodness; this is also what is meant by "correct teaching.
What is the correct teaching?
This means that when one speaks correctly, it is a skillful exposition.
For this reason, the merit obtained from those three kinds of sympathetic joy, compared to the merit of giving, is immeasurable and incomparable.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and yet another immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a world named Akampya.
In that realm, there was a Buddha named Ratnagiri-vyūha-tathāgata."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the All-Knowing One, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World,
the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world—
he who has attained great mastery, who subdues all, and who is fully endowed with liberation for eternity.
Having crossed to the other shore, he is supreme, most wondrous, most excellent, and peerless;
he can act as a great refuge for sentient beings, provide great protection for sentient beings, and cure the diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings.
He penetrates the three periods of time with complete clarity and, relying on the Dharma he has realized by himself, teaches it to sentient beings.

The Dharma he teaches is good in the beginning, middle, and end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its words are skillful and elegant, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life (brahmacarya). For the sake of all sentient beings, he constantly teaches in this manner.

"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaparvata resided in a royal city named Vairanirghāta, together with a great assembly of thirty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas—all of whom were still in training (śaikṣa), who still had things to be practiced, things to be abandoned, and things to be attained, and who were worthy of receiving offerings from the devas and humans of the world."
"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnaparvata arose from samādhi and had this thought:

'Now these three hundred billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas of mine are all still in training; they have not yet accomplished what was to be done and have not yet reached the further shore. I should now teach them according to the Dharma so that they may all swiftly attain the exhaustion of outflows.'"
"Ākāśagarbha! At that time, the Buddha Ratnagiri-vyūha extensively manifested such great supernormal powers that the entire trichiliocosm was filled with smoke and ablaze with fierce flames."

“Āśūnyadarśin! At that time, when those śrāvakas witnessed the Tathāgata performing such extensive and great supernormal feats, they were filled with joy and rapture throughout their entire bodies—just as a bhikṣu who has entered the fourth dhyāna, so too was the physical and mental bliss of those śrāvakas.”
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
At that time, after that Buddha had displayed such miraculous feats during the stillness of the night, he addressed the assembly of śrāvakas, saying:
'O bhikṣus, you should observe this trichiliocosm filled with billowing smoke and ablaze with fierce, blazing flames.'"
"Monks! All conditioned phenomena are likewise impermanent. Monks!"
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are of the nature of suffering are likewise so. O bhikṣus!
All dharmas are without self or what belongs to a self; they lack solidity, being false and unreal, subject to breaking and destruction, and characterized by total cessation.
"O bhikṣus!

I have now briefly explained all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), up to and including the instruction to relinquish them all and not cling to them, so that you may give rise to profound weary detachment (*nirveda*) and be naturally liberated."

“Ākaśagatā! At that time, those thirty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas, having received such Dharma and such instructions from that Tathāgata, all attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) and realized all dharmas; they became unimpeded regarding all dharmas and dwelt securely in them, crossing over the net of doubt.”
Having heard and received the Dharma from the Teacher, he attained complete fearlessness regarding all phenomena and uttered these words in a loud voice:
"So it is, Bhagavān!"
"So it is, Blessed One!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
So it is, Blessed One!"
"All conditioned phenomena are suffering.
"So it is, Blessed One!
All phenomena abide but momentarily."
"So it is, World-Honored One!
All phenomena are shattered and cannot be relied upon.
So it is, World-Honored One!"
All phenomena are ablaze, just like grass, wood, and stone walls.
Thus it is, Blessed One;
all conditioned formations—even those that can be released, abandoned, reviled, and escaped from—are likewise so.

"Aśūnyapratibhāsa! At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagiri-alaṃkāra, through these three kinds of manifestations—such miraculous powers, such preaching of the Dharma, and such instructions—transformed the assembly of śrāvakas, causing them to enter the three gates of liberation, namely emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Furthermore, there were thirty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas who were all destined to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Aśūnyadarśin! At that time, for the sake of those thirty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, that Buddha preached this King of Jewels Samādhi. Having thus revealed it, and furthermore, for the benefit of the world of devas and humans, he turned the wheel of the true Dharma for eighty-four thousand billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of years. Only then did he enter parinirvāṇa in that realm of nirvana without remainder."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many assemblies of bodhisattvas did that Tathāgata Ratnaparvata-vyūha teach and transform in his presence?”
"Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, for how long will the Dharma remain?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati, saying:
"Akṣayamati!..."
While the number of all the stars in this trichiliocosm may be known, the limit of the quantity of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Adorned with Jewel Mountains is difficult to know.

After that Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for a full eighty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of years, and the Semblance Dharma remained in the world for twenty billion years.
Not long thereafter, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Maitrīcaryā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; his lifespan was immeasurable, and the height of that Buddha’s body was a full yojana.
At that time, the bodies of sentient beings were six *krośas* in height, measured from their feet.

The lotus thrones—those large ones being thirteen *yojanas* high and the small ones still six *yojanas* high—completely covered the earth; all sentient beings, whether walking back and forth, moving about, going, standing, sitting, or lying down, each remained upon a lotus throne.

"At that time, the world was named Abundant Lotus. Its ground was as soft as sheep’s wool, and when sentient beings touched it, it felt like the exquisite garments of the devas. Its color and luster were like the yellow-white stone of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and those sentient beings experienced happiness just like those in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas."
Those sentient beings who wish to cross the Eastern Sea reach the opposite shore in the space of a single moment;
it is likewise with the Southern, Western, and Northern Seas—whenever those sentient beings set their minds upon going anywhere, they arrive immediately.
"When that Tathāgata Maitrīcaryā first attained Buddhahood, his realm was vast, extending to the very limits of the four oceans.

At that time, the great earth was perfectly square, measuring eighty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of yojanas in length and breadth, and it was entirely filled with the assembly of śrāvakas. Among them, most were arhats who ate in a single sitting, with the sole exceptions of the attendant Ānanda, Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, Asita, and others."
Furthermore, there was an assembly of eighty nayutas of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression.

When those bodhisattvas requested the profound and wondrous gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-dharmaparyāya*), and when the Tathāgata Maitrakārī revealed and displayed that profound dharma-gate for the sake of the bodhisattvas, the World-Honored One Maitrakārī uttered this verse with a single voice:
"If a person seeks to leave the household life through skillful means, They should focus their mind one-pointedly on the wondrous Dharma.
He will surely crush the army of Māra, Just as a fragrant elephant destroys a thatched hut.
Who seeks to swiftly achieve great Bodhi?
One should constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of the world; And if one wishes to purify this most supreme ground, This joy of samādhi can indeed accomplish it.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Nine: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.

This concludes the remainder of the "Chapter on Cultivating Samādhi. At that time, when the great transformation of the Tathāgata Maitrīcaryā was nearing its end, there was a bhikṣu named Śālavṛkṣarāja who extensively expounded this samādhi for the sake of sentient beings, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.

After the parinirvāṇa of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, during the period of the True Dharma, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Devendra, endowed with majesty and virtue, possessing great supernormal powers and the seven precious jewels, including the golden wheel; he ruled the world according to the Right Dharma.
"Aśūnyadarśin!

The great city where that Lord of Devas resides is named Indravatī—translated in the Sui language as 'City of the Lord of Devas' and also as 'Imperial Banner'—and it is twelve yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly square."
The towers, pavilions, terraces, and palaces both inside and outside that city were all composed of the seven treasures in various colors, and they were further covered above by golden galleries.
"Avalokiteśvara!

That city had three gates on each of its four sides; as for the description of its various adornments, they were identical to those of King Vīryabalasusthita’s Great City of Good Abiding, being magnificent, exquisite, and unsurpassed.
"Aśūnyatādarśana!

Later, at a certain time after midnight had passed, while that Lord of the Gods was still asleep and had not yet awakened, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven descended to the king's presence and caused the king to see him in a dream; therein, he spoke to the king the name of this Dharma-gate of the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*:
'Great King!'"
You should seek this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. Why is this?

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to achieve this samādhi, they will never be separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; furthermore, they will clearly understand all mundane and supramundane letters, phrases, sounds, names, and languages, and being endowed with eloquence, they will spontaneously and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Ākaśagatā! At that time, King Devendra, having seen the deva in his dream, immediately awoke and addressed that deva, saying:
‘Among the hosts of devas and humans, who is able to uphold such a samādhi?’”
The deity replied,
"Great King! Have you not heard?"

Now there is a bhikṣu named Śālavat, who is currently able to receive and uphold such a samādhi, extensively analyzing and expounding it for the sake of the world, thereby benefiting all the great assemblies of humans and devas.

"Aśūnyadarśin! When that Lord of the Gods heard the name of this samādhi, he was immediately able to receive, uphold, contemplate, and examine it, while also reciting and remembering the name of that bhikṣu."

When that night had passed, at the break of dawn, he immediately renounced his status as a Wheel-Turning King over the four continents; he likewise abandoned eighty billion hundred thousand nayutas of ladies of the inner palace, queens, and female attendants, and furthermore cast aside all the various requisites for the five desires—all of this being solely for the sake of this King of Samādhis.
At that time, the king again joined ninety-six billion, one hundred thousand nayutas of sentient beings in seeking that bhikṣu to renounce his home and go forth into homelessness.
"Aśūnyadarśin!

At that time, the Bhikṣu King of Trees was surrounded on all sides by the fourfold assembly—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and humans and non-humans. Furthermore, ninety billion devas of the desire realm stood to his left listening to the Dharma, while eighty nayutas of bodhisattvas stood before him praising and expounding this King of Samādhis, analyzing and explaining its profound meaning.

When that King of Devas arrived at his location, he immediately scattered various jewels over the bhikṣu; only then did he prostrate himself with his five limbs touching the ground and, with single-minded devotion, pay homage at the feet of that bhikṣu.

Furthermore, he took eighty precious caskets, each with a capacity of one *hu*, filled them completely with golden flowers, and scattered them upon it; he also scattered celestial flowers—namely, the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *māndārava*, and *mahāmāndārava*—upon it.

Furthermore, they scattered upon it various celestial exquisite incenses—namely, celestial agallochum, tagara, tamālapatra, gośīrṣa sandalwood, black agallochum sandalwood, powdered incense, and so forth.

"Having extensively prepared these various offerings, he then invited [the Buddha] to become his disciple as a bhikṣu. On that very day, together with ninety-six billion hundred thousand nayutas of ministers and subjects, he shaved off his hair and beard before the bhikṣu, donned the saffron robes, and left the household life in weariness with the world, all for the sake of seeking this wondrous samādhi."

"From then on, that bhikṣu Lord of Devas was constantly able to attend upon and make offerings to as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, together with his retinue of ninety-six billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus; this was all for the sake of this supreme samādhi."
“Āśūnya-darśin!

At that time, that bhikṣu Devendra, for eighty-four billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of years, served and made offerings to that bhikṣu Vṛkṣarāja with various kinds of requisites, seeking this samādhi; he recited it, upheld it, practiced according to its teaching, and instructed his disciples, never for a moment becoming weary.”
Furthermore, that assembly of bhikṣu followers was courageous and diligent, never wearying in their efforts. "Aśūnyadarśin!

That Lord of Devas bhikṣu and his retinue conceived a heart of deep respect for the Dharma Master Śālavṛkṣarāja, regarding him as a Buddha. Hearing him preach the sublime Dharma, they received and upheld it with single-minded devotion, practicing with diligence through the long night without ever resting."

The bhikṣu Vṛkṣarāja had fully accomplished all these things; those nine billion six hundred million bhikṣus who practiced the bodhisattva path and dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression subsequently entered parinirvāṇa, and all of their followers likewise passed away.

“At that time, there appeared in the world another Buddha named Jambudhvaja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Therein, the bhikṣu Indradeva, together with his retinue, further sought out and inquired of that Jambudhvaja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding this profound sūtra of samādhi; they read, recited, received, and upheld it, contemplated its meaning, practiced according to the teaching, and explained it for others, in order to benefit all devas and humans in the world and to realize unsurpassed great bodhi.”
Furthermore, for the sake of this unsurpassed and supreme samādhi, that bhikṣu Devendra extensively analyzed and expounded the profound sūtras proclaimed by all the Buddhas.

After three thousand kalpas have passed, he will then become a Buddha; furthermore, he will be able to teach and transform immeasurable multitudes of beings, causing them all to reach maturity, to ultimately abide in the stage of non-retrogression, and to receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:
"You should now know this:
was that King Devendra at that time anyone other than you?"
He is none other than the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha of Supreme Conduct.
Therefore, you should not harbor any doubt now. Furthermore, Anagamin!
"You should now contemplate and observe with single-minded focus the depth of the roots of goodness and the extent of the merit of this king of samādhis; I shall now explain it to you only in brief."

If those immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the world merely hear the name of this samādhi with their ears, they will certainly attain equal and perfect enlightenment in the future.

How much more so for these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have personally heard me extensively expound this King of Samādhis, whether before me or behind me—those who read and recite it, uphold it, contemplate its meaning, practice it, or are able to proclaim and explain it widely for others?
"Aśūnyatādarśin!

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling in the bodhisattva vehicle who hear this samādhi sūtra reach their ears and hearts, they too shall before long certainly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas of the Bodhisattva Vehicle who dwell in the first stage shall swiftly realize the stage of non-retrogression, and for them, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* will no longer be distant.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
It is like when the night is nearly spent and the sun has not yet risen, at the moment the first light of dawn appears in the east; there are none among the people of Jambudvīpa who do not rejoice."

Why is this? Because one knows that before long the solar orb shall appear, extensively providing great illumination for the world, so that the people of Jambudvīpa may all behold whatever is good or evil, and perceive all pure and impure forms so as to carry out their activities.
Thus it is, Aśūnyatādarśin!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who merely hear this *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha* with their ears, they shall all before long attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Therefore, you all should form a resolute mind regarding this samādhi, give rise to indestructible faith, and neither produce divergent views nor harbor a web of doubt.
"Furthermore, Anagata-darśin!
Just as when a kalpa is about to end, on the appearance of the sixth sun in the world, the entire great earth of this trichiliocosm will emit smoke;
once the smoke has issued forth, one should know that before long the seventh sun will appear, and the entire world will be completely ablaze.
Thus it is, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family—whether they have already entered that Bodhisattva vehicle or have not yet entered it—whoever has previously heard this *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha* with their ears, or at some time has recited it, or has received and upheld it, or contemplated its meaning, or practiced according to its teaching, or even been able to explain it extensively for others, they will certainly and swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!

It is like a person digging a well who, upon seeing moist earth that soils his hands and feet, or perhaps seeing mud mixed with water, would know that water is not far away. A wise person should understand this."
Thus it is, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, correctly receive and uphold it, contemplate it with true intent, discern its principles, and extensively proclaim and explain it to others, you should know that those good sons and good daughters will before long spontaneously attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
It is as if there were a person who swallowed a vajra pellet; you should know that this person will surely die before long. Why is this?
Because that vajra-ball cannot be digested,
so it is, Emptiness-Seer!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who merely hear this samādhi, or further contemplate it, or constantly draw near to it, or practice it, or are able to proclaim it, you should know that those sons and daughters of good family will before long certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? This samādhi is the true vajra, pure and accomplished through the contemplative cultivation of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, present, and future; it is without falsehood and indestructible.
Furthermore, it is able to teach and transform the bodhisattvas, causing them to dwell securely, because bodhisattvas are certain to abide peacefully in the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Anagamin!
Just as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven experience peace and happiness upon seeing the Nandana Grove, so it is, Anagamin!"
All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by virtue of hearing the name of this samādhi, are able to swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

By means of the name of this samādhi dharma-gate, it has been praised by all Buddhas of the past; they have extensively expounded it for others, explained its principles and meanings, and revealed and displayed its collection of names, phrases, and syllables. It is complete and perfect, abiding within the dharma-realm, protected and sustained, and serves to teach and increase the great bodhisattvas, causing them to delight in the true path, becoming upright, pure, and harmonious, and always experiencing peace and bliss.

"Aśūnyatādarśin! For this reason, you should know this: if any bodhisattvas hear of this samādhi even for a moment, such sons and daughters of good family will before long realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“Amoghadarśin! For this reason I say to you: you should understand this well.

If any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing this profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, are able to receive and uphold it, those sons and daughters of good family will naturally and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
"Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

You should uphold this samādhi and constantly bear it in mind, proclaiming and explaining it extensively for all those in the world—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; as well as kings, ministers, and counselors; kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras; all mendicants; and others of various non-Buddhist paths, such as the Nirgranthas, Carakas, and Pārivrajakas."
Why is this? Because by the great virtue and majestic power of this samādhi, they are able to swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyapratibhāna!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, with pure faith and a reverent mind, clearly understand that this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* has been praised by the Buddhas of the past and is endorsed by all Tathāgatas;
having understood it thus, they should immediately read and recite it, should immediately receive and uphold it, should immediately practice it, and should immediately expound it."
Furthermore, one should reflect in this way:
"This samādhi is an inconceivable mass of great merit.
Having reflected thus, one should further believe and revere it, further respect it, further penetrate it, and further realize it.

Why is this so? This samādhi is that which has been taught by all Buddhas; it is the sphere of practice of all Buddhas; it is that which is approved by all Buddhas; it is the true teaching of all Buddhas; it is the eloquence of all Buddhas; it is the awakening of all Buddhas; it is the discernment of all Buddhas; it is the activity of all Buddhas; it is the wealth and treasure of all Buddhas; it is the treasury of all Buddhas; it is the hidden store of all Buddhas; it is the granary of all Buddhas; it is the seal of all Buddhas; it is the śarīra of all Buddhas; and it is the essential nature of all Buddhas.
"Aśūnyadarśin! If those sons and daughters of good family can understand in this way, they will immediately attain immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness.

By virtue of this merit, wherever they are born, they will always dwell in great Kṣatriya families, great Brāhmaṇa families, and all other families of great majesty, great honor, or among the abodes of gods of great virtue, until they eventually realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? O Aśūnyadarśin!
It is because by means of this samādhi, one is fully able to attain the inconceivable mass of supramundane fruits and rewards.
"Aśūnyadarśin!

If those sons or daughters of good family merely hear the name of this samādhi with their ears, they shall obtain an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit, and they shall likewise perform immeasurable and boundless meritorious deeds."
However, the mass of merit, roots of goodness, meritorious conduct, and virtues attained by them are vast and profound, beyond calculation, beyond reckoning, beyond measure, and impossible to know.
"Furthermore, Aśūnyadarśin!
Though the description has been as detailed as this, the meaning is not yet clear.
I shall now provide you with further analogies so that those of wisdom may understand it even slightly."
"Amoghadarśin!

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with single-minded faith and joy, practices the dāna-pāramitā by giving at three times each day—at the first part of the day, by means of supernatural power, he causes the seven treasures and all other requisites to fill those worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and then offers them up to Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with their assemblies of disciples and śrāvakas;
and just as he practices such giving during the first part of the day, so too does he practice giving during the middle and the latter parts of the day."

He practiced giving in this manner three times each day, continuing thus for immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas without ever ceasing or desisting, all the while seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Amoghadarśin! What do you think?
Could the merit obtained by that bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices such giving for so long a time be said to be great?"
Amoghadarśin said:
"Very many, World-Honored One!
They are immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, incomparable, and inconceivable."
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, saying:
“Amoghadarśin! I shall speak further to you; you should listen attentively.”

Even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to practice the dāna-pāramitā in such a manner, the roots of goodness they plant and the mass of merit they acquire would indeed be vast; yet it still would not equal even a small portion of the merit of these sons and daughters of good family who merely hear the name of this samādhi, or at times write it down, or read and recite it, or believe and understand this profound and subtle Dharma-gate taught by the Tathāgata.
"Amoghadarśin!

Yet, the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family merely through hearing the name of this samādhi already surpasses the aforementioned blessings—being immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and incomparable. How much more so for those sons and daughters of good family who fully hear this samādhi and are able to immediately transcribe it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, contemplate its meaning, and skillfully proclaim and explain it extensively for the great assemblies of devas and humans?"
"Amoghadarśin!

You should now know that I have merely briefly described the merits of this samādhi; if one were to describe the roots of goodness of this concentration in detail, even if one were to spend many kalpas, one could never reach the end."
Chapter Fifteen: The Original Deeds of the Bodhisattvas, Section on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
At that time, there were the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Subhūti, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Suprītiprabha, and the Bodhisattva Anantadarśin.
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantaprabha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantavyūha,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantadhvaja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantaprabhāsa,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantayaśas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantadhyāna, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantajñāna.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantacāra-rāja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ananta-vaśavarti-rāja,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantacintita-parama, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvadharmacintitārtha,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ākāśacintitārtha, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Asaṅgacintita.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Manas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantaratnamati,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvabhayapraśamanakṣama, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suviśuddhamati,
and other such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas as leaders, together with ninety billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Bodhisattvas.
The Mahāsattvas all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground,
and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One!

Having heard from the Buddha these merits and benefits of the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, we ourselves shall certainly transcribe, recite, uphold, contemplate its meaning, and explain it extensively to others, and cause others as well to practice according to what has been taught.
Why is this? World-Honored One, it is because we desire to embrace and uphold *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One!

Regarding these profound sūtras on samādhi spoken by these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, we shall cause all sentient beings to hear them and rejoice; we ourselves shall also augment their vigor and bestow upon them peace and happiness.

Why is this? Because if they are able to practice progressively according to these Mahāyāna sūtras—having heard them, copying them, reciting them, upholding them, reflecting upon them with discernment, and explaining them extensively to others, as well as causing others to explain and interpret them—they will certainly attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were single-mindedly seeking [the Dharma], smiled.

It is the nature of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, that when they smile, various lights are emitted from their faces—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, musaragalva, and pearl. From within all these jewel-like lights, there further emerge immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of diverse colors; all of these issue forth from the World-Honored One’s face, travel throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, reach as far upward as the Brahma palaces, and return to rest upon the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, erects a jeweled banner that is upright, radiant, and glorious, bringing joy to all who behold it;
so too was this trichiliocosm adorned with such magnificence and splendor that its subtle beauty was beyond compare.
At that time, when the assembly of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had witnessed these miraculous displays of adornment, they all marveled in astonishment:
"How marvelous! How rare is the supernatural power of the World-Honored One!"

Then, from within the assembly, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named *Yìzhìdìngzhìshéntōng* (Power of Samādhi and Wisdom of Sovereign Intent). He rose from his seat, maintained perfect dignified deportment, and with palms joined in reverence, prostrated himself before the World-Honored One. He then offered celestial aloeswood incense, *tagara* incense, *tamālapatra* incense, ox-head sandalwood, and powdered sandalwood, scattering them over the Buddha.

Furthermore, having made offerings to the World-Honored One with celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *kicaka* flowers, and *mahākicaka* flowers, they spoke these verses in praise:
"The World-Honored One is an incomparable tamer; A person endowed with a golden body and the marks of excellence.
His radiance and majestic virtue pervade the ten directions, Appearing like flowering trees within a forest."
Your wondrous conduct is perfected and your wisdom is boundless; with great majesty, you are able to benefit the world.
Pray, expound upon these most excellent skillful means; for what reason do you smile once more?
The World-Honored One possesses peerless and boundless wisdom; transcending all classes of beings, who could possibly surpass you?
You who possess unsurpassed majesty and virtue should now proclaim: for what reason do you smile once more today?

Now this world throughout the great trichiliocosm, with flowers blooming everywhere like the trees of the gods in the celestial realm, all sentient beings are filled with joy; for what reason do you now smile again?
The blind can see, the deaf can hear, the mute can speak, the lame can walk, and those who were deranged and lost their minds have regained their original mindfulness;
for what cause and condition do you now smile again?
The herds of beasts leap for joy and all let out their roars; the exotic birds rejoice and emit pure melodies;
the various musical instruments sound spontaneously without being struck—by what cause do you now smile once more?
All musical sounds arise simultaneously; originally not struck by gods or humans, yet they bring peace and happiness to gods and men.
Now you smile once more—what is the cause for this?
That deity gazes upon this person with clear illumination, and this person now likewise beholds that deity;
as gods and humans both give rise to thoughts of rare wonder, by what cause do you now manifest a smile?
Unsurpassed Great Being, refuge of the world, Great Honored One, today you have proclaimed it for me;
If one hears this and smiles out of great compassion, How could one ever repay such profound joy and gratitude?

At that time, the World-Honored One proclaimed for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Yathāmaty-Adhiṣṭhāna-Jñāna-Abhijñā the sublime questions of that Great Being, and likewise proclaimed the names of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The verses say:
"All you sons of noble family, having heard the wondrous voice of the Dharma King,
those sixty-eight thousand have all resolved to attain Bodhi."
Furthermore, in a future age, when the True Dharma is being destroyed,
the World-Honored One himself will protect and uphold such profound and wondrous scriptures.
Having heard of his great renown, I shall never grow weary.
This inconceivable Dharma-gate is that which all Buddhas have taught.
Listen now as I speak: this assembly of bodhisattvas has not, at the instance of only a single Buddha, given rise to such a heart of sincere reverence.
I recall my past births, numbering sixty-six billion nayutas;
at that time, I too arose in this very manner, solely for the sake of protecting and upholding this profound Dharma.
Furthermore, in the past prior to this, at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
I have been foremost in practicing reverent devotion and have upheld the most supreme and wondrous Dharma.
For the sake of the Dharma, these great beings are able to relinquish even their precious lives; how could they cherish their own bodies?
How sweet is the Dharma to them that they do not dread suffering, seeking only the realization of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Inconceivable Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, possessing immeasurable majesty and virtue,
all rose up with reverence at that time, solely because they cherished and delighted in this Dharma.
Ratnaprabha, Arciṣmat, Mahāprabha Buddha, Vidyutprabha, Samantaprabha, and Acintya—
These three classes have upheld the Dharma; Seeking the unsurpassed path of Bodhi,
Only through my supernormal power can I know you, And today the fruits of your retribution are all clearly manifest.

"Amogha! You have long since made this vow, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of past lives; before the Great Teachers, the Buddhas, you have brought all inconceivable practices to full completion."
Constantly engaged in the practice of singing praises to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, and having cultivated great vows through ascetic practices,
by virtue of the excellent causes and conditions accumulated in the past, you have now obtained this verse of praise for the Great Dharma King.
In a former age, the World-Honored One was named Sunetra, Also called Agnidhvaja and Anantatejas;
at that time, these individuals were their leaders, Because they sought supreme, perfect enlightenment.
In the past there was a Buddha named King Adornment; his realm was like the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.
Most of these beings were supreme noble ones who, at that time, had already attained great enlightenment.
In the past there was a Buddha named Emitting Light, Also Boundless Light and Immeasurable Marks;
among those followers he was their leader, And first sought this wondrous samādhi.
The Buddha Great Maṇi-jewel Radiance, the Teacher of Universal Radiance-Gathering,
at that time first gave rise to the gathering of the Dharma, seeking the peace and bliss of bodhi.
Great light, solar radiance, and inconceivability;
immeasurable diligence and boundless concentration—these arise as the foremost among the dharmas he gathers, for the sake of seeking the bliss of bodhi.
The Buddha Fine Flower Fragrance and Golden Flower, the Tathāgata Untainted and the One of Non-contentious Conduct—
during that time, they were all leaders in protecting the Dharma, seeking such supreme enlightenment as this.
Thus, for the sake of upholding these three types [of merit], I pray for the supreme Buddha-enlightenment of all the Tathāgatas of the past—
those Honored Ones of Boundless Wisdom and Honored Ones with Feet Like Elephant Trunks.
Eighty thousand great men and realized sages, having attained the foremost, wondrous Bodhi, shall,
by virtue of these supreme roots of goodness, serve the Awakened One among humans in the future.
Wherever they are born, they shall always dwell in noble and eminent families; all evil realms are forever eliminated for them.
Assembling as companions in the Dharma, they shall never be far removed from the Awakened One of the World.
Forever parting from all non-Buddhist teachers, And abandoning all friends of false wisdom, One gathers unspeakable merits;
This merit shall surely lead to enlightenment.
In the future, they shall meet the Honored One Maitreya; at that time, this assembly shall all gather together.
By thus maintaining and protecting the Dharma through the three karmas, they will thereby be able to achieve supreme enlightenment.
Furthermore, after the parinirvāṇa of Maitreya, there will be a Buddha, a Lion, a Tamer of Men;
he too shall seek that Dharma and maintain it through the three karmas, thereby attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
The future thousand Buddhas, the Unsurpassed Honored Ones, are the guides for sentient beings in this Auspicious Aeon;
these Dharma masters constantly preach in the world, and thereby realize the wondrous form-body of unimpeded liberation.
After these Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa have passed away, there shall again be a Perfectly Awakened One of immeasurable majesty,
and another Tathāgata whose name is Bhadra, as well as the World-Honored One Vipaśyin.
After the passing of Bhaiṣajya and Vipaśyin, there appeared another Buddha named Śāla;
at that time, the wise all gathered together and extensively prepared various requisites to offer worship.
When the World-Honored One Śāla had entered nirvāṇa, there was a Tathāgata named Avalokita;
because these people sought the Dharma from him, they further made offerings to that King of the Sublime Dharma.
After observing the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there was a Buddha, World-Honored One, named Samantadarśin;
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin, there was a Buddha whose name was Padmottara;
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Padmottara, there was a Buddha titled Utpala.
At that time, those wise ones sought the Dharma again, serving and making offerings to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
After the Buddha Utpala had entered parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Puṣpa;
after that Tathāgata Puṣpa had entered parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled Alaṃkāra.
After adorning the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Vijñāna;
these people also sought the Dharma from him, establishing boundless offerings.
After the Tathāgata Vijñāna entered parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Sudarśana;
after the Tathāgata Sudarśana entered parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Susthita;
after the Tathāgata Susthita entered parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha named Vinīta.
He too was sustained by these three kinds of dharmas, seeking only to realize this path to bodhi.
After the Buddha Endowed with Dignity entered nirvana, there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One, named Immeasurable Dignity;
after the Buddha Immeasurable Dignity entered nirvana, there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One, named Victorious King.
After the Tathāgata Jina-rāja had entered parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Pratyutpanna;
after the Tathāgata Pratyutpanna had entered parinirvāṇa, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Saṃjvalana-rāja.
At that time, for the sake of the Dharma, these [Buddhas] extensively established inconceivable offerings.
So too shall all the World-Honored Ones of the future, whose supreme worldly wisdom transcends all,
have no attachment or stinginess toward their own bodies or lives, seeking only to realize the Buddha’s Bodhi.
By virtue of such supreme roots of goodness, may I in the future serve those of supreme majesty—
those Buddhas who are the foremost among men, like that Tamer Amitābha.
In the presence of that most excellent World-Honored One, desiring to cultivate and realize supreme enlightenment,
one should always exert oneself with diligence in seeking the Dharma and provide boundless, wondrous offerings.
In all the worlds throughout those directions, far removed from decay and affliction, with the five sensory objects eliminated,
they seek only the joy of the Dharma to benefit all sentient beings, making offerings to billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In the future, attaining the boundless wisdom of Buddhahood, Able to bring great benefit and extinguish all sufferings,
For the sake of seeking peace and happiness for all sentient beings, I shall make offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas.
When he attains Buddhahood, his great fame shall spread;
that land will be adorned in ways inconceivable, composed entirely of various jewels for all to behold with joy, as vast and magnificent as the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Many billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, all receiving the Buddha’s prediction as the Honored One among Men,
with the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddhas, thus praise and extol the Great Dharma King.
I shall now speak for your sake; all you members of the great assembly, gods and humans alike, whoever seeks the truth of perfect enlightenment will ultimately realize it just as the Tathāgata has.
If one can aspire to and delight in supreme enlightenment, they shall be called a superior person and receive divine protection;
the devas, nāgas, and ghosts, the kumbhāṇḍas, garuḍas, and yakṣas will all guard them.
If one wishes to pray for the attainment of enlightenment and constantly delights in cultivating the Buddha’s supreme path, [they shall be protected].
The World-Honored One regards [us] with compassion as if we were his only son; his body is golden, and he possesses great power, wisdom, and extensive learning.
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Chapter Ten: "The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha."
